paragraphs.text: The house looked and smelled very old. Eleven-year-old Vinnie didn’t want to live there. Neither did his nine-year-old sister, Mandy. But the children had no choice. Six months ago their parents gave them some shocking news.
"We’re moving to the country," they announced.
"Why?" asked the startled children.
"You need the fresh air," Mom explained.
"You’re going to love the new house," added Dad.
"But what about our friends?" Vinnie and Mandy cried.
"You’ll make new ones," said Mom firmly.
The family arrived at their "new" house. It was actually a hundred years old. It needed many repairs. Mom and Dad got busy painting the outside of the house. Vinnie and Mandy had lots to do inside.
"Vinnie?" Mandy walked into the living room. Her brother was tearing old wallpaper from the wall.
"What?" he asked, annoyed at everything. Vinnie threw down the scraper. "This is a stupid house!"
"Well, complaining isn’t going to help," said Mandy. Vinnie shrugged. "Dad said I have to clean out the attic," Mandy continued. "But I’m scared to go up there by myself."
"You aren’t afraid of ghosts, are you?" Vinnie grabbed an old sheet from one of the chairs. He pulled it over his head. Flinging his arms in the air, he made scary noises.
Grinning, Mandy pulled the sheet off Vinnie’s head. "Will you come with me or not?" she asked.
Vinnie led the way upstairs. In the dusty attic, they were surrounded by books, maps, and cobwebs. Vinnie did not like spiders. He brushed a sticky spider web off his face.
Mandy was more interested in the books. They were everywhere—in boxes, on shelves, and in tall piles against the wall.
"Oh!" she said clapping her hands excitedly. Mandy loved to read. "Do we know anything about the owner of this house?" she asked.
Vinnie shook his head. "Maybe he was a writer." Then he looked around for creepy spiders.
Mandy read the book titles in one box. All the books were about history or traveling. "Well, he must have loved history," she said.

Vinnie walked over to a shelf of books. "Mandy, look at this!" Vinnie called, excitedly. He held a thick, dusty green album. The children flipped through the first few pages. Each page had one black-and-white photograph. Something was written below each photo.
"I wonder if this is the owner." Mandy pointed to the elderly man in one of the pictures. He had a friendly smile.

Vinnie turned to the first page. "Hey, Mandy," said Vinnie, "look at this one. He’s in a boat and . . ." Vinnie looked closer. "Cool! Here’s a pyramid and an eagle in the background. He must be in Egypt."
"Vinnie, this picture is . . ." Mandy paused. "different."
"What do you mean?" asked Vinnie.
Mandy rubbed her eyes and stared at the photo again. "Look at the pyramid," she whispered. "It’s glowing."
Vinnie slammed the album shut. "Did you see that?" he asked, his voice shaking. "That pyramid was glowing!"
Mandy nodded slowly. "Should we tell Mom and Dad?"
Vinnie shook his head. "No, this is our little secret."
"There was something written below the picture," Mandy said. "Maybe we should read it."
Vinnie nodded and opened the album. The handwriting was small and neat. "‘August 24, my first photo travels,’" Mandy read aloud.
"Photo travels? What’s that?" Vinnie interrupted.
Mandy continued to read. "‘I found this photo album in my uncle’s attic. It didn’t look special on the outside. But once I opened it, it changed my life forever.’"
"So he found the album in an attic too," said Vinnie.
Nodding, Mandy continued to read. "‘People say I’m crazy. Maybe I am. But I have traveled to the past. I even have proof—this photo album.’"
"Travel to the past? Like in a time machine?" Vinnie asked excitedly. "Go on reading!"
"'My first travel—to Egypt . . .'" Mandy held her breath. "'A glowing pyramid called to me.'"
"Mandy, do you think it’s calling to us too?" Vinnie asked. He pulled the photo out of the album.
Mandy continued, "’When I looked into the light, my adventures began.’"
"But how did he go back in time? And why do the pictures glow?" Vinnie stared at the photo.
"Vinnie, maybe we should forget all this." Mandy looked at her watch. It was almost noon.
"Let’s just go and have lunch."
But Vinnie did not hear her. His eyes were fixed on the photograph.
"Vinnie, you’re scaring me! Stop it!" she cried.
"But what if it’s real? What if we really could go back in time?" Vinnie said in a dreamy voice.
"I’m going downstairs," Mandy insisted.
Vinnie grabbed her arm. "Don’t you want an adventure, Mandy?" he said excitedly.
"I do, but I’m also scared," she said honestly. "How do we travel to the past? And I’m worried about how we’d get back home again."
"Mandy," her brother suddenly shouted. "The pyramid is getting brighter!"
Sure enough, the pyramid was glowing with a bright yellow light.
Now the children really couldn’t take their eyes off the light.
"’When I looked into the light, my adventures began.’" Vinnie repeated the words written in the album.
The heat from the light felt hot against their faces. It forced them to close their eyes. Now they could see the pyramid in their minds. It seemed to be coming closer.
"Vinnie, I’m scared," cried Mandy.
Suddenly, the children felt their feet lift off the ground. Vinnie grabbed his sister’s hand and shouted, "Hang on, Mandy!"
He held her hand tightly. "I’ve changed my mind! I don’t want to do this!" Vinnie cried. He tried to open his eyes, but couldn’t. It was too bright.
"Mandy!"
"Vinnie!"
Still holding on to each other, the children screamed. They began to fall down a deep dark tunnel.
Without warning, the children landed at the bottom of a tunnel with a loud thud.
"Ouch!" shouted Vinnie.
"Oomph!" cried Mandy.
They opened their eyes. The bright light was gone. The darkness of the tunnel was gone, too. They both lay on the ground, not far from each other.
"Are you okay?" Vinnie called to his sister.
They had landed on the bank of a long river. They could see ducks and geese flying by. Men with nets and spears were fishing from boats and from land.
"Mandy?" Vinnie called to her again. As he got up and moved closer to Mandy, Vinnie could see why she didn’t answer. Standing in front of her was a boy about Vinnie’s age. He was dark and slender.
"Are you the gods of the Nile?" the boy asked, falling to his knees.
"The Nile?" Vinnie questioned. Then he realized where they were. "We’re in Egypt!" he shouted at Mandy.
"Please don’t hurt me," the strange boy cried, his voice shaking.
"No, we are not gods," Vinnie said to the boy. "I’m Vinnie and this is my sister, Mandy."

The stranger wore only a short white skirt, tied with a sash around his waist. Suddenly Vinnie looked down at himself. That’s all he was wearing, too! Vinnie’s face turned red. Mandy was also dressed differently. Her body was covered by a straight white dress. Her feet were in sandals. Her hair was in a long braid.
"But I saw you fall from the sky," said the boy, getting back up on his feet. .
"We have . . . special powers," she paused and looked at Vinnie. He was still holding the photograph, which he stuck inside his sash.
The stranger gasped and fell to his knees again.
"Don’t worry. We’re not going to hurt you," Mandy said kindly. "We need your help."
"I am Akhom," the boy said, "and I promise to help you."
"Thank you, Akhom," said Mandy.
They heard voices coming toward them from the distance. Vinnie and Mandy froze.
"Oh, those are my friends," Akhom explained. He held up an odd shaped ball in his hand. "I left them to look for my ball. Then I saw you."
Vinnie and Mandy looked at each other.
"Please don’t tell them about us, Akhom," they both said.
Akhom nodded. "Yes, it would be best for you to hide. My friends are not accustomed to strangers."
The loud shouts came nearer. "Akhom! Are you looking for cobras again?" shouted one boy.
"Cobras?" whispered Vinnie. Vinnie hated snakes even more than spiders.
"Cobras, hippos, crocodiles. They’re all over the Nile," Akhom whispered back. "Crocodiles!" Vinnie mouthed, his eyes getting very big.
"Akhom! Where are you?" the voices shouted again .
Akhom threw the ball back to his friends. Then he signaled to Vinnie and Mandy.
"Quickly follow me!"
Vinnie and Mandy ran after him. Out of breath, they arrived at a small house with windows high up on the walls. Its white surface had many cracks from the hot sun.
"Welcome to my home," Akhom said warmly.

4.title: Akhom's Home and the Village Market

paragraphs.text: Akhom took his new friends through his home. To Mandy and Vinnie, the one-room house seemed quite empty. Then he led them up the stairs to the roof.
The roof was flat and square, just like the house. It had straw mats, a wooden chest and baskets filled with fruits and grains.
"There are more things here on the roof than inside the house," Mandy commented.
"During the hot season, we sleep and eat up here," he explained.
"Why?" asked Vinnie.
"It’s very hot inside the house. On the roof, it’s much cooler," Akhom explained.
"What a lovely house," said Mandy.
Akhom bowed proudly. "My father, brothers, and I made all the bricks ourselves."
"How?" asked Mandy.
Akhom brought over a pan. "In this pan, we mix mud from the Nile River with straw and stones. We shape the mixture into bricks. Then we take them out into the sun to dry."
Akhom held out a basket. "Are you hungry? Would you like some dates?"
"Thank you," Mandy replied. She bit into the dark soft fruit.
"What other foods do you eat?" asked Vinnie, taking another date.
"Mostly bread . . . Oh no!" Akhom cried, looking up at the sun.
"What’s the matter?" asked Mandy.
"I must take lunch to my father and brother." Akhom grabbed a small basket. He filled it with bread, figs, and dates.
"We’ll come with you," said Vinnie.
"We must hurry," gasped Akhom. "My brother has to eat before removing the organs."
Puzzled, Vinnie and Mandy said together, "Organs?"
"They just received a new dead body today," Akhom said, nodding. "Today Tau, my brother, will embalm his first body."
"Embalm?" Vinnie repeated.
"That means preparing a dead body to make it into a mummy," explained Mandy. She had read about this in one of her books.
"Mummies?" Vinnie’s eyes got big. "Cool!" He ran after Akhom. Mandy had no choice but to follow them.

Akhom and Vinnie raced through the village market. Mandy followed, but soon stopped to catch her breath. The outdoor market was crowded. All kinds of things—fruits, vegetables, spices, pottery, wigs, and jewelry—were displayed on mats and stools.

Curious and no longer afraid, Mandy wandered more slowly down the street. She saw a woman trade a cucumber for a small bag of spices. Another man traded a sack of grain for a skinny cow. Smiling, Mandy stopped at a fruit stall.
"What’s this?" Mandy picked up a large red fruit. She had never seen anything like it before. It was bigger than an apple. The skin felt like an orange.

"How many do you want?" The fruit seller barked at Mandy. She was so startled that she dropped the fruit. It rolled down the road. The skinny cow that was being led away stomped on it. Red juice burst everywhere.
"My cow is bleeding! You sold me a sick cow!" the owner yelled at the merchant. The two men started to argue loudly.
"You better pay for my fruit!" the fruit seller shouted at Mandy.
Mandy was in big trouble.
Racing past the market, Vinnie followed Akhom down some stairs. The chamber below was cool and the air smelled strange.
"Stay right here and wait for me," Akhom whispered. Akhom left to look for his father.

"We’re going to see a real mummy, Mandy!" cried Vinnie. He turned around to speak to Mandy. But Mandy was nowhere to be seen. In a panic, Vinnie left his spot and walked down a dark hallway. He needed Akhom to help find his sister.

When he heard voices coming from a room, he looked in. Three men were standing over a body on a flat table. One of the older men spoke to the youngest person. Vinnie guessed this must be Akhom’s brother, Tau.
"Tau, please explain what we are going to do."
Tau replied, "First we will remove the organs." He gulped. "Then we put them in the clay jars." He pointed to the jars standing against the wall.
"Then what do we do with the natron?" The man pointed to a large jar. It was filled with white powder that looked like salt.
"Put it inside and outside the body," replied Tau.
"Why?" the man asked.
"So the body won’t spoil while it dries up," explained Tau.
"When can we wrap it in linen bandages?" asked the man.
Tau swallowed before answering. "In forty days, Father."
"Whoa," Vinnie said under his breath. "So that’s how to make a mummy!"
Suddenly, a cold hand touched his arm. "What are you doing here?" Akhom whispered angrily. He pulled Vinnie away from the room.
When they were in the hallway, Vinnie told him about losing Mandy. "We have to find her," he said urgently.
"Let’s go, then," Akhom said.
"When you grow up, do you have to learn that too?" Vinnie asked, pointing behind him.
"Yes, I must," replied Akhom. "My father is an embalmer. So my brothers and I will be embalmers too." Vinnie was glad his dad was an architect.
Meanwhile at the village market, Mandy was wishing she had followed Vinnie. The fruit seller tried to grab her.
Near her, several men walked in a long line. Each carried a large bundle of long green sticks on their backs. Mandy ran into their line, hidden by the men and their bundles.
"Stop! Thief!" yelled the old man.
"I’m very sorry!" Mandy called back. But she walked with the men and their reeds, hidden from her pursuer.
The man in front of her laughed. "What did you steal?"
"Nothing," she replied. She changed the subject. "What are you carrying?"
"Papyrus reeds, of course," he answered. "We’re going to the workshop now."
"What do you make with papyrus?" Mandy asked. The man looked at her strangely.
"Papyrus is used to make paper and other things. Surely you know that," he said.
She quickly responded, "I mean, what are you going to make with that papyrus?"
"Come join us and see," said the friendly man.
Mandy was now on her own adventure. In the papyrus workshop, groups of men were making different things. Mandy saw a young boy make a ball like Akhom’s. Another person worked on a pair of sandals.
"These reeds are for making paper," the friendly man explained. He took a long reed from his bundle. "First you cut the reeds to make them shorter. Then you strip off the green skin."
The inside of the papyrus was white. The man used a knife to cut it into thin sheets. "You can do this part," he said to Mandy. "Just put these sheets on this block," he explained.
Mandy sat down in front of the block.
"Cover the papyrus with this cloth," he continued. He gave Mandy a hammer. "Now beat the cloth evenly."
She gently hit the papyrus sheets. "This is amazing," she exclaimed.
Nodding, the man said, "Papyrus is a gift from the gods."
She lifted the cloth. The papyrus still felt thick and rough. "After the papyrus dries," the man explained, "we will use this to make the surface smoother." He picked up a shiny stone.
"It’s time to go, Issa," said another man, motioning to his friend.
"Where are you going?" Mandy asked.
"We must take the papyrus rope to the pyramid," Issa replied. He pointed to coils of thick rope.

Mandy had almost forgotten her brother and the glowing pyramid. "Can I come with you?" she asked her new friend. Shaking his head, Issa said, "That is no place for a young girl. You shouldn’t even be here."
"I promise not to get in the way," she begged.
Issa gave in. "But you must stay in the boat," he warned.
Suddenly Mandy missed Vinnie. "Come on, Vinnie," she said in her mind. "The glowing pyramid is where we both want to go." She hoped her brother was thinking the same thing.
Meanwhile, Vinnie and Akhom walked back to the market. "I don’t see her anywhere!" cried Vinnie.
"Where would she go?" asked Akhom. Vinnie thought for a moment. "Wait!" He pulled out the photograph. The pyramid was now glowing blue.
"Great Amon-Ra!" Akhom shouted, when he saw the photo.
"Don’t worry," comforted Vinnie. "It’s just a photo."
"A what?" Akhom opened one eye.
"Never mind," said Vinnie. "I think Mandy may be going there." He pointed to the pyramid. "Do you know where this is?"
Akhom cautiously studied the picture and shuddered. "Yes, it is the Pharaoh’s tomb along the Nile."
"Can you take me there?" asked Vinnie. Akhom did not answer. "Please, Akhom, I must find my sister," begged Vinnie.
Akhom finally agreed. "But we must be very careful because it is forbidden."
The boys looked for a way to get to the Pharaoh’s pyramid.
"There!" Akhom pointed. "We can sail to the Pharaoh’s pyramid in that boat!"
"It looks like half a banana," laughed Vinnie, describing the large sailing ship.
"No. That small one," corrected Akhom. The big boat was pulling a smaller one. Men were loading baskets onto the smaller boat.
"Someone special must be going to visit the site," said Akhom.
"How do you know?" asked Vinnie.
"All those baskets are food," explained Akhom. "They only prepare that much food for the royal family. They must be going for a visit to the pyramid."
"Let’s jump on!" said Vinnie. The boys snuck into the small boat and hid among the food baskets.
In the larger boat, twenty men picked up their long oars. They pushed and pulled the oars. The wind filled the gigantic sail and the small boat followed. The boys sailed down the Nile.
From the boat, Vinnie could see all kinds of interesting things off shore. A farmer pushed a wooden plough through a field of wheat.
Another large ship sailed beside them. It carried a huge white block of stone. "What’s that?" he whispered to Akhom.
"That’s one of the blocks used for building a pyramid," Akhom answered. "Pyramids are made of hundreds of heavy blocks of stone."
"That must take a lot of time and work," said Vinnie.
"Some say we make more stones than there are stars," explained Akhom. "Thousands of people work on the Pharaoh’s pyramid. They started to build it before I was born."
"When will it be finished?" Vinnie asked in a surprised voice.
Akhom shrugged. "Perhaps in a couple of years. Maybe by the time I marry."
Suddenly Vinnie saw a pair of blinking eyes staring from the water. "Akhom! Is that a crocodile?" Vinnie pointed.
Akhom shook his head. "No, that’s a hippo. Look! There’s a crocodile!" Akhom pointed to a reptile lying in the sand.
Further on the shore, they could see the Pharaoh’s pyramid. The boats slowed down. Men shouted orders at each other. "When we reach the shore, run for the pyramid," Akhom instructed.
When the boys jumped off the boat, Vinnie was surprised by the sight of the pyramid in real life. "Whoa!" he said, as he stopped to look up at the huge structure.

Facing the sunset, the pyramid looked very majestic. Each side of its base was the length of two soccer fields. Though it seemed already quite tall, the workers were adding more blocks. Vinnie saw thousands of men pulling the heavy white blocks of stone.
The boys climbed a ramp that led into the pyramid. Behind them, a voice shouted, "You, boys, stop! What are you doing here?"
"The guards!" yelled Akhom. "Run, Vinnie! Run!"
The boys ran up a ramp toward the pyramid. The guards followed closely behind.

The boys were small and fast. They lost the guards before they entered the pyramid. Inside, Vinnie followed Akhom through a long narrow passage that led to a chamber. Inside the chamber, Vinnie stopped and stared. The walls were covered with paintings and symbols.
"Who is that body with a dog’s head?" Vinnie pointed to a painted figure.
"That is Anubis, the guardian of the dead," Akhom replied. "Pharaoh must prove to Anubis and the other gods that he has lived a good life. Only then will he be able to rest peacefully after he dies."

Akhom explained, "This is one of the false burial chambers that leads to another passage. You must pass several passages and chambers. Finally you come to the secret chamber filled with gold and jewels. The secret chamber is where the Pharaoh will be buried."
"But we can’t go there today," said Vinnie anxiously. "We have to find my sister." Akhom led Vinnie to the other side of the pyramid.

When the boys left the pyramid, they saw a small boat pulling up to the shore. Several men leaped out, dragging a long papyrus rope toward the pyramid. Mandy was the only one left in the boat. She stood up to admire the pyramid.
"Mandy!" Suddenly Mandy heard her brother’s voice. She looked for him on the crowded shore.

Just then, the loud noise of horns began to sound. It came from the grandest ship in the river. "It’s the Pharaoh!" whispered Akhom. He fell to his knees. Everyone at the pyramid site stopped and fell to their knees. Only Vinnie remained standing.
"Get on your knees!" Akhom whispered. But Vinnie wanted a good view of the Pharaoh.

The Pharaoh appeared. He wore a blue and gold headdress and held a golden staff. Suddenly the Pharaoh stopped. He stared at the one small standing figure. When the Pharaoh lifted his staff, three armed guards ran toward Vinnie.
"Vinnie!" Mandy yelled. "Quickly, get into the boat!" The guards were close, but the boys managed to jump into the boat. Akhom and Vinnie grabbed the oars.
"I’m so glad to see you!" Mandy cried.
"Me too," gasped Vinnie.
As they paddled away, Mandy looked up at the pyramid again. "Do you think this is the pyramid in our picture?" she asked.
Vinnie pulled out the photo. The pyramid now appeared in a glowing red light.
"This must be it!" exclaimed Mandy. "And look! We’re in a boat too, just like the old man in the picture."
"But there is an eagle in this picture," Vinnie pointed out.
"That’s my name," Akhom said. "Akhom means eagle."
Suddenly the sky turned very bright. The children were forced to shut their eyes. Akhom’s voice began to fade.
"We're going home. Good-bye, Akhom!" Mandy shouted.
Vinnie and Mandy fell into a dark tunnel once again. Then with a loud thump, the children fell onto the hard attic floor.
Opening his eyes, Vinnie cried, "We’re back home!"
"Vinnie! Mandy! Time for lunch." They heard their mother calling them.
They stared at each other in confusion. Mandy looked at her watch. It was almost twelve noon, the exact time they had left for Egypt.

The next morning, Vinnie overslept. He ran to the attic. He wanted to make sure their trip to Egypt wasn’t a dream. He hoped Mandy was already there. But she wasn’t. Disappointed, Vinnie came downstairs and went outside. His dad was about to mow the lawn.
"Dad," said Vinnie, "where’s Mandy?"
"She went shopping with Mom," Dad replied.
He couldn’t believe it. "Doesn’t she want to go on another photo trip?" he thought. Suddenly Vinnie had an idea. "What if I go by myself? Mandy won’t even know I’m gone!"

Vinnie raced back to the attic. He took the photo of Egypt out of his pocket. He stared. The picture had changed. The old man and the eagle in the boat were gone. In their places sat Vinnie and Mandy.
"Every time we come back from a photo trip," Vinnie thought, "will we be in the picture? There’s only one way to find out."

Vinnie carefully put the picture of Egypt into the photo album. His heart began to race as he turned the page. In the next photo, the old man was sitting near a brightly glowing object. He was at the bottom of some steps. Vinnie took the photo out.
"The next adventure begins," Vinnie said excitedly.
Suddenly, the attic door swung open and Mandy ran in. "I knew you’d be here!" she shouted angrily.
"No time to argue!" Vinnie said, grabbing her arm. "Look!" He showed her the new photo.
Mandy stared. "Where is this?" she asked.
Before Vinnie could answer, the picture glowed very brightly. The children had to close their eyes. Soon they were falling down a deep dark tunnel.
"Whoa!"
"Ouch!"
Vinnie and Mandy landed heavily on wet ground.
"We landed in mud!" Mandy said. Their clothes were changed. She wore a sleeveless cotton dress. Vinnie wore something like a short skirt.
"Where are we?" Mandy looked around.
"We’re on a tiny island!" Vinnie cried. "I think we’re in a lake!"
Vinnie noticed that Mandy wore a sparkly bead bracelet. "What’s that?" Vinnie asked.
"Mom bought it for me," said Mandy. "It’s an early birthday present."
"Why did you come home from shopping so quickly?" her brother asked.
"Mom forgot her grocery list, so we had to come back." Mandy remembered that Vinnie almost went on this trip alone. "Hey! You went to the attic without me," she scolded.
"So?" said Vinnie. "You didn’t have to go shopping!"
The children argued, forgetting where they were. Suddenly someone jumped out of the water. Mandy screamed and startled Vinnie. He jumped backward, slipped, and fell into the lake.
The person in the water turned out to be a boy. He was holding a large basket of mud. Coughing, Vinnie climbed back onto the tiny island.
"Who are you?" the boy asked.
"I’m Vinnie. This is my sister, Mandy," Vinnie replied, shaking his wet hair.
"Where is your family garden?" the boy asked.
"We don’t have one," admitted Vinnie. "We’re just visiting. Do you need help?"
The boy thought a moment. "Yes," he said. "Collect mud from the lake. Then pile it on here." He pointed to the island. He had dark skin and was dressed like Vinnie.
"Why do you need mud?" Vinnie asked.
The boy looked at them, surprised. "It helps the crops grow strong," he said. "Corn and beans grow best on this soil. Our corn was very good last year. So we are making more floating gardens."
"What a great name!" Mandy clapped her hands. The tiny islands did look like floating gardens. Each one had a different crop.
For the next hour, Vinnie and Mandy helped the boy. They piled mud on the island. Mandy smoothed the mud with a stick. A canoe went by.
"Look, Vinnie!" she called. "People use canoes to move from one island to the next."
"Who are you, little girl?" someone behind her asked. Mandy turned around. A man was sitting in a canoe with a big pile of corn. He had kind eyes.
"We’re friends of . . ." Mandy paused. She didn’t know the boy’s name.
"Of Mazatl? I see. Where is my son now?" he asked.
"He’s getting mud from the water, sir," she replied. Mandy thought Mazatl looked very much like his father.
"Good," Mazatl’s father nodded. "Tell Mazatl I will be at the market. I want to go early to get a good spot." He paddled away.
As Mandy watched him leave, she wondered, "Where are we?"
When the boys returned, Mandy told Mazatl what his father said.
"I must hurry and join Papa at the weekly market," said Mazatl.
"May we come with you?" asked Vinnie.
"Yes, but come to my house first," said Mazatl. "We can take a bath and change our clothes."
"Thanks, Mazatl," Mandy said. "What a great place this is."
Mazatl nodded.
She really wished she knew where she was.
"Our gods are good to us if we are good to them," Mazatl said.
"How are you good to the gods?" Mandy asked.
"We make sacrifices regularly."
"What kind of sacrifices?" asked Vinnie.
Mazatl stared at them suspiciously. "Our Aztec gods are offered only the best sacrifices—humans!" he said proudly.
"Aztec? We’re in ancient Mexico?" gasped Mandy.
"Human sacrifices?" cried Vinnie.
Mazatl’s house was very simple. It was made of adobe clay bricks. The house was one big room divided into separate areas. Vinnie and Mandy met Mazatl’s mother. She was making flat pancake-like bread.
"These corn tortillas are for your papa," she said to Mazatl. "But please take a bath first."
Mazatl led them to another building. "This is our bath hut," he explained.
Vinnie and Mandy saw a mud hut. It had a chimney on the side with a hot fire.
"The chimney heats the walls inside. We throw water on the walls. And we get lots of steam. We come here to get clean, but also when we are sick," Mazatl explained.
"Does it make you better?" asked Mandy.
"Oh yes!" replied Mazatl. "I once had bad pains in my chest. The steam and heat made me well again. You go first," he said to Mandy.

Mandy had a quick steam bath. So did Vinnie. When they came out, Mazatl had fresh clothes for them. Vinnie got a short skirt and a cloak to wear over one shoulder. Mandy got a colorful sleeveless shirt and a skirt.
"My mother and sister wove these clothes," Mazatl said. "You can return them later."
"Thank you, they’re beautiful," replied Mandy.
Then Mazatl bathed and changed too.
"Mazatl and his family are so nice," Mandy whispered to her brother. "I can’t believe the Aztecs make human sacrifices."
Vinnie didn’t want to think about it.
Taking the tortillas from his mother, Mazatl led Vinnie and Mandy to a canoe.
They got to the crowded market. Vinnie and Mandy were amazed! People arrived in canoes or carried their goods on their backs. They could hear voices arguing loudly.
"I need to find my papa," said Mazatl. They walked past people selling many interesting things.
"Are those bear skins?" Mandy asked, pointing to a stack of fur.
"Bears? Those are puma and jaguar skins. Only the rich can afford them," Mazatl explained.
Vinnie also noticed a man holding a bag of something.
"I will give you three rabbits for those cocoa beans!" a buyer yelled at the man.
"Give me five rabbits and two geese," the seller shouted back.
"Are you mad? I don’t have that many animals!" the buyer screamed.
"I’m offering you a bargain! Take it or leave it!" the seller shouted.
"Oh, no!" Mandy said. "I think those two men are going to fight."
Mazatl laughed and said, "Don’t worry. The judges are watching them."
"Judges?" asked Vinnie.
Just then a tall man walked over. He said a few words to the buyer. The man nodded and walked away.
"Our judges are wise and fair," Mazatl said.
"What exactly do the judges do?" asked Vinnie.
Mazatl looked at his new friends strangely. "Judges make sure people behave fairly. We must obey what they say. Surely you know that."
The judge moved to another stall in the market. Mazatl stared dreamily. "I wish I could be a judge someday," he sighed.
"Maybe you can," Vinnie said.
Mazatl shook his head. "Papa is a farmer, so I will be one too. Judges come from rich homes. I do not."
"That’s not fair," said Vinnie.
Mazatl shrugged. "Only the gods can direct your life. I was meant to be a farmer, I guess."
Vinnie felt sorry for Mazatl.
Mandy noticed that the Aztec people didn’t use money. They traded things they had for the things they needed. She remembered the man selling cocoa beans. "Are cocoa beans worth much?" Mandy asked.
Mazatl nodded. "We use cocoa beans to make a chocolate drink. It’s our favorite. But it is too costly for my family."
That gave Mandy an idea. As Mazatl and Vinnie walked along, Mandy went to the cocoa bean seller. "Sir, I would like to buy your beans," she said.
He looked at her and laughed. "What will you give me, little girl?" he asked.
"Something very precious," she said bravely.
The bean seller looked at her coldly. "Show me."
Mandy held out her arm. Her bead bracelet sparkled.
The man’s eyes grew greedy. "Where did you get that?" he demanded.
"From a faraway land," she replied. The man stared and then handed over the beans. Mandy gave him the bracelet. "Good day, sir," she said, and ran to find her brother.
Vinnie and Mazatl were going to meet Mazatl’s papa. Suddenly, Vinnie heard people cheering and shouting. Attracted by the sounds, he left Mazatl’s side.

Not far away, Vinnie was amazed to find a large outdoor stadium. Two teams were playing a game similar to basketball. The players were trying to get a hard rubber ball into a high hoop. They did not use their hands or feet, only their elbows, hips, and knees.

"That’s impossible!" Vinnie said. Then something else caught his eye. Behind the stadium was a tall tower. It looked like a pyramid, but the top was flat and had two buildings on it. Many steps led up to the top of the pyramid. "I wonder what that is?" he said.
Meanwhile, Mandy found Mazatl near his father’s stall. She handed him the bag of cocoa beans.
"But how?" Mazatl asked, amazed.
"Please, it is my gift to your family. You have been so kind to us," she said.
"Who are you?" he asked suddenly. "You are different from us."
But before she could reply, loud drums began beating.
"Mazatl!" said his father. "The sacrifices are about to begin. Let us go to the temple immediately."
Mandy looked around. "Where’s Vinnie?" she asked.
Mazatl and his father had traded all their corn. In return, they received goods their family needed. The market was closing. Most sellers were quickly wrapping up their blankets.
"What’s going on?" Mandy asked. "Mazatl, where’s Vinnie?"
"The priests will make an offering to our gods," replied Mazatl. "Follow me to the temple. I’m sure Vinnie will be there."

Vinnie heard the drums beating faster and faster. He turned and saw a parade leaving the ball court. The game was over. Men in animal costumes danced around. Some pretended to fight. Other people sang and chanted loudly. People were playing flutes too. Vinnie thought it was a victory celebration. "Who won?" he asked a young boy.
"Who cares?" replied the boy. "All the players are prisoners. Today the losers will die. But all the prisoners will be given to the gods someday soon."
The crowd was now heading toward the pyramid.
"What? The losing team is going to die?" gasped Vinnie.
"Their blood will be given to the gods," said the young boy. "In return, the gods will give us good weather for our crops."
Vinnie could not believe it!
He watched the players who had lost. Tied together, the group was being pushed forward by the temple guards. Vinnie didn’t want to see what was about to happen. But the crowd shoved him up front.
"Mandy! Mazatl!" he shouted as loud as he could. But the drums continued to beat louder. No one could hear him.
Mandy followed Mazatl to the temple.
"It’s amazing!" she remarked when she saw the tall pyramid. She asked Mazatl about the two buildings on the top.
"Those are where the sacrifices are held," he explained.
"Why are these people being killed?" she asked carefully.
"Today is a festival to honor our gods," said Mazatl.
Mandy understood. To Mazatl, the gods controlled the lives of his family. Sacrifice was important to the gods. So people had to die for the future well-being of the Aztecs.
"Mazatl, do you see Vinnie? Oh, where is he?" she cried.
"I don’t see him. He must be trapped in the crowd somewhere," replied Mazatl.
Mandy yelled for Vinnie. Worried, she ran as fast as she could toward the temple.
Meanwhile, Vinnie managed to break away from the crowd. "Whew! I can breathe!" he said, wiping his forehead. A single line of men moved slowly in front of him. Vinnie felt someone push him hard.
"Hey!" Vinnie turned angrily.
The person pushing him held a spear—it was a temple guard! Only then did Vinnie realize where he was. He was in the line to be sacrificed. He tried to explain. "There’s been a mistake!"
But the guard only pushed him forward again.
Vinnie fought back tears. "How did this happen?" he cried. The prisoners began climbing. The Aztec priests were standing at the top of the pyramid. Vinnie’s heart beat faster with each step.
Mandy ran toward the temple. "Vinnie!" she screamed. She could not find her brother. Suddenly she saw the prisoners on the temple steps. The last person in line looked very small and very familiar.
"Mandy! Stop! It’s too dangerous!" Mazatl called to her. But Mandy kept pushing through the crowd.
"Go back, little one!" a guard yelled. But Mandy was too quick. She ran up the stone steps.
"Vinnie!" She grabbed her brother’s arm.
"Mandy! What are we going to do?" Vinnie said in a shaky voice.
"The photo, where is it? Maybe it can help us," she said.
"The old man!" gasped Vinnie. "I remember, he was on some steps." Vinnie took the picture out. It was glowing blue. "We must be very close," he said.
"What are those?" Mandy pointed to the glowing objects in the photo. She looked around. "Vinnie! Look!" She pointed to the bottom of the steps. Statues!
Mandy looked at the photo again. "I can’t tell what they are!" she shouted.

Vinnie peered at the photo. Then he looked down at the stone objects. "There’s only one way to find out!" he said. He grabbed his sister’s hand and headed back down the steps. The guards began running toward the children. The crowd below went wild. The drums beat louder.
"Hang on!" Vinnie climbed onto a huge stone ramp. He slid all the way down. Mandy followed. They got to the bottom and saw that the statues were dragons. The photo glowed red.
"Vinnie! Mandy!" Mazatl called.
They looked at their new friend.
"Thanks for everything, Mazatl!" Mandy called out. "Don’t worry about us."
"We’re going home," Vinnie shouted. Vinnie and Mandy held hands and closed their eyes. The noise of the crowd faded as the children fell down the dark tunnel.
"Ohhh!"
Vinnie and Mandy landed safely back in the attic.
"That was a close call," Mandy said. Vinnie nodded.
"Mandy!" Mom called from below. "Where are you?"
"I’m coming!" she yelled. She winked at Vinnie and ran downstairs.
"What were you doing? We’re late!" Mom asked. She looked at Mandy. "What happened to that bracelet I bought you?"
"Um, I left it in the attic. Come on, Mom, let’s go!"
Vinnie looked out the window.
His dad was looking up while mowing the lawn. "Vinnie, come and help me!" he shouted.
Vinnie smiled and waved. "Okay, Dad! I’ll be right there."
After his close call with the Aztecs, mowing the lawn didn’t seem that bad.
A whole week went by. Vinnie and Mandy could not go to the attic. Mom and Dad kept them busy all the time.
On Saturday morning, Vinnie and Mandy got their chance. Vinnie woke his sister up. It was still dark.
"What time is it?" Mandy asked, rubbing her eyes.
"It doesn’t matter. Come on," Vinnie whispered.
The children crept up the stairs. Mandy opened the photo album. "Look at the Aztec photo," she said.
Vinnie looked. "Yeah, that’s us!" he said. He shivered as he remembered their Aztec travels. "Where will we go next?" he wondered aloud.

Mandy turned the page. This time the old man stood in front of a very long ship. The ship had a huge sail. It glowed brightly. Along the side of the ship were 16 large round plates. They were glowing too.
"What is this?" Vinnie pulled the picture out. He stared at the glowing photo.
"It looks like . . ." Mandy began. She couldn’t finish her sentence. The children fell into the dark tunnel.
"Ow!" grunted Vinnie as he landed on a wooden floor.
"Ugh!" groaned Mandy. "That hurt. Where are we?"
The children sat up and looked around. They were surrounded by wooden chests. A chilly breeze brushed their faces. They were rocking gently.
"I think we’re on a ship," whispered Vinnie. The ship suddenly moved up and down. Vinnie lost his balance. "Whoa!" he cried. He fell backward, flinging his arms wildly.
"Ouch! You hit me," said a voice. A boy slowly sat up, rubbing his arm.
Startled, the children stared at him. The boy’s fair hair and skin were dirty. He wore a pair of dark pants, fur boots, and a wool cloak.
"Where did you come from?" the boy asked.
"We . . . " Vinnie struggled to answer.

Mandy got up and looked around. They were on a large open boat. There were many wooden benches along both sides of the ship. About ten men were rowing gently with big oars. Other men were sleeping on the benches, snoring loudly. One very large man was snoring louder than all of them.
"Hey—you're a girl!" the boy suddenly said, staring at Mandy.
"So what?" Mandy replied loudly.
"Shh, be quiet," said the boy. "You’ll wake him up."
"Who?" asked Mandy, turning quickly. As she turned, she knocked over a bag. It was on top of a barrel and full of iron nails. The nails scattered loudly all over the wooden deck.
"Him?" Vinnie asked, pointing to the large man. "Uh-oh, too late. He’s already awake."
The man stood up and pulled out a long sword.
"Who dares to board the Sleeping Dragon? " he growled.
Vinnie and Mandy froze with fear. All the sailors stopped rowing or woke up. They stared at the children. The large man walked over to Vinnie and Mandy. Mandy guessed he was the captain.
"Gunnar! Explain! Who are they?" the captain asked the fair boy.
"Sir, I don’t know," the boy replied.
"Why did you hide here? Do you want to be warriors like Gunnar?" The captain pointed his sword at Vinnie and Mandy.
"Yes, sir!" Vinnie shouted.

"Ah, true Viking spirit!" the captain said. "I like your courage, boy." The captain slapped Vinnie on the back. Vinnie nearly fell over. The captain stopped and glared at Mandy. "But you! Little girls should not be sneaking onto a Viking ship. Especially one as weak as you," he sneered.
Mandy threw back her head proudly. "I may look weak, sir," she replied in a clear, loud voice. "But I am as strong as a horse."
"Land ho!" the lookout shouted.
"Finally!" the captain said. "Get ready to go ashore." Turning to Vinnie and Mandy, he said, "You two—stay with Gunnar."
Mandy let out a sigh of relief as the captain turned away. "Vinnie! I don’t think he likes me being on the ship," she said.
"Don’t worry. You were really brave," Vinnie replied. He turned to Gunnar. "Where are we going?" he asked.
"This port is Kaupang. It is a Viking village where we trade and sell our goods," Gunnar said proudly. "The captain is the best bear hunter! He brought bear skins from our village in the icy North."
"Here we go, Vinnie. Look!" Mandy grabbed his arm.

The Sleeping Dragon pulled smoothly into port. Several other Viking ships were already docked there. Each ship was long and slender. Viking sailors carried large chests out of the ships. Some carried smaller boxes of jewelry.
"Gunnar!" the captain called out. "Take this to Old Dirk, the blacksmith." The captain handed Gunnar a jewelry box. "Tell him I sent you. He will know what to do."
"Yes, captain," said Gunnar as he took the box.
"Do not disappoint me," the captain roared. "And keep an eye on those two." He pointed to Vinnie and Mandy.
"Come on!" Gunnar called.

Vinnie and Mandy followed him off the Sleeping Dragon . Kaupang was a busy open market. People exchanged furs for iron weapons. Others bought bear skins, walrus tusks, and whale bones with silver coins. Finally the children arrived at the blacksmith’s workshop.
The boy introduced himself to the blacksmith. "I am Gunnar. Captain Skull-Crusher sent me."
Vinnie and Mandy stared at each other. "Skull-Crusher?" they gasped.
Gunnar took Vinnie to the back of the blacksmith’s shop. He wanted Vinnie to see the Viking swords.
Mandy watched Old Dirk, the blacksmith, open the jewelry box. It was filled with bracelets, rings, and necklaces. "Where did those come from?" Mandy asked.
"When people do not have anything else that is valuable," Dirk said, "Vikings take their gold."
"You mean . . ." Mandy tried to calm herself. "You mean, they stole these?"
"We Vikings take what we want," Dirk said proudly.
"May I ask one more question?" said Mandy.
"Sure," answered the blacksmith.
"Why is the captain called Skull-Crusher?"
Old Dirk laughed. "Vikings are given nicknames for their fighting skills," he explained. He started sorting the gold from the jewelry box.
"What’s that?" Mandy asked, spotting a small wooden bear carving. "It’s so cute!"
Old Dirk picked it up and looked it over. "Hmm. I don’t know. It shouldn’t be in here with the jewelry. Would you like to keep it?"
"Yes, thank you," Mandy said with a big smile. She put the little bear in her pocket.
"Gunnar, this will take a while," Old Dirk called to the boys in the back. He started melting the gold. "You’ll have to come back later."
Outside the workshop, Gunnar faced Vinnie and Mandy. "I don’t even know your names," he said.
"Oh, sorry. I’m Vinnie and this is my sister, Mandy," said Vinnie.
"Strange names," Gunnar remarked. He shrugged and began walking away.
"So Gunnar, how long have you been with . . ."—Vinnie paused—"with Skull-Crusher?"

"Just one year," Gunnar replied. "I want to be a Viking warrior like my father. But he was killed. No one would teach me to fight. So I hid on the Sleeping Dragon. The captain was upset at first, but he let me stay. Now I’m his aide!"
Passing through Kaupang village, Mandy’s view of the Vikings began to change. She saw many farmers and fishermen. So they weren’t all robbers and warriors. In fact, they seemed just like most people.
A group of children were playing a game on a field. A crowd gathered to watch.
"What are they playing?" asked Vinnie.
"Knattleikr," replied Gunnar.
The children paused to watch for a while. There were two teams. Some players had wooden sticks. They were hitting a ball around.
"It looks like hockey," remarked Mandy.
Suddenly one player caught a flying ball. He threw it to another player who had a stick. His teammate hit the ball. But the ball flew wildly in the wrong direction.
Konk! The ball hit Vinnie right on the head. He fell to the ground. His eyes were closed. He did not move.
"Vinnie!" screamed Mandy.
The crowd gathered around.
"Is he okay?" asked someone.
"Let’s take him to my house," said a boy, coming forward to help. Gunnar and the boy picked Vinnie up. Mandy followed, very worried.
Vinnie was taken to the home of the boy, Dag. His house had stone walls and a roof made of straw. His mother and sister, Birgitta, were inside. Dag explained what happened.
Dag and Gunnar laid Vinnie down on a bench. It was covered with bear skins. Dag’s mother hurried over to Vinnie. "Birgitta, bring me the whale bone," she said.
"Whale bone?" asked Mandy. "What is that for? Is Vinnie going to be okay?"
"Don’t worry," said Dag’s mother. "There are magic symbols carved into the whale bone. It will help your brother heal quickly."
Birgitta gave the whale bone to her mother. Her mother placed it under the bear skins beneath Vinnie. Vikings believed that symbols had magical power.
Soon after, Vinnie opened his eyes. "Oh, my head," he groaned. There was a big bump on his forehead. He tried to sit up. "Where am I? Where’s my sister?"
Mandy knelt down beside Vinnie. "Are you okay?" she asked.
"Except for a headache, yes," he replied.
Mandy turned to Birgitta and Dag’s mother. "Thank you so much," she said.

Now that Vinnie seemed better, Mandy looked at the inside of the house more closely. It was just one long room with no windows. In the middle of the room was a fireplace. She was surprised to see animals—a cow, two sheep, and four pigs—in a pen at the far end of the house.
"Why do the animals live in your house?" she asked Birgitta.
"It’s too cold to keep them outdoors," she explained. "And having them inside keeps us warm too."
"Birgitta," called her mother, "take this soup to our old neighbor Hilda. She’s been sick for three days."
Birgitta took the pot of soup. "Come with me," she said to Mandy.
While the girls were gone, Vinnie watched Gunnar practice sword fighting with Dag. They used wooden swords.
"Gunnar, do you really want to be a warrior?" asked Vinnie.
"Yes, I do," Gunnar said. "I practice my fighting skills whenever I can. There is nothing better than being a Viking warrior. I want to be the next Leif Erikson!"
"Who’s that?" asked Vinnie.

"You don’t know about him?" said Gunnar, surprised. "He’s one of our most famous explorers. Leif Erikson discovered a new land far across the sea. He and his men saw many forests. The wood was perfect for building longships. They said the fish were bigger than me!"
Vinnie and Gunnar laughed. Then they heard a loud noise at the door.
"I finally found you little ship rats!" yelled Skull-Crusher.
"My Captain!" Gunnar bowed his head.
The red-faced captain stood in the doorway. He was very angry. "Where is my good-luck charm?" Skull-Crusher demanded.
Everyone trembled in fear. The captain of the Sleeping Dragon circled the room. He was breathing heavily. "Where is my good-luck bear charm?" He stopped in front of the boys.
"Sir, I swear, I don’t know," Gunnar pleaded.
"Silence! My father gave that bear charm to me when I killed my first bear. Its power has made me the best bear hunter! It’s my most precious treasure." The captain poked Gunnar hard.
Gunnar grabbed Vinnie and said in angry voice, "Vinnie! Did you take it? I trusted you!"
"No, no, I didn’t take it," cried Vinnie.
Skull-Crusher looked around the room and roared, "Where is the girl?"

At that moment, Mandy and Birgitta were returning from the neighbor’s house. They were about to enter Birgitta’s home through a door near the animals. The girls could hear an angry voice inside. Mandy stuck her head in the door.
"It’s Skull-Crusher!" she whispered urgently. "He looks very angry."
"What should we do?" asked Birgitta anxiously. "The last time he was this mad, he smashed up our house."

Mandy looked at the animals. She noticed a lit oil lamp by the door. She had an idea. "When I say so, let the animals loose," she instructed Birgitta. Mandy picked up the lamp. She placed the flame near one pig’s tail. "Now!" she cried.
Just as Birgitta opened the pen, the pig felt the heat and rushed forward. The other animals cried as well and ran through the house.
"Vinnie!" Mandy cried. "Over here!"
Vinnie tried to sneak away, but the captain saw him.
"Stop! Where are you going?" shouted Skull-Crusher. A fat pig blocked the captain’s way. Vinnie ran and made it to the back door.
"Mandy, I have to ask you something," he gasped.
Mandy grabbed his hand and started running. "Ask me later, Vinnie. Right now, we have to run!"
They kept running until they reached an open field. It looked like a shipyard.
"Why is the captain so angry?" Mandy asked, taking a deep breath.
"Somebody took his bear charm," said Vinnie. "He thinks we did it!"
"His charm? You mean this?" Mandy took the little carved bear from her front pocket.
"So you have it!" Vinnie shouted.
"Old Dirk gave it to me!" Mandy cried.

"Well, we have to give it back," said Vinnie. "And we have to get out of here." Vinnie pulled the photo out of his pocket and studied it. The sail in the photo was still glowing yellow. "It shows a ship with sails," he said. "But I didn’t see any sails."
Mandy pointed at the photo. "What are those glowing things on the ship’s side? They look like big round plates."
"I don’t know," replied Vinnie. "But I think we should head back to the harbor."
"And return Skull-Crusher’s charm," said Mandy.

Vinnie and Mandy looked around. They were in the shipyard. A group of men were building a Viking ship. It wasn’t as big as the Sleeping Dragon. Still, the construction was amazing. Strong men dragged planks of oak wood. Others carefully carved the wood to shape the frame.
"I remember reading in school about Viking ships," said Vinnie.
"What did you learn?" asked Mandy.
"Vikings were the best shipbuilders and seamen of their time. Their ships were so fast that nobody could catch them," said Vinnie.
"I caught you!" Someone grabbed the children from behind. The children had not heard Gunnar sneaking up on them.
"You scared us, Gunnar," cried Vinnie.
"I thought you were my friends," he said. "Why did you steal from my master?"
"We didn’t," said Mandy. She explained what happened.
"Oh!" said Gunnar. "The captain didn’t mean to put his bear charm in that box." A silly mistake had caused all this trouble. "So, do you have the charm?" Gunnar asked.
Mandy held it out to him.
"We must return it," said Gunnar.
Suddenly the sound of a horn rang loudly through the air.
"The battle horn," Gunnar said excitedly.
"What does that mean?" asked Vinnie.
"It is calling the men to set sail." Gunnar ran toward the sound. Vinnie and Mandy followed.

When they got to the harbor, the entire village was there. All the Viking warriors were hurrying to their ships. They wore leather helmets and carried wooden shields. The men swung their swords high in the air. The battle horn kept blaring. Old Dirk was watching the ships.
"What’s happening?" Gunnar asked.
"New land needs to be conquered," Old Dirk explained. "All the ships will sail together to fight."
The children searched for the Sleeping Dragon. "There it is!" Mandy shouted. "Vinnie, the photo!"
Vinnie took the photo out. It was now glowing blue. "But what are these round plates?" Vinnie counted. "There are 16 in the picture."
"Look! They’re the Vikings’ shields!" Mandy cried.
On both sides of the Sleeping Dragon were round wooden shields. They marked the places where each Viking warrior sat.
"But I count only 15," said Vinnie.
"I must go," Gunnar said. "Do not worry about Skull-Crusher. I will give him the bear charm. Good-bye, my friends."
He ran to the ship without looking back.
"Gunnar is true to his name," Old Dirk said.
"What does his name mean?" asked Mandy.
"It means ‘warrior.’"
Vinnie and Mandy stared at the photo. The old man was next to a longship. They looked up at the Sleeping Dragon. Suddenly one more shield appeared on the ship. It was Gunnar’s! Now they could see 16.
The glow in the photo turned red. The children’s eyes started to close. Then they were falling down the dark tunnel again.
"Yow!"
"Hey!"
The children landed in the attic. It was still dark, but the sun was just about to rise.
The rest of the day, Vinnie and Mandy were busy. They had many chores to do! So the next morning, the children headed straight for the attic.
"Where’s the photo?" Mandy asked.
"Here." Vinnie pulled it out of his pocket. "Mandy!" he cried. "The sail and shields stopped glowing!"
The old man was gone from the photo. Instead, Vinnie and Mandy were standing by the Viking ship. Vinnie put the picture back in the album. Then he turned the page.
"Mandy, look at this!" Vinnie exclaimed. "Here’s a new glowing picture!"
Mandy stared at the photo.
The old man stood next to a statue of a woman with a tall helmet. The helmet was glowing. The tall statue had a small winged figure in one hand. The other hand held a shield.
"Where is this?" asked Vinnie.
"I don’t know," said Mandy. She took the photo to look more closely.
Suddenly, they heard footsteps climbing the stairs.
"What are you doing up there, kids?"
It was Dad.
"What should we do?" Mandy whispered.
"Our adventures can’t stop now!" Vinnie said.
They stared at the glowing helmet on the statue. They closed their eyes and fell down the deep dark tunnel.
"Ow!" yelled Vinnie as he landed on a hard floor. "Hey!" he shouted as Mandy fell on top of him.
"Sorry!" Mandy cried. "I can’t help where I land."
The children were in a room with baskets filled with thread. The rolls of thread were many different colors. A beautiful piece of cloth hung from a large wooden frame.
"What’s that?" asked Vinnie, pointing.
"I think it’s a loom," guessed Mandy. "You know, to weave cloth."

"Look at what we’re wearing!" Vinnie stood up to admire his clothes. He wore a short white tunic. Mandy had on a white tunic too. But hers reached to her ankles. Both tunics were fastened with small pins at the shoulders.
The children heard voices.
"Someone’s coming!" whispered Mandy.
The children looked around for a place to hide. Too late—the door opened. Vinnie and Mandy froze. Two young girls walked in. One girl, dressed in blue, stared at them.
"What are you doing here?" she demanded, pointing at Vinnie.
"Uh, well, I, uh . . . ," stuttered Vinnie.
"How dare you step inside the weaving room!" she shouted. "My father will not allow this!"
"How did you get into my room?" the young girl in blue asked.
"We’re lost. We’re looking for a statue of a woman," Mandy said quickly.
"Lydia, bring Jason," the girl in blue said. "He’ll know what to do."
The other girl bowed and left.
"Is Lydia your friend?" wondered Mandy.
"No, she is our slave. Most Greeks have slaves," said the girl. "Who are you?"
The children introduced themselves.
"My name is Callia," said the girl. But she did not smile.
"This cloth is very pretty," Mandy said, trying to change the mood. "Do you weave?"
"Yes, I do. I am making cloth for my wedding," said Callia. Her anger was almost gone. "After the Olympic Games, I will be married."
"Married?" Mandy cried. "You’re so young!"
Now Callia smiled. "You’re not from Athens, are you? Girls here marry when they are 14 years old."
"Callia!" a boy’s voice called.
"Jason!" Callia cried, running to greet him. Jason was careful not to step into the room. Callia introduced the children to her brother.
"You are lucky my sister has a good heart," said Jason. "Father will not hear about this. This room is only for women and girls. Men and boys are not allowed here."
Vinnie quickly moved to stand beside Jason.
"They say they need to find a statue of a woman," said Callia.
Jason burst out laughing. "Athens has many statues of women!" he said. "Can you tell us more?"
"She has a big helmet," said Mandy, "and holds a smaller woman with wings in her right hand."
"Wait, you speak of Athena," said Jason. "She is the goddess of our city. That statue is in her temple, the Parthenon. It is at the top of the Acropolis."
"The Parthenon!" cried Mandy.
"I’ll take you there," said Jason. "But I am going to the gymnasium first."
"Thank you," said Vinnie and Mandy.

The children followed Jason through the house. The home was built around a courtyard. Mandy noticed a kitchen and a workshop. People were coming and going. One room had couches. Some people carried small barrels into this room. One person carried what looked like a flute.

"We hold symposia there," Jason said. "No girls allowed." He smiled at Vinnie. "Symposia are dinner parties. We eat and drink. We discuss many important things." Jason winked at Vinnie. "Of course, we have a lot of fun too!"
Jason led Vinnie and Mandy out of the house.

"We'll pass through the agora. It is the heart of our city," said Jason. "This is where people buy and sell things. We make the laws of Athens here too. Men, women, and slaves can be together in the agora."
Suddenly, Mandy pulled Vinnie’s arm.
"Look at that!" She pointed upward.
"Whoa!" Vinnie said, stopping. He stared up at a tall, rocky hill. Many stairs led up to the top. At the top were many buildings.
"There’s the Parthenon," said Jason. "Isn’t it great?" He pointed out a large building surrounded by tall, white columns.
"It’s beautiful!" Mandy gasped.
"I can surely tell you’re not from here. Where are you from?" Jason asked.
"From New Jersey." Vinnie said nervously.
"I have never heard of New Jersey," said Jason, frowning.
They reached the agora. People were everywhere.
"Jason!" a man called. "Here’s some bread. You have to eat a lot to win the race!" He held out a loaf.
"Thank you!" said Jason.
Another voice yelled, "Jason, your lyre has been fixed! Come by later to pick it up."
"Can you play that instrument?" asked Vinnie.
"Sure," said Jason. "I learn music at the gymnasium."
"Good luck, Jason!" called out three more voices.
"I will compete in the sprint race at the Olympic Games," said Jason. "The race will be held in Olympia. I am the youngest runner, but I am the fastest."
"I love watching the Olympics!" said Mandy.
Jason stared at her with his mouth wide open. "Women are not allowed to watch the games!"
"Jason!" a tall man called out. He was a few years older than Jason. He walked up to Mandy and Vinnie. "My name is Milo. I am the fastest runner in Athens!"
"But I thought . . . ," said Vinnie, pointing to Jason.
"Did he tell you he was the best? Ha-ha!" laughed Milo. "Everyone knows that I will wear the olive wreath of victory this year!"

"Milo, stop bragging," said Jason with a half smile. "After the race begins, you will see me far ahead of you!" He turned to Mandy. "You must stay in the agora now," Jason said. "We’re going to the gymnasium."
Surprised, Mandy cried, "No, I want to come with you!"
Jason shook his head. "Girls aren’t allowed inside. You must wait here until we come out."
Mandy stamped her foot. She hated being left out.

Alone, Mandy walked through the agora. "How could they just leave me!" she thought. "It seems boys get to do anything they want here. But girls don’t!" She wandered around the marketplace. It was hot and she was getting tired. "I hope Vinnie comes back soon," she thought.
Finally she stopped to wait in front of a small house. She noticed some sheep’s wool pinned to the door. "That’s odd," she said to herself.
"Ah, you have a new baby sister," a voice said from behind her.
Mandy turned to look at the speaker. He was a short man in a long white robe. He had a full white beard.
"I beg your pardon?" Mandy said.
Pointing to the wool, the man said, "That means a new baby girl. For a boy, your family would hang olive leaves."
"Why do they hang wool? Or olive leaves? Or anything at all?" Mandy asked.
"Everyone in the city knows this," said the man. "Yet you question it. Why?"
Mandy looked the man right in the eye. "Because I don’t understand," she replied.
"Ah! You seek understanding," he said.
Three men walked up. They seemed excited.
"Great Socrates," said one of the men, "your students are waiting."
Mandy’s mouth dropped open. "S-S-Socrates?" she stuttered. "He is one of the greatest teachers of all time!" she said to herself.
Socrates smiled at Mandy. "Let’s walk to the Parthenon," he said.

Meanwhile, back at the gymnasium, Vinnie looked around. The gymnasium was huge! He saw some young men wrestling. Others threw a ball back and forth. A musician played a lyre while a group of boys listened.
Jason wrapped long strips of leather around his knuckles. He was getting ready to box. "Vinnie, come train with us!" he cried.
"No, thanks," Vinnie said shyly.
"Come on," said Jason. "Boxing will make you strong!"
"Oh really?" a voice boomed. "Everyone knows wrestling is better!"
"Not again," said Jason. "It’s Milo."
Milo showed them a thick rope. He tied it around his head. "Watch this!" said Milo. "You are about to see an amazing feat of strength!"
"Don’t show off," groaned Jason.
Milo took a deep breath and held it. His face turned very red. He held his breath even longer. The veins in his forehead swelled. His head looked like it might explode. Everyone watched closely.
Pop! The rope broke!
All the boys shouted and clapped.

Mandy sat on a step in front of the Parthenon. Socrates’ students gathered around. Mandy listened as Socrates spoke. He was glad Mandy was sitting with them. Socrates was saying that girls should go to school, just like boys. Suddenly Mandy remembered the photo in her pocket. She took it out.
"It’s changed colors!" she said a bit too loudly.
In the picture, the helmet on the statue was glowing blue.
"What is that?" said a man sitting next to Mandy. He was pointing at the photo.
"Nothing," she said nervously.
The students gathered around to look at the strange picture.
One of the students held out his hand. "Give me that," he said.
"No, I won’t," Mandy replied. "I can’t get home without it."
The student tried to grab the photo. Mandy stood up. She tried to hide the photo. But more students noticed the glowing helmet.
"Gods above!" someone said. People started shouting. Their eyes grew wide with fear. Because of the fuss, Socrates came over to Mandy.
"Who are you?" he asked.
Mandy did not answer. She turned and ran up the rest of the steps into the Parthenon.
Back at the gymnasium, Vinnie was thinking about Mandy. "Jason," he said, "I think I should find my sister. She’s probably wondering where I am."
"Sister?" the other boys laughed loudly. "Isn’t she at home cooking?"
The boys started teasing Vinnie, but Jason did not.
"Do not say such things about our sisters!" Jason yelled. He and Vinnie walked out of the gymnasium.
"You are close to your sister," he said to Vinnie. "Like me and Callia."
"Yes, I’m worried about her," said Vinnie.
"Maybe Mandy went back to my house," Jason replied.
The boys ran back to Jason’s house. Callia was in her room, weaving.
"Callia, is Mandy here?" Jason asked.
Callia shook her head. "Weren’t you going to the Parthenon?" she asked.
"That’s right! Mandy must be there!" Vinnie shouted.
Waving good-bye, the boys ran out of the house. They ran through the agora. They climbed the steps to the Acropolis.
"Jason!" gasped Vinnie. "Wait for me!"
Jason really was a fast runner. Vinnie could hardly keep up.
"Sorry, Vinnie," grinned Jason. "I’ll slow down."
The boys made it to the top of the hill. Vinnie took a deep breath and looked down. The view was amazing.
"You can see all of Athens from here," Vinnie remarked.
Jason nodded proudly. "Yes, it truly is a beautiful city. Come, Vinnie, let’s find Mandy."
Mandy gasped for breath beside a temple column. "I wish Vinnie were here," she said.
Jason and Vinnie headed toward the Parthenon. But Socrates stopped them.
"It may not be wise to enter the temple," Socrates warned.
"Great Socrates," said Jason, bowing. "Why?"
"That name sounds familiar," thought Vinnie.
"Inside, a young girl is holding a strange light," Socrates said.
It was Mandy! "Jason, that’s my sister," Vinnie said. "She won’t harm anyone."
"But Socrates said . . . ," cried Jason.
"He doesn’t understand. We both need your help," said Vinnie. He looked straight into Jason’s eyes.
"Then I will help you, Vinnie," Jason said.
Together they ran up the stairs.
"Mandy!" Vinnie called.
"Vinnie! You’re here!" she cried.
Vinnie took the photo from Mandy.
"Look! The helmet is glowing brighter!" Vinnie said.
"Where is the statue?" cried Mandy. "I thought it was in the Parthenon!"
Jason stepped forward. "It is here. I can take you," he said. He was glad Mandy was safe. "On the way, I will tell you the story of Athena."
As Jason talked, the children passed scenes carved on the walls. Some scenes showed men in chariots. Another scene showed girls carrying water for the goddess.

"Both Athena and the god of the sea wanted to rule our city," Jason said. "So they decided to hold a gift-giving contest. The god of the sea gave the city water. But it was salty. Athena’s gift was an olive tree. This tree gave people food. The people of Athens were very happy. Athena won and became the goddess of the city."
At last they stopped in front of the statue of Athena. It was huge!
"Wow!" Mandy cried.
The children were stunned. The entire sculpture was gold except for the face and arms. They were white like polished ivory.
"The winged woman in her right hand is Nike," explained Jason. "She can fly and run faster than anyone. Nike is the goddess of victory!"
Vinnie took the photo out of his pocket. In the photo, Athena’s helmet was glowing red. The light hurt the children’s eyes.
"We’re going home!" Vinnie shouted. "Good luck at the Olympics, Jason!"
"Vinnie! Mandy! What is happening?" Jason shouted. His voice faded as the children fell through the dark tunnel.
"Ow!" grunted Mandy, as she hit a solid floor.
"Ugh!" moaned Vinnie.
The children opened their eyes. They were back in the attic. They heard footsteps. They quickly shut the album as the door swung open.
"Didn’t you hear me calling?" Dad asked. "What are you doing up here?"
Vinnie and Mandy looked at each other and smiled.
After lunch, Mom went outside to weed the garden. Dad went to the hardware store. Vinnie and Mandy quickly did the dishes. Then they ran up to the attic.
"Our photo trips still feel like a dream to me," Mandy said.
"Do you think anyone would believe us?" asked Vinnie. He opened the attic door.
Mandy shook her head. "No, they would think we were crazy."
Vinnie picked up the photo album. He opened to the picture of Greece.
"I wonder if Jason won his race at the Olympics," he said.
"Where are we going now?" Mandy asked.
Vinnie turned the page. The next photo was puzzling. The old man was standing beside a fountain. Behind him, frogs were glowing.
"Where is this?" asked Vinnie.
"We’ll soon find out!" Mandy replied. The light forced them to close their eyes. The children fell down the deep tunnel once again. This time they landed in a tree.
"Something’s tickling my arm," giggled Mandy. It was a small red apple.
"Oh, Mandy, I think I’m going to—," began Vinnie.
The tree branch broke. Vinnie and Mandy fell to the ground—hard. Apples fell all around them. Someone screamed "No!" in a high voice.
The children turned around.
An old man was stamping his feet angrily. "Look at what you have done!" he shouted.
The children quickly jumped up.
"Look!" Vinnie said, grabbing his sister’s arm.
All around them grew different kinds of fruits and vegetables. Pear and peach trees were next to pumpkins on the vine.
"How many apples did you ruin?" the man cried. He looked around in a panic. "His Majesty will be most upset. He won’t stand for this. No, he will not."
"We’re so sorry," Mandy said.
"My poor garden!" the man cried. "Who are you?"
"We’re—," Vinnie began.
The man held up his hand. "I don’t care! Get out! Leave at once!" he shouted.
The children looked around for a way out. They saw the most amazing sight. A fabulous palace stood right in front of them!
"Wow!" the children said together.
"Where are we?" Vinnie asked aloud.
"You little monsters!" the old man said, ignoring Vinnie. "I should—" But he suddenly became quiet. He bowed his head.
The children turned to look. A group of men and women walked toward them. A man in a feathered hat was in front. He wore white stockings and long robes. He carried a cane.
Vinnie could tell he was very important.
"You, gardener!" The man pointed his cane at the old man. "What have you done to my apples?"
The old man was very nervous. All he could do was mumble.
"Excuse me, sir," interrupted Mandy. "I can tell you what—"
There was a loud gasp from the group. Dozens of eyes stared at the children angrily.
"How dare you speak to the Sun King!" one man scolded.
"Do you not recognize your king?" A man pushed his face close to Mandy. "This is King Louis XIV! He is the greatest king in the world!"
"Louis who?" Vinnie whispered to Mandy. She pinched his arm to make him keep quiet.
"That’s enough, my Duke," the king said. "The children will go to their work now." King Louis waved his hand and walked away very slowly. His followers moved as slow as snails too.
Vinnie giggled and pointed to their pointy shoes. "No wonder they can’t walk fast," he said.
"Shh!" said Mandy.
The women wore long full skirts. The men wore wide lace neckties and long coats. Both the men and women wore big curly wigs.
"Didn’t you hear the king? Go to your work!" the gardener shouted again. His voice was back now that the king had moved on.
"But, sir, we do not know where to go," said Mandy. "We . . . uh . . . we are new here."
The old man sighed and pointed to the next building.
"Go inside to the kitchen and ask for Mary!"
The children thanked him. Vinnie and Mandy headed for the kitchen. But someone was watching them.
"So we’re in France. Then this place must be—," Mandy began.
"Versailles!" A girl jumped out from behind some tomato plants.
"Ahhh!" Vinnie and Mandy screamed.
"Oh, I’m sorry!" the girl giggled. She was about Mandy’s age. "I’m Helene." She pointed to the old man. "He is my father. He’s the gardener of the king’s kitchen garden."
The children introduced themselves.
"Do you work here at Versailles?" asked Vinnie.
Helene nodded. "I was born here," she said. "My family lives here to serve the king."
"What about school?" asked Mandy.
Helene laughed loudly. "You’re so funny, Mandy. I don’t go to school. You are new here. Let me show you around."
The children saw orange trees and more gardens along the way.
"How many gardens are there?" asked Vinnie. He was already tired of walking.
"Lots and lots," giggled Helene. "And we have over 1,300 fountains, 300 statues and vases, and . . ."
"What?" Vinnie stared at her. "There are 1,300 fountains?" He was thinking of the fountain in the photo. "How will we ever find the right one to get us home?" he wondered to himself.
Mandy was thinking of something else. "And all of this is for just one person?" she asked.
"Yes, it’s all for the king of France. He can have whatever he wants." Helene smiled again. "Where do your parents work at Versailles?"
"Uh, well . . ." Vinnie thought quickly. He remembered that Dad went to buy something for the roof. "Our parents are working on the roof."
Helene looked up at the top of the palace. She seemed puzzled. "Maybe we can look for them later," she said, shrugging.
Vinnie and Mandy looked at each other and smiled.
The children heard the lovely sound of a low horn.
"What’s that?" asked Mandy.
"It’s the hunting horn. The hunt is about to begin!" Helene yelled.
"Everyone goes hunting with the king. Everyone but the servants, of course."
A man with a pack of dogs appeared. The dogs were barking and pulling at their leashes.
"What are they hunting?" asked Vinnie.
"Most likely fox," Helene said.
Another horn rang out. They heard horses trotting.
"Do they hunt every day?" asked Mandy.
"Of course!" said Helene. "Hunting is the king’s favorite sport. Yesterday he got a deer."
Mandy burned with anger. She whispered to Vinnie, "Hunting is not a sport! It’s killing poor animals!"
Helene took Mandy’s hand. "Since the king is out hunting, I’ll show you the palace," she said.
The children all ran into the palace.
"Ooh!" said Mandy.
"Wow!" said Vinnie.
"Shh!" said Helene. "If you want to see it all, you have to be quiet."
Everything in the palace sparkled. Paintings of the king were on the walls and ceilings. The furniture was covered in gold and velvet.
"There are about 700 rooms in Versailles," Helene explained. She stopped in front of huge double doors. Helene looked around. She wanted to make sure no one was watching.
"And this room is the most beautiful of all!" cried Helene. "It’s my favorite!"
She opened the double doors wide.
Vinnie and Mandy followed her inside. Their mouths dropped open.
It was a large hall. There were 17 glass doors that looked out to the gardens. On the walls were large decorated mirrors.
"This is the Hall of Mirrors. It has 357 mirrors!" said Helene. "King Louis meets very important people in here. I make believe this is my dancing room."
Helene twirled across the floor. She did not see two guards with long spears enter the hall.
"You children!" one shouted. "In the name of His Royal Highness, stop!"
"Uh-oh!" Helene stopped dancing. "Follow me!"
Helene led the children down a hallway. Along the walls, gold statues held up crystal lights.
"Stop!" yelled the other guard. The guards ran after them.
"What happens if they catch us?" asked Vinnie.
"Don’t worry," giggled Helene. "We can get away through the gardens. But we’ll have to hide first!"
Helene turned a corner and went into a room. Lace and ostrich feathers were everywhere. A group of women sat sewing. One woman saw the children.
"Are the guards chasing you again, Helene?" she smiled.
Helene blew the woman a kiss. Then she led the children out another door.
Helene ducked into another room.
"How does she know this place so well?" gasped Mandy.
Vinnie hurried right behind. He wondered the same thing.
Suddenly, he bumped into a woman, and her head rolled off.
"Ahhh!" he screamed.
Vinnie watched the head roll across the floor. Luckily, it was only a wooden head from a wooden body.
"Where are we?" he asked loudly.
"Keep your voice down, Vinnie," said Helene.
Helene peeked out to see if the guards were still following them. Vinnie and Mandy walked around the room. It was full of wigs.
"Hey, look," said Mandy, as she tried one on. The white wig was huge, with lots of curls. "It’s very heavy!"
"Look at me!" cried Vinnie, trying one on too.
"Shush, Vinnie," said Helene.
"Why does everyone wear wigs?" asked Mandy.
"It’s the fashion. And King Louis sets the fashion," said Helene. "He changes his clothes many times a day. What he likes, everyone wears."
"People change their clothes when the king does?" asked Mandy.
"Of course," said Helene. "I think it’s safe to go now."
The children silently followed her out. Walking through the palace, the children noticed many servants.
"There are over nine thousand servants," whispered Helene. "They do many different jobs."

The children slipped out of the palace through a back door. Then they went down the steps to the gardens. The horses from the hunt had returned. The dogs were back too. Important aides rushed over to the king. The children were pushed to the side. One gentleman removed the king’s jacket. Another took his gloves. King Louis did not look at anyone. He walked straight into the palace. His group followed close behind.
"Children!" said a big man wearing a white apron. "Grab that game. Bring it to the kitchen!" He pointed to some dead rabbits. The animals were tied behind one of the horses.
Helene instantly obeyed, but Mandy stood back.
"Vinnie, I’m going to be sick," she said.
"Just don’t look," Vinnie said.
"I have to get away!" Mandy cried. She ran back into the palace.
"Mandy!" Vinnie shouted after her.
"Boy! Come in here!" The big man pulled Vinnie into the kitchen.

Mandy didn’t know where she was going. She ran until she was out of breath. She found a door slightly open. She peeked in. Inside, a young lady stood before a large mirror. Mandy counted seven servants in the room. Each one held a different piece of clothing.
"What is the king wearing?" the lady asked.
"He is upset," said an older servant. "He caught only four rabbits. He will probably be wearing dark blue."
"Then you know what dress to bring," the lady said.
Mandy felt someone poke her. It was another servant. "What are you doing here?" the woman whispered sternly.
Mandy quickly moved aside. The servant knocked and entered the room. Mandy overheard her saying: "My lady, the king will be changing to white and green."
"Then bring my green gown," the young lady ordered.
Mandy remembered what Helene said: everyone does what the king does.
The cook led Vinnie and Helene to the kitchen. She put the rabbits on a long table. The kitchen was full of busy people.
"You!" The cook pointed to Vinnie. "Start peeling!" Vinnie sat down at a pile of onions. Sighing, he began to peel them. Vinnie wondered what happened to Mandy.
"I haven’t seen you here before," said a kitchen boy. He grinned at Vinnie.
"I’m new," said Vinnie. "Why is everyone so nervous?"
"Our king is very picky. He likes his food cooked a certain way. If it isn’t"—the boy shuddered—"you’re in big trouble!"
"What will he do?" Vinnie gulped.
"You don’t want to know," said the boy.

Meanwhile, Mandy was trying to find her way out of the palace. "I wish I knew where Helene was!" she cried. She walked down a dark flight of stairs. "This part of the palace is very different," she thought. The rooms were small and shabby.
Mandy knocked on a door. She poked her head in. "Hello?" she said.
"Elise? Is that you?" someone called.
Mandy walked in. She found a sick woman in a bed. The room was damp.
"I’m looking for Helene," said Mandy.
The woman coughed. "Helene? Simone’s daughter? She’s not here."
Mandy felt very bad for the woman. "Can I bring you some tea?" she asked.
She shook her head. "If His Highness knows I am sick, I will be thrown out. Please do not tell."
Mandy promised she wouldn’t. "King Louis and his friends live in luxury," she thought. "But the servants do not. How do the rest of the French people live?" wondered Mandy.
In the kitchen, Vinnie’s eyes were watering. The onions made his eyes sting. He stood up to wipe his eyes. Vinnie’s elbow hit a bowl of green leaves. The bowl tipped and spilled on the table.
"Uh-oh," he said.
"Be careful with that!" said the kitchen boy. He was heading into the next room. "It looks like parsley. But that bitter herb can make you sick if you eat too much."
Vinnie scooped the bitter herb back into the bowl.
The cook called out, "Give me that parsley! I need it for the soup!"
Vinnie looked at him, puzzled. "What parsley?" he asked.
"In your hand!" the cook yelled.
"But this isn’t—," Vinnie began.
The cook grabbed the bowl. "Get back to the onions!" he screamed. Then he poured the bitter herb into the soup.
Vinnie’s eyes grew big. "But, sir," he began.
It was too late. The cook put the soup on a tray.
"This is the king’s favorite," the cook said to a servant. "Take it to him at once."
Vinnie looked so worried that Helene ran over to him. "What’s wrong?" she said.
Vinnie explained. "I have to keep the soup away from the king," he cried.
"I’ll help," said Helene.
They followed the servant carrying the tray of soup.
