In the palace, Mandy was still searching for Helene. She walked down another hallway. She heard noises. Quietly she opened the nearest door. The room was full of billiard tables. Men, including King Louis, were playing.
"Oh, Your Majesty," one man laughed. "You win again! You are truly the champion of this game."
King Louis smiled. Then he walked into the next room. Mandy followed, keeping out of sight. It was a dining room with a long table. Waiting servants held trays of food.
"Bring me my soup!" said the king as he sat down.
Mandy saw her brother and Helene right behind the servants. They looked scared. Mandy waved, but they didn’t see her.
"Ah, my favorite soup!" the king said.
At that moment, Vinnie jumped out.
"Don’t eat that!" he yelled.
Startled, the servant dropped the soup into the king’s lap.
"You idiot!" King Louis leaped from his seat.
"Your Majesty, are you all right?" cried the servant. Everyone ran to the king. They tried to wipe off the spilled soup.
"Vinnie! Helene!" Mandy shouted loudly.
They ran to her.
"We’d better get away!" Helene cried.
"Oh, look at the royal clothing," said someone.
"His coat is ruined," said another.
"And his best hat," a servant whispered. "What a mess!"
The king looked up and screamed: "That boy! Stop him!"
Everyone looked around. In the confusion, the children had escaped.
The children ran down a long hallway. "Over here!" cried Helene. They stopped to catch their breath in a corner. The guards were far behind.
Vinnie pulled out the photo. "We have to get to a fountain with golden frogs," he said.
"You must mean the Fountain of Latona," said Helene. "It has many frogs on it. It’s behind the palace. I’ll show you." The children followed her.
Along the way Mandy asked: "Why did you stop King Louis?"
Vinnie explained.
"Would the king really kill someone because of his soup?" asked Mandy.
"Only if it was truly poisoned!" laughed Helene.
"Look, Mandy! The frogs in the picture are glowing blue!" Vinnie shouted.
"What?" asked Helene.
"Nothing," said Mandy.
"There it is!" Helene pointed ahead. "The fountain was inspired by an ancient Greek goddess. She turned people into frogs if they insulted her."
"Wow, sounds cruel," gulped Vinnie.
Helene giggled. "Some people think King Louis built it to send his people a message: obey your king! Anyway, I have to get back to work. See you later?"
Mandy gave her a hug. "Well . . . good-bye," she said, then paused. "I am so glad I met you!"
Helene looked confused.
When Vinnie and Mandy got to the fountain, they looked back. Helene was walking up the steps waving. The grand Palace of Versailles was as beautiful as ever.
"The frogs are glowing red," said Vinnie. "We’re going home."
Vinnie and Mandy stood on the lawn with their parents. They were all looking at their house.
"Just a few more things we'll do," Dad said proudly. "Then our home will be perfect."
"Today we’re going to clean that attic," said Mom.
"Yep, it’s filled with junk," Dad said firmly.
Speechless, Mandy poked her brother hard.
"Ouch! We’ll do it, Dad!" said Vinnie, rubbing his arm.
"That’s okay. I’ll take care of it," Dad replied. He went into the house.
"We have to get the album!" cried Vinnie. "Come on!" The children ran into the house.
"Whoa! Where are you going?" Dad shouted as they ran past him.
"We have to do something!" Vinnie cried. They raced up the attic stairs and slammed the door shut.
"Vinnie! Grab the album!" cried Mandy.
Vinnie opened the album to another page.
"Mandy! Look!" Vinnie showed her the new photo.
"We don’t have time . . . ," Mandy began. But her eyes were drawn to the beautiful photo.
The old man was standing in front of a large group of Indians. They were standing in a circle. One Indian was holding something like a big belt. It glowed brightly.
"What’s going on up there?" Dad shouted angrily from below.
Those were the last words the children heard. Their eyes closed and they fell down the dark tunnel. They landed on soft soil.
"What’s that smell?" Vinnie moaned.
"Something’s burning," replied Mandy.

The children were in a village surrounded by a tall fence. Around them, long buildings with curved roofs were covered in bark and animal skins. A large fire burned in the middle of the village. People were throwing pieces of cloth into it.
A young girl came out of a nearby house. She gasped loudly when she saw them.
"How did you get in here?" she said, looking shocked.
"Well, we just . . . ," said Mandy nervously.
Like the girl, Vinnie and Mandy were wearing shirts made of animal skin. Vinnie wore pants underneath. Both Mandy and the girl wore a skirt.
The girl stared angrily at Mandy. "You are white. You don’t belong here," she said.
Vinnie and Mandy did not know what to say. Just then, an old woman appeared from the same house. She looked at Vinnie and Mandy curiously.
"Who are you?" she asked.
The children introduced themselves.
"Do you know where you are?" the woman asked.
"Uh, not really," Vinnie replied truthfully.
"This is the village of the Iroquois," said the old woman.
"So go home!" the girl said in a mean way.
"Onatah, it is the time of the Green Corn Festival," the woman said softly. "It is a time of thanksgiving and forgiveness."
"I know, Grandmother," Onatah mumbled.
Nodding, the old woman looked at Vinnie and Mandy again.
"I am Clan Mother. The People of the Longhouse welcome you," she said.
"You will be kind to visitors," Onatah’s grandmother said. "These two can join the festival after Busk." She gave Onatah some old animal skins. "Put these in the fire."
The children walked over to the large fire.
"What is Busk?" Vinnie asked.
"During the Green Corn Festival, we clean our homes completely," said Onatah. "We burn everything we do not use." Onatah threw the skins into the fire.
People were staring at them.
"Who are they?" asked one man.
"Vinnie and Mandy," shrugged Onatah. "Grandmother welcomed them."
"Then you are guests of the Onondaga," said the man.
"Onondaga?" asked Mandy.
The girl nodded proudly: "We are Onondaga, the People of the Hills. But Magua is Mohawk." She pointed to the man.
"Five Indian nations make up the Iroquois, the People of the Longhouse," said Magua. He held up one hand. He counted five fingers: "Oneida, Cayuga, Onondaga, Seneca, and Mohawk."
"Five nations?" asked Vinnie.
"Yes, five nations became one people—the Iroquois!"said Magua, closing his hand into a fist. "Vinnie, do you like to fish?"
"I’ve never tried it," said Vinnie.
"I’ll teach you how we fish," said Magua.
"Is it safe to split up?" Mandy asked Vinnie.
"It’ll be fine," said Vinnie. He followed Magua.
"Come," said Onatah, warming to her new friend. "I’ll show you around. Then we’ll go to my house."
They walked past the longhouses. Mandy saw an animal sign above every door.
"What do these signs mean?" she asked.
"Iroquois people belong to different clans. Clans are like big families that grow from one woman born long ago," explained Onatah. "Every clan has its own longhouse. I belong to the Bear Clan."
The girls arrived at Onatah’s longhouse and went inside.
"Let’s make a corn husk doll," suggested Onatah. She gave Mandy some corn hanging from the ceiling. Mandy also saw floor mats made from corn husks.
"Is corn your main crop?" Mandy asked.
"It is one of three vegetables we call the Three Sisters," Onatah replied. "Beans, squash, and corn must grow together as sisters do."
Mandy and Onatah husked the corn.
"Let’s get some beaver skin for a doll dress," said Onatah. The girls ran out the door.
Vinnie and Magua got into a canoe. They paddled out on a nearby stream.
"This is for you," said Magua. He gave Vinnie a long spear that was in the canoe.
"You catch fish with this?" asked Vinnie, looking at his spear.
"Watch," smiled Magua. He carefully aimed his spear and quickly pierced a fish.
"Wow!" yelled Vinnie. "Is this how everyone does it?"
"Only when we fish alone or with a friend," said Magua. "Mostly, we use the fish traps we’ve built."
"Fish traps?" asked Vinnie.
"The stream guides the fish into the trap," said Magua, pointing to a large circular dam made out of sticks. "Then we use a net to catch them."
"Why are you in the Onondaga village?" asked Vinnie.
"I am only visiting. My people live toward the rising sun," said Magua. "We are the Keepers of the Eastern Door. Mohawks protect the Iroquois from the whites in the East."
Raising his spear, Magua moved with great speed. Then he speared another big fish.
Vinnie and Magua returned to the village. They had caught plenty of fish. Families were gathering for the Corn Festival dances. Everyone was celebrating!
"Come, Vinnie, we must eat," said Magua. Baskets of food were passed around.
"This is great!" Vinnie bit into some corn bread. He also had some corn soup and roasted corn. He was so hungry!
Suddenly, Magua groaned. He held his stomach.
"What’s the matter?" asked Vinnie.
"I feel sick," Magua said weakly.
Clan Mother walked over to them. "What’s the matter, Magua?" she asked.
Vinnie explained.
"Call the healers," she ordered. "Bring them to my house."
Inside the longhouse, Magua lay on a bed by the wall. Soon, Vinnie heard strange noises. People were shaking rattles and chanting.
"What’s that?" he asked.
"The healers are here," Clan Mother said.
Vinnie heard scratching sounds at the door.
Clan Mother let them in.

People wearing ugly masks danced into the room. Vinnie almost screamed. The carved masks were scary. A large tongue hung out of the mouth of one mask. The healers called out in screeching voices and jumped around.
Vinnie was afraid. But Magua did not look frightened. He only looked sick.
The masked group came closer. They threw ashes on Magua. They leaned over him and chanted louder.
"Stay away! He’s my friend!" Vinnie shouted.
At that moment, Mandy and Onatah came into the house. Onatah held their corn husk doll.
"What’s going on?" asked Mandy. She saw the masked dancers around Vinnie and screamed. "Don’t touch him!" she cried. Mandy ran and stood in front of her brother.
The dancers stopped. They murmured to each other.
"Vinnie! Mandy!" Clan Mother was angry. "You should never stop the healers! It is our tradition. It is how the sick get well."
Vinnie and Mandy were embarrassed. "We’re sorry," they apologized.
"Clan Mother," Magua called weakly. He tried to sit up. "I’m feeling better. Maybe I ate too much corn bread." He smiled weakly.
"Clan Mother, what are we to do?" asked one of the healers.
Clan Mother looked at Magua.
"He seems better," she replied. "You have cured him. Your magic is good."
The dancers left the house.
"We were very scared," Mandy said.
Clan Mother nodded and said: "You do not understand the magic of the Iroquois. That is why you fear."
"I don’t know much about your people," said Vinnie. "But Mandy and I would love to learn."
Clan Mother placed a hand over her heart. "I will tell you how the Iroquois became the Five Nations. It was through one man’s journey for peace—Deganawidah.Here is his story."

"Long ago," said Clan Mother, "the People of the Longhouse were always fighting. Mohawk warriors killed Cayuga. Oneida killed Seneca. Too many people were dying. Too many people were crying. The Onondaga chief, Tadodaho, was very cruel and wild. His hair was full of snakes.
"One day a spirit appeared to a young Indian woman. The spirit told her, ‘Your son will plant the Tree of Peace at Onondaga.’ Her son was Deganawidah.

"Deganawidah grew into a young man. One day, he took his mother to a tree on a hill. ‘Mother, you must come to this tree every year,’ he said. ‘Cut the tree. If blood flows, I have failed in my journey for peace. But if sap flows, I am alive and doing well.’
"Deganawidah made an amazing canoe out of white stone. He crossed the river into Onondaga land. He found a friend there―Hiawatha. The name Hiawatha means ‘the one who combs,’" said Clan Mother.
"Combs what?" asked Vinnie.
"Combs the snakes from Tadodaho's hair," explained Clan Mother. "Someday, Hiawatha would calm the wild chief.

"Hiawatha and Deganawidah went to the land of the Mohawks. But no one there believed in his journey for peace. So Deganawidah climbed a very tall tree by a deep river. ‘Cut down this tree,’ he said. ‘If I live, you will know my words are true.’ The Mohawks did as he said."
"Did he die?" interrupted Vinnie.
"Hush," Clan Mother said. "The next day, the Mohawks found Deganawidah. He was alive. The Mohawks believed his message of peace.

"Hiawatha and Deganawidah went into Oneida land. The Oneida people were great friends of the Mohawks. So they quickly joined in the peace journey. Soon the Cayuga and the Seneca joined too. They all became Deganawidah’s people," said Clan Mother.
"What happened to the man with snakes in his hair?" Vinnie asked.
"Patience," Clan Mother smiled. "The four nations now went to see Tadodaho. ‘We are to be united as Iroquois,’ declared Deganawidah.
"‘Why should I join you?’ Tadodaho roared. ‘Onondaga is powerful on its own!’
"‘But think how strong you would be if all of us were one people,’ said Deganawidah. ‘If you agree, you will be head chief.’

"So Tadodahhoh agreed. Hiawatha combed the snakes from his hair. And there, in Onondaga, Deganawidah planted a tree. Its roots spread all over the earth. People everywhere who wanted peace could follow the roots to its source: the Tree of Peace.
"‘Above this tree I place the eagle that can spy out danger,’ said Deganawidah. ‘It will prepare you for battles.’

"Deganawidah also placed antlers on the heads of fifty chiefs. They would be the ones to rule the Five Nations. Then he made a promise to his people. ‘Call my name and I will return,’ said Deganawidah.
"And that is how the Five Nations became united." Clan Mother dropped her head to her chest and closed her eyes.
After the story, Onatah brought Magua a drink. He looked much better.
"How many families live here?" asked Mandy, looking around.
"Our longhouse has six families," said Onatah. "I live with my grandmother, aunts, uncles, and cousins."
A man entered the home. He whispered something to Clan Mother. She looked very serious.
"Onatah, take Vinnie and Mandy to the Green Corn dance," Clan Mother said.
"What’s wrong, Grandmother?" asked Onatah.
"Don’t worry. Go out and join the others," said Clan Mother. "I will call you when I need you."
The children left the longhouse.
"Everyone calls your grandmother ‘Clan Mother,’" said Mandy. "Why?"
"Women head all our families. Women are wise," said Onatah. "People always come to my grandmother for advice. She is the oldest woman in our clan."
Mandy thought of the other places she had visited. Men were always the most important ones. Among the Iroquois, women were more respected than men.

Many people were gathered in the middle of the village. Everyone looked excited. The dancers were dressed in colorful clothes. Some were holding feathers in their hands. Others wore them in their hair. People were singing and playing small drums.
"We thank you for the harvest," people sang. "We planted. We gathered. We ate."
The dancers pretended to plant corn, beans, and squash.
"Iroquois always plant the Three Sisters together in a small pile of soil," said Onatah. "And we use the shoulder blades of deer as hoes."
Then Onatah jumped into the dance. Vinnie and Mandy did too. The rhythm of the loud drums matched the beat of their hearts. Everyone was smiling and laughing.
After the dance, Onatah’s grandmother spoke. "Something important has happened," said Clan Mother. "We must get ready for the council. They are coming."
The people began to whisper.
"The council?" asked Mandy.

"Remember the story Grandmother told you?" said Onatah. "Deganawidah chose fifty chiefs to look after the Iroquois. Each nation has ten chiefs. They come together to make important decisions for the Iroquois." Onatah looked at her grandmother.
Clan Mother looked sadly at Vinnie and Mandy.
"What is it?" asked Mandy.
"The whites have come into our land," Clan Mother sighed. "A fight may begin soon."
Vinnie and Mandy looked at each other.
"Maybe we should call Deganawidah’s name," said Vinnie. "He promised to return."
Clan Mother smiled and patted him lightly. "We will wait to hear from the council."
Everyone stood near the central fire. People looked worried. No one danced or laughed anymore.
"When are the chiefs coming?" asked Mandy nervously. "Will it be soon?"
No one answered her.
Vinnie took the photo out of his pocket.
"I think it’s almost time for us to go home," he said. Vinnie pointed to the glowing object. It was glowing blue.
"But what is it?" asked Mandy, looking at the photo.
"They are coming," said Magua. He pointed to the village gate.
A long line of chiefs slowly walked in. Each wore his traditional headdress. Mandy was amazed by their colorful clothes.
"Should we hide?" whispered Mandy. But it was too late. One of the chiefs stopped when he saw the children.
"The enemy stands on our land," he said.
Vinnie gulped loudly. Mandy felt tears in her eyes.
"We are a peaceful people," Clan Mother said. "Remember Hiawatha’s wampum belt."
"Yes, it is the belt of harmony among the Iroquois," the chief said to Clan Mother. "But not harmony with the whites!" He pointed to Vinnie and Mandy.
"These children have done no harm to us," said Clan Mother.
"What is a wampum belt?" whispered Vinnie.
"A wampum belt is made of small beads made from shells. It is very important for the Iroquois," explained Magua. "Hiawatha’s belt was made long ago when the Five Nations was first formed."
Respectfully, Magua and Onatah came up to the chief. "It is true," they said. "Vinnie and Mandy came in peace."
Vinnie and Mandy were very moved by the words of their new friends.
"They’re trying to help us, Vinnie," said Mandy, wiping her eyes.
"Very well. The children may stay," said the chief. Onatah walked back to Mandy and Vinnie. Magua stood behind the chief.
It took a very long time for all the chiefs to gather around the fire.
"Sorrow has come to our people," one of the chiefs said.
"There is a time for peace and a time for battle," said another.
"Oh, Vinnie," whispered Mandy, "there’s going to be war."
"The Iroquois will not be divided," said another chief. "We must stand strong against the whites." He held up a purple and white belt in both hands.
"Wow!" cried Vinnie. "That’s Hiawatha’s belt! It’s the one Magua told me about." The belt was decorated with white and purple shells.
"The Great Tree of Peace is in the center of it," said Onatah. "And the row of white shells is like a path for anyone who seeks peace."
"The Iroquois want peace," the chief said. "But if we must fight, we will fight as one people!"
Everyone cheered.
"Vinnie! The photo! The wampum belt!" cried Mandy.
Sure enough, the belt in the photo was glowing red. Mandy looked around for her friend. But Onatah had disappeared into the crowd.
"Come on, Mandy," Vinnie said, gently taking his sister’s hand. They fell down the dark tunnel.
The children opened their eyes. They were in the attic. At that moment, Dad opened the door.
When Vinnie and Mandy finished the Iroquois trip, Dad had opened the attic door suddenly. Then he slipped and twisted his ankle.
"Oh, that hurts!" Dad said in pain. He was sitting in his favorite chair in the living room. Mom held a bag of ice on his swollen foot.
"I was going to clean up the attic, but I can’t now," Dad said. "Can you kids do it?"
Vinnie and Mandy clapped their hands excitedly.
"Sure, we’ll take care of it," said Vinnie cheerfully.
"What’s so special about that attic?" Dad asked Mom as the kids ran off.
The children raced up the attic stairs. Mandy grabbed the photo album.
"Let’s guess where we’re going next," she said.
"Okay, I’m going to guess Africa!" said Vinnie.
"I think it’s going to be China!" said Mandy, opening the photo album.

They were both wrong. In the photo, the old man was standing in front of a large tower. There were big black birds flying around his head. A group of men with spears were marching together. The spears were glowing.
"Where is this?" asked Vinnie.
"It looks like . . ." began Mandy. The light forced them to close their eyes. The children fell down the dark tunnel.
Mandy landed first. She opened her eyes. Two horses pulling a wagon were coming straight at her. Screaming, Mandy jumped out of the way. Then she tripped, fell, and scraped her knee badly.
"Whoa!" The driver of the wagon stopped the horses. "Where did you come from, miss? I didn’t see anyone walking in the street." The driver scratched his head.
"I . . . I’m terribly sorry, sir," Mandy stammered. Her legs felt shaky. "Where am I?" she wondered. "And where is Vinnie?"
Vinnie landed on the same street. A carriage came toward him. Vinnie quickly stepped aside. Looking around, he did not see Mandy. She was hidden by all the wagons and horses in the street.
"To be or not to be!" cried a voice.
Vinnie saw a boy behind some barrels. He was reading from a piece of paper. The boy did not see Vinnie.
"That is the question!" continued the boy.
"Ahem," said Vinnie, clearing his throat.
"Hey, stop spying on me!" said the boy, hiding the paper. "Who are you?"
"My name is Vinnie. Who are you, and what are you reading?"
"My name is Edward," said the boy, bowing dramatically. "I am reading a play by Shakespeare!"
The name sounded familiar to Vinnie.
"Someday, I will be England’s greatest actor!" shouted Edward. "Someday, I will perform before the queen!"
A baker came out of his shop and stared at the boys.
"Edward, you’d better get back to the tailor shop," said the baker. "Your master will be angry."
"I don’t care," said Edward. "I was born for the stage. I don’t want to be a tailor!"
"Are you a tailor?’ asked Vinnie.
"No, I am an apprentice," said Edward.
"Apprentice?" asked Vinnie.
"Young boys need to learn skills for different jobs," said Edward. "My master, the tailor, is teaching me to sew."
"Do you like making clothes?" asked Vinnie.
"It’s all right," said Edward. "But my talent is wasted sewing shirts and coats. I’m an actor!"
"Really?" said Vinnie, impressed.
"Where do you work?" Edward asked Vinnie.
"Oh, I’m not an apprentice," said Vinnie. "I go to school."
"You are very lucky," said Edward. "My family is poor, so I must live with the tailor."
Suddenly, the boys heard a man calling angrily, "Edward! Where are you?"
"That is my master," sighed Edward. "I have to go, Vinnie. I can’t practice now. But someday the queen will see my great talent!"
"What queen?" asked Vinnie.
"Why, Queen Elizabeth of England!" cried Edward.
"Queen Elizabeth?" Vinnie scratched his head. "Isn’t she the queen of England now? " he thought. Mandy might be able to explain it to him. But where was his sister?
Meanwhile, Mandy felt like crying.
"How did we get separated?" she wondered. "Now I’m all alone. How will I get home?" She lifted her skirt to check her scraped knee.
A carriage drove up alongside Mandy. A woman wearing a fancy hat looked out.
"Are you all right?" she asked Mandy. "Oh, you’re bleeding!"
"It’s okay," Mandy said, sniffing.
"Where do you live?" asked the woman.
Mandy bowed her head and didn’t answer.
"Let me clean up your knee. Charles will take you home later," said the woman.
Undecided, Mandy paused for a moment.
"Charles," she said to the driver, "open the door for the little girl."
"Yes, Lady Katherine," replied the driver.
Mandy stared at the woman and then got into the carriage. "She must be very rich!" she thought. "I wish Vinnie could meet her!"
However, Vinnie was seeing a different side of London.
Vinnie and Edward arrived at the tailor shop. Master Crossland, the tailor, was standing in the door with his hands on his hips.
"So you’re hanging out with actors again!" said the tailor, looking at Vinnie.
"I’m not an actor, sir," said Vinnie.
"In that case, you are welcome, young man," said the tailor. "Come, it’s one o’clock and time to eat. After lunch, maybe you can help Edward with his work."
The tailor then turned to Edward and said, "When will you stop dreaming of Shakespeare?"
On the ride to Lady Katherine’s home, Mandy introduced herself. Then she asked: "Where am I?"
Lady Katherine thought Mandy was confused after her accident.
"Why, child, you’re in London, England. Elizabeth is our queen," said Lady Katherine in a comforting way.
Mandy had read about Elizabeth I of England. She thought it would be great to actually meet her.
"Is the queen as kind as people say?" asked Mandy.
"Her majesty is good and fair," replied Lady Katherine. "England has never been so peaceful."
Mandy looked outside. She noticed how busy the streets were. Women wore long dresses and some carried baskets. Men wore fancy hats decorated with feathers. Horses and carriages filled the streets.
They arrived at Lady Katherine’s home. A servant opened the door.
"The girl has been hurt," Lady Katherine said. "Please take care of her."
When her knee was cleaned up, Mandy was led into a big room. Two other servants brought trays of cakes, gingerbread, and almond milk.
"Thank you," she said to them.
The servants smiled at her.
"Have you been with Lady Katherine a long time?" asked Mandy.
"Our family has always served Lady Katherine’s family," said one servant.
"Oh! Do you like to work for Lady Katherine?" asked Mandy.
"Lady Katherine is very good to us. We are treated like part of the family," replied the other servant.
Meanwhile, Vinnie and Edward were having lunch with Master Crossland. The tailor and his family lived above the shop. They all shared one small room.
"If you’re looking for work," said the tailor, nodding to Vinnie, "I could use your help today."
Vinnie looked at Edward, and the boy nodded, smiling.
"Sure," Vinnie replied. He ate some more bread.
After the meal, Master Crossland took the boys back down to the shop. He showed Vinnie how to cut some cotton cloth. Vinnie had to be very careful.
"Oops! I cut too much!" Vinnie cried.
"You’ll get better with practice," said the tailor.
Vinnie had trouble cutting the cloth. But Edward was very good at it.
"You will make a fine tailor one day," Master Crossland said to Edward.
"Maybe I can make the costumes for the Globe Theater," said Edward. "Then I could meet Shakespeare and . . ."
"Get those crazy ideas out of your head," said the tailor. "Working at the Globe will not feed your family."
Suddenly, a well-dressed man came into the shop. He wore a cloak with a high collar.
"Welcome, Lord Crumley!" said the tailor. "Lads, bring me those three rolls of silk!" He pointed to a corner.
Edward and Vinnie went to get the silk.
"Quick," said the lord. "I’m in a hurry!" He frowned as he took off his cloak.
Lord Crumley was a very rich man. But he did not seem very kind.
Lord Crumley stood in the center of the shop. Master Crossland knelt beside him. He was measuring the lord’s leg from the knee to the foot.
"We have very nice silk from Italy," said the tailor. "Edward, please show the golden silk to Lord Crumley."
Edward carried the silk over to Lord Crumley. The nobleman hardly looked at it.
"Is that all?" he yawned in a bored voice. "Ouch! Be careful! You’ve pinched my leg!" he yelled at the tailor. Then he kicked him.
Edward put down the silk and jumped on a nearby stool.
"How dare you treat my master like that!" shouted Edward in his most dramatic voice. "Have you no shame? Have you no pity?"
"Ssh, Edward," said the tailor. "Get down."
"What are you doing?" whispered Vinnie to Edward.
Lord Crumley was angry and turned bright red. He looked as if his head would explode.
"My lord, I’m so sorry," said the tailor. "My apprentice didn’t mean to upset you."
"This is your apprentice?" shouted Lord Crumley. "Throw him out immediately!"
"But, my lord, he’s just a boy," said the tailor.
"Toss him into the streets!" cried the angry man.
"That’s fine!" shouted Edward. "I’ll leave. I won’t spend my life measuring cloth for lords and ladies. Come on, Vinnie!"
Edward grabbed Vinnie’s arm and they both ran out of the shop.
At that same moment, Mandy and Lady Katherine were also leaving the house.
"Have you been to the Globe Theater, Mandy?" asked Lady Katherine.
"No, my lady," replied Mandy.
"William Shakespeare and his actors are performing a great play," said Lady Katherine. "It is called Romeo and Juliet. Would you like to go?"
"You are so kind to me, Lady Katherine," said Mandy.
Lady Katherine smiled at her. "If you don’t have a family, you may stay at my home," she said. "You will be treated well."
"Thank you . . . but . . ." Mandy could not finish her answer. She was thinking about Vinnie. "Where is he?" she wondered.
Then Mandy and Lady Katherine got in the carriage.
Edward and Vinnie were running fast through the streets. Edward ran down lanes and jumped over fences. Vinnie had a hard time keeping up with him.
Finally, Edward stopped on the corner of a wide street.
"Vinnie, do you want to see something wonderful?" said Edward, out of breath.
"What do you mean?" asked Vinnie.
"England has more than just servants and lords," shouted the boy. "We have the theater!"
"But isn’t Master Crossland going to be angry?" asked Vinnie.
Edward wasn’t listening. "We’re finally going to the Globe, Vinnie!" he said. "Follow me!"
Vinnie and Edward ran down the streets of London. When they got to the Globe Theater, it was full of people. Edward paid and they went inside.
"Wow!" said Vinnie, looking around.

The stage rose above the ground about one meter. The seats formed a half circle around the stage. They were on three levels, three stories high. The theater had no roof. Many people were standing on the ground in front of the stage.
"What’s the show?" asked Vinnie.
" Romeo and Juliet, " said Edward.

Mandy was sitting with Lady Katherine on the second level. The richer people sat there because the seats were more expensive. The poorer people didn’t have seats. They just stood in front of the stage. Mandy looked down and saw a familiar face.
"Vinnie!" she shouted.
Vinnie heard her. He looked up.
"Mandy!" he yelled, and waved.
"Vinnie, I’ll be right down!" cried Mandy.
"Stop!" snapped Lady Katherine. "My servants do not shout like street people!"
Mandy apologized. "That’s my brother," she said. "I have to go to him."
"You may not leave without my permission," said Lady Katherine.
"But I have to," said Mandy.
She got up and walked to the stairs.
Vinnie ran to the steps, but a guard stopped him.
"You can’t go up there," the guard grunted. "That level is for lords and ladies!"
"But my sister . . ." Vinnie said, pointing.
"Go back!" shouted the guard. "You’re probably a thief!"
"Come, Vinnie," said Edward, "I know of a secret stairway backstage."
He took Vinnie behind the stage. Actors were getting into their costumes. Vinnie noticed something very strange.
"Is Juliet a man?" he asked Edward.
Edward burst out laughing. "All the actors are men! Women are not allowed on stage!"
Suddenly, the guard was right behind them. "You are a thief!" he yelled, shaking his fist angrily at Vinnie. "Trying to steal from the actors!"
He grabbed Vinnie and threw him on the floor.
Just then, Mandy ran backstage. She looked around and saw Vinnie lying on the floor.
Vinnie jumped up and grabbed Mandy’s hand. "Run, Mandy!"
"I’ll keep the guard busy!" Edward shouted behind them.
Vinnie and Mandy ran through the crowd, out of the theater, and into the street. Suddenly, Mandy screamed. Two large carriages almost ran over them. The drivers shouted angrily.
A tall man got down from one carriage.
"Are you children crazy?" he said. "Watch where you’re going!"
"They were running from someone," said a woman’s voice from inside the carriage.
The man held out his hand to the woman. She took his hand and stepped out of the carriage. She was dressed in a deep-purple gown.
"Bow before your queen," the man said.
Everyone on the street stopped and bowed to the woman.
"Is that . . . ," Vinnie gulped, " . . .Queen Elizabeth?"
"Search them," she ordered.
Two guards began searching Vinnie and Mandy. One guard found the glowing photo.
"Your Majesty!" he gasped. With shaking hands, he handed the picture to the queen. She looked at it. Then she looked at the children.
"Magic is not allowed in my kingdom," she said calmly. "Take them to the tower."
Vinnie and Mandy were put into the other carriage, under guard. The guard was too frightened to hold the glowing photo. He gave it back to Vinnie.
"Witches," the guard said under his breath.
"We’re not!" cried Vinnie.
As they rode, Vinnie told Mandy all about Edward and the tailor shop. "I didn’t even get to say good-bye," Vinnie said sadly.
Mandy told him about Lady Katherine. "She was nice to me," she said. "But she wanted me to be her servant. I didn’t like that."
Mandy looked through the carriage window. They were crossing a long bridge. She could see a stone building with many towers in the distance.
"What’s that?" Vinnie asked, pointing.
"The whole area is called the Tower of London," said the guard. "The queen lives in the White Tower. But you’re going to the Bell Tower."
"What’s in there?" asked Vinnie.
"It’s a prison," replied the guard. "The queen will decide what to do with you later."
Vinnie and Mandy looked at each other.
"Prison?" Vinnie whispered. "We’re going to prison?"
"Why?" asked Mandy.
The carriage stopped. The guard pulled the children from the carriage. Queen Elizabeth’s carriage pulled up slowly. The queen got out and walked over to the children.
"I am not a cruel woman," she said to them. "However, I will not permit witchcraft in my kingdom."
"But we’re not witches," began Vinnie.
"Silence!" cried the Queen. Then she asked, "Where are your parents? Are they witches too?"
Vinnie and Mandy did not answer.
"Witchcraft is against the law in England. I have no choice but to send you to the Bell Tower," Queen Elizabeth said.
Two guards grabbed the children.
"Let go of me!" Vinnie yelled.
Suddenly, the birds in the trees flew into the sky.
"Vinnie! Look!" Mandy pointed to the large black birds. "The photo had black birds in it!"
Vinnie took the photo out. The picture was glowing blue.
"The tower ravens have been here for many years," said one guard. "You will get used to them!"
Right after that, a group of men in black hats and red uniforms marched up to Vinnie and Mandy. They carried long spears.
"Take these children to the tower!" shouted the queen.
"Look, Mandy!" cried Vinnie.
"That’s it!" Mandy said excitedly. "The ravens and the spears are in the photo!"
Vinnie noticed the spears in the photo were glowing red. The children closed their eyes and fell into the deep dark tunnel.
Back in the attic, Vinnie and Mandy let out a sigh of relief. It was good to be home.
It turned out Dad’s ankle was badly sprained. He could not walk for two weeks.
"Since I can’t work, let’s all take a little vacation," Dad said cheerfully.
"We can spend more time in the attic," whispered Vinnie to Mandy.
They started up the stairs.
"Mandy? I need your help," Mom called from the kitchen.
"Coming, Mom!" Mandy yelled. Then she turned to Vinnie.
"Wait for me," she said.
"Well, you’d better hurry up!" he replied, running up the stairs.
In the attic, Vinnie picked up the photo album. He wanted to open it so badly. He listened for Mandy’s footsteps. He looked at the clock on the attic wall. Fifteen minutes had passed by.
"Come on, Mandy!" he said aloud.
Impatiently, Vinnie opened the album. He stared at the next photo. The old man was standing in front of a large domed building. It had four tall towers around it. The towers were glowing.
"Sorry, Mandy," Vinnie said, as his eyes closed.
He fell down the dark tunnel. He landed on something hard, though not as hard as the ground. But he wasn’t alone.
"Ouch!" Vinnie cried.
"You tried to leave me again!" Mandy was pinching him.
"I waited but you were taking too long," Vinnie said, rubbing his arm.
"You couldn’t wait ten more seconds?" asked Mandy.
Suddenly, something under them began to move.
"Hey!" cried Vinnie. "What’s happening?"
"Vinnie! We didn’t land on the ground," whispered Mandy. "We’re on a camel!"
The children were sitting in two saddles on a very large camel.
"Where are we?" Mandy asked aloud. She looked around.

Donkeys were pulling wagons loaded with wooden boxes of different sizes. Other wagons carried barrels. Some people rode on horses. Carpets were piled on top of camels. Everyone in the group moved slowly.
"There are so many people!" said Vinnie.
"And lots of animals too," added Mandy.
"I wonder where we’re going," said Vinnie.
"Let me see the photo," said Mandy. Vinnie gave it to her. Mandy studied the photo for a moment.
"It looks like a temple," she remarked.
Their camel stopped suddenly. Everyone else had stopped too. A man on a horse stopped next to them. He was wearing a long robe and turban.
"We are about to enter the city," he shouted to the travelers. "Look after your goods and animals. We don’t want any strangers coming after our caravan."
"Strangers?" Vinnie gulped.
The man pointed ahead and cried,"To Istanbul—the greatest city in the great Ottoman Empire!"

The caravan entered Istanbul. The streets were crowded. Most men wore hats that were shaped like an upside-down flower pot. Each hat had a silk tail on top of it. Women wore long coats, and some covered their faces with a cloth.
As the caravan passed by, people on the street called out to the travelers.
"What goods have you brought this time?"
"Do you have any Chinese silk?"
"Come to the Grand Bazaar!" shouted someone from the caravan. "Then you can see what we have!"

The caravan stopped in front of a beautiful building. Through the main doorway, Mandy could see stalls and shops. They were filled with colorful items. People from the caravan were unloading things to sell.
"Wow! I’d like to shop here!" exclaimed Mandy.
"What’s that in your hand?" asked Vinnie.
Mandy held up a pair of diamond earrings. "I forgot—Mom asked me to put these in her drawer!" she cried.
"You’d better not lose them," warned Vinnie. "She’ll be really upset."
Mandy shrugged and put them in her pocket. "They’re not real diamonds anyway."
"How do we get off this animal?" said Vinnie, looking down. The camel stood quietly.
"Maybe we can jump," suggested Mandy.
"If you jump, you will break your leg or your neck," a man’s voice said from below.
Vinnie and Mandy saw a man staring at them.
"How did you get up there?" the man asked, petting the camel. "Kiraz the camel was not carrying any people earlier."
"Uh, well, we …" Vinnie tried to explain.
The man spoke to the camel and Kiraz knelt down. The children climbed off his back.
"Thank you, sir," said Mandy.
"Who are you?" the man asked.
The children introduced themselves.
"I am Ali," said the man. "I sell carpets and other things."
The camel opened his mouth and stuck out a gray tongue.
"I think Kiraz likes you!" laughed Ali.
Vinnie and Mandy helped Ali carry rolls of carpets into the building.
"The Grand Bazaar is the biggest market in the world," Ali explained. "It is one of the best places to buy and sell."
"It’s amazing," Mandy remarked. "It looks like the mall!"
Many shops lined each side of the long building. People strolled down the middle, looking and buying.
Ali stopped in front of one shop. A woman and a boy were already there. They were setting out beautiful pieces of jewelry and dishes.
"This is my family," Ali said. "As you see, we sell many things, including carpets!" He turned to his son. "Berk, take this bag to the coffee shop. Ask Hasad the owner to exchange it for silver."
The boy nodded.
"Can we go too?" asked Vinnie.
Berk looked at his father.
"Sure! The coffee shop is always fun to visit," Ali said. "But don’t stay too long."
"Do you ride with the caravan too?" asked Mandy.
"Sometimes," replied Berk. "My father and I have traveled the entire empire."
"That must be fun!" said Vinnie.
"Most of the time, it is," Berk said, smiling.
They arrived at a coffee shop. Men were outside sitting and drinking coffee. The children went in. Some men were smoking from a big pipe.
Berk gave his father’s bag to Hasad, the shop owner. Hasad gave Berk a bag in return. Hasad spoke to Berk quietly. Then a man stood up and raised his hands. "Time for a story!" he shouted.
The crowd cheered.
"We are happy to have Duman the storyteller with us!" the man said.
Everyone clapped.
Then, a man wearing a colorful robe stood up in the middle of the shop. It was Duman the storyteller, and he began to speak.

"Prince Babar wanted to see the world. His father, the sultan, would not allow him to go. The sultan wanted the prince to stay in the palace and marry. ‘But Father,’ said the prince, ‘I must see our great empire before I marry.’"
Duman pulled out a bright handkerchief. He waved it in front of his face. Then his voice changed.
"‘You can see the empire after you marry!’ At that moment, the prince’s mother came in."
Duman waved the handkerchief again. This time his voice was high, like a woman’s.
"‘Babar! I’ve found the perfect bride for you. She looks exactly like me.’"
All the men in the coffee shop laughed loudly.
"He’s doing all the characters himself!" giggled Mandy.
Berk stopped talking with Hasad and stood next to Vinnie.
"Isn’t he funny?" Vinnie pointed to the storyteller.
Berk smiled, but then suddenly froze. In fact, everyone stopped laughing. A group of men wearing uniforms walked in. They had long swords in their belts.
"We want coffee," demanded one of them. "You," he said to the storyteller, "Go on with your story."
Duman nervously continued.
"Who are they?" Vinnie asked Berk.
"The Janissary," explained Berk. "They used to be slaves from outside the empire. They’re trained to be the best fighters. The Janissary protect the sultan."
"You, children! Come over here!" one guard shouted.
The children walked over to him.
"Who are you?" he asked.
"Our caravan just arrived in Istanbul and . . . " began Berk. The guard grabbed Berk’s bag and looked inside.
"This bag is full of silver!" he said. "Young thieves were seen in the palace this morning."
"I wasn’t with them, sir. That silver is for my father," Berk explained.
"And what do you have in your pockets?" another soldier asked the children.
Berk and Vinnie had nothing in their pockets. But Mandy did. She pulled out her mother’s glittering earrings.
Berk looked at her in shock. So did the soldiers.
The soldier took the earrings from Mandy. He held them in his palm and stared at them.
"This jewelry surely does not belong to a little girl!" the soldier said.
Suddenly, Duman the storyteller threw his handkerchief in the air. He wanted to change the mood and amuse the guards. The men looked up and forgot about the children for a moment.
"Run!" shouted Vinnie.

Mandy grabbed her mother’s earrings from the guard. Berk didn’t have time to grab his silver. The children ran out of the coffee shop. They thought the guards would chase them. The children ran up one street and down another. Finally they stopped, gasping for breath.
"Do you hear that music?" said Mandy.
"We can’t stop to listen!" Berk said sharply. "I need to go back to the bazaar right away."
"Wait just a minute," Mandy insisted. She and Vinnie walked toward the music, and Berk slowly followed.
"What’s going on?" Mandy asked. They saw musicians and dancers in an open field. Food was being served. Everything smelled good.
"A wrestling match is about to begin," said Berk.
"Can we stay and watch?" asked Vinnie.
Berk looked around nervously. He thought the guards might be nearby.
"No, we shouldn’t. These matches can last for days," Berk replied.
A loud horn signaled the beginning of the match. Two big men walked to the middle of the crowd.
People cheered and shouted as they watched the wrestlers.
"Please, we must leave," said Berk. He motioned for Vinnie and Mandy to follow him.
They returned to the Grand Bazaar. Berk explained to his father what had happened.
"The sultan’s guards are fair men. They will give back the silver," said Ali. "Let me see the earrings." He took them from Mandy. "Where did you get these?" he asked.
"They’re my mother’s," Mandy replied. "I didn’t steal them."
Ali looked at Mandy and said, "I’m worried about you."
"Why?" asked Vinnie.
"You are strangers and these earrings look expensive," said Ali. "The Janissary won’t stop looking for you."
Vinnie gulped loudly. "But we didn’t do anything wrong!" he cried.
"You took back the earrings and ran away," said Ali. "They think you are hiding something."
Just then they heard loud voices.
"They’re here!" cried Berk. He hid behind his father.
The guards from the coffee shop came into the bazaar. They stopped at every shop to look for the children behind curtains and under tables.
"We have to go, Mandy," Vinnie said. "We can’t stay here!"
"Thank you for your help," Mandy said to Berk and his family. "We’re sorry for any trouble we caused."
"May Allah give you peace," said Berk. "Pray to Allah and all will be well."
Vinnie and Mandy turned to leave. But Vinnie tripped over a carpet. He bumped into a table with colorful tiles on display. Everything fell with a loud crash.
"There they are!" shouted the guards. "Stop, thieves!"
Vinnie and Mandy ran down the road and happened to see a domed building. It had six towers. The guards were still chasing them.
"Isn’t that in the photo?" Mandy called, pointing.
"Yes!" Vinnie said happily.
The guards were very close. But the children weren’t worried.
"We’re going home," thought Vinnie.
They closed their eyes. But nothing happened.
"What’s wrong?" cried Mandy, scared. She looked around. People were walking toward them carrying small rugs. "We’d better hide."
"Come with me!" cried Vinnie. He grabbed Mandy and joined the crowd walking through a large door.
The guards ran up and looked around.
"Where did they go?" one guard said.
Vinnie and Mandy walked into a courtyard. Soon, they met a boy and a girl.
"Where is your mother?" asked the girl. She had a scarf covering her head.
"Where is your father?" asked the boy.
"We’re alone," said Vinnie.
"Then come," said the girl. "My name is Feyza and this is my brother, Nesim."
Mandy and Vinnie introduced themselves.
"Welcome to our mosque," said Feyza. She smiled and took Mandy’s hand.
"So it’s a mosque, not a temple!" thought Vinnie, as Nesim led him to a different door.
"Women and men pray separately," said Feyza. "Here is a scarf, Mandy. Girls must wear them in here."
Mandy put the scarf on as they walked along.
"Take off your shoes," said Feyza. "Shoes are not permitted in the mosque."
The girls walked barefoot to a fountain.
"Let’s wash our feet," she said. "Muslims always wash before praying to Allah."
"Is Allah the name you use for God?" asked Mandy, putting her feet in the water.
"Yes. And we pray five times a day," said Feyza.
The girls finished washing and walked upstairs to a balcony.
"Don’t be afraid. Just do what I do," said Feyza.
Meanwhile, Vinnie watched Nesim closely. They were on the main floor. Vinnie and Nesim joined the men who were kneeling and bowing side by side.
Then Nesim got up. "Noon prayers are over!" he said.
The boys went outside. Mandy and Feyza were waiting.
"Thank you for showing us your mosque," said Mandy.
"You’re welcome," said Feyza. "We have to go home now. I’m glad that we met you!"
Mandy and Vinnie were now all alone in the street.
"I felt so safe in there," said Vinnie.
"Well, we’re not safe out here," said Mandy.
Vinnie took out the photo.
"Why couldn’t we return home? The building looks the same," said Vinnie.
Mandy looked at the picture and looked up. This mosque had six towers.
"It’s the wrong place!" Mandy said.
Suddenly a guard appeared and grabbed the children.
"The sultan wants to see you!" he said.
The guard took the children to the palace. Vinnie and Mandy were scared, but they had never seen a place so grand. There were so many courtyards and fountains. Everything glittered with gold.
"This place is big!" said Vinnie.
"Bigger than Versailles," Mandy added.
Two more guards came out of a palace gate. They walked over to the guard who was holding the children. All the guards began whispering at once. Their faces were angry.
"It is time," said one guard.
"We hoped the sultan would raise our pay," said another guard. "But he only cares about his own riches."
"We have no choice," said the first guard. "We must act!"
The guards huddled together, and the children were forgotten.
"Come on!" cried Vinnie. He pulled his sister’s arm. "Let’s get out of here!"
The children ran into a nearby building. It was a huge kitchen made up of ten large rooms. Each room had a tall chimney.
"This is a kitchen?" Vinnie said, amazed.
Many people were rushing around. Everyone was busy cooking, washing, or chopping.
"How many people do you cook for?" Mandy asked a young cook.
He wiped his face. "Over four thousand people," he replied. "Sometimes, we cook six thousand meals a day."
Mandy could not believe it. "Look at all those dishes!" she cried. Then she saw more Janissary guards entering the kitchen.
They looked very angry. She poked Vinnie.
"Vinnie! They found us!" Mandy pointed at the door. "What should we do?" she whispered, looking for a place to hide.
But the guards ignored the children. Instead, they picked up big pots. The kitchen workers looked frightened.
"What’s happening?" Vinnie asked one of the cooks.
Each guard was carrying a large pot.
The leader of the guards called out, "We will make the sultan listen!"
All the guards cheered loudly and marched from the kitchen.
"Where are they going?" Mandy asked the cook.
"They want more money," said the cook. "The guards have been angry with the sultan for a long time. They want the sultan to fill the pots with gold."
People started shouting throughout the palace.

"Mandy, let’s go!" cried Vinnie. The children ran out of the kitchen. They followed the Janissary up some marble steps and through a large door. Soon, Vinnie and Mandy were in a big colorful room. A man wearing a turban with a white feather sat on a red throne just inside.
"That must be the sultan," cried Mandy.
"We can’t stay. Let’s get out of here and find a way back home," said Vinnie.
The children ran out of the throne room and into a courtyard.
"I hope you know where you’re going," Mandy said.
"Don’t worry, Mandy" said Vinnie as they ran.
Soon they were outside of the palace.
"Look! Over there!" Vinnie pointed. Another mosque was nearby. The dome shone brightly in the sun.
Vinnie took out the photo. It was glowing blue.
"Four towers . . . " he said, counting the towers around the mosque.
Then, the photo started to glow red.
"Mandy, this is it!" Vinnie grabbed his sister’s hand. "We’re really going home!"
Mandy’s hair was wet from her bath. She heard a knock on her door.
Vinnie came into her room. "I need to talk to you," he said.
"We can talk tomorrow," Mandy said sleepily.
"It’ll be too late. We have to talk now," Vinnie said.
Mandy sighed. "Okay, what?"
"Jordan and Scarlet are coming over tomorrow," Vinnie said.
"Oh no!" she cried.
Their cousins Jordan and Scarlet were seven-year-old twins. And they were completely wild! They loved to play hide-and-seek. But this game mostly involved poking around in other people’s stuff.
"What if they go in the attic?" asked Vinnie.
"We can’t let them find the album!" Mandy whispered.
"We have to hide it," said her brother.
Mandy nodded. Quietly the children went up to the attic, and Mandy picked up the album.
"Where should we put it?" she asked. She looked around. But now, Vinnie was thinking of something else.
"Hey, let’s take one more trip," he said.
Mandy shook her head. "I’m too tired, Vinnie."
"But with Jordan and Scarlet here," said Vinnie, "we may not be able to go for a while."
"But I just had a bath," Mandy whined.
"Come on, it’ll be fun." Vinnie took the album from her hands. He opened it up.
"Wow! Look at this," he said with excitement.
The old man was standing inside a large arena. The seats were filled with cheering people. Behind the man was a long stage. Some things were glowing at the end of the stage.
"What are those?" Vinnie pointed to the glowing objects.
"I count two of them," Mandy said, looking carefully at the photo. "They look like fish."
"Where do you think this is?" wondered Vinnie.
"We’ll soon find out," Mandy said, as the glowing light got brighter. The children’s eyes closed as they fell down the dark tunnel.
"Ow!" cried Vinnie. He banged his knee on something hard.
Mandy landed right beside her brother in front of an arched doorway.
As soon as they stood up, someone touched their arms.
"Move along, children," said a man wearing a long white robe. "You must not block the entrance."
The children moved aside as some men walked into the large building.
"Wow!" Vinnie cried as he looked around.
"Are we back in Greece?" asked Vinnie. Everything he saw reminded him of Greece.
"I don’t think so," said Mandy. She tried to look through the doorway.
"Women and girls use the door on the side," the large man shouted.
"You come with me, dear," said a woman. She grabbed Mandy’s arm.
"But . . . but . . . " Mandy tried to explain.
The woman led her away.
Mandy was taken into a room full of women. They were taking off their clothes and putting on thin robes. Women and girls were talking and laughing.
"Time to bathe," the woman said.
"I just had a bath," said Mandy. But the woman ignored her and left.
Mandy walked through a hallway and started looking around.
"What is Vinnie doing?" Mandy wondered.

Vinnie was also in the bathhouse. He was sitting in a large bathing pool with some men. No women were there. Some men were lying on tables getting rubbed with oil. Others were exercising. Most of the men just sat in the pool talking.
"Ah, there is nothing like a hot bath," said a young man sitting next to Vinnie.
Vinnie smiled nervously. He wasn’t comfortable bathing with strangers.
"Some say Asian baths are better," continued the young man, "but I say Roman baths are the best."
"The best in the world!" someone said. Everyone cheered.
"We’re in Rome!" thought Vinnie.
"I’m Varius," said the young man.
"Hi," said Vinnie, introducing himself.

Mandy kept her clothes on and walked through a doorway. It led her into a large steam room. Women were silently sitting on benches enjoying the warm room. But two women were whispering, and Mandy could hear them.
"It’s all set," one of the women said. "The poison will be put into the horses’ water."
"How?" said the other woman.
Mandy could not hear what the first woman said next.
"Aquila will lose the race. Brutus will be the champion!" said the other woman excitedly.
Mandy was very upset. Someone was going to poison horses! She had to find Vinnie.
Vinnie was now outside the bathhouse with Varius.
Suddenly, Mandy came running up to them.
"I heard something in the bathhouse," she cried.
"Calm down," said her brother. He introduced Mandy to Varius.
"Why are you upset?" asked Varius.
Mandy told them what she had heard. "Why would anyone poison horses?" she cried.
"Are you certain you heard the names Aquila and Brutus?" Varius asked.
Mandy nodded.
"Who are they?" said Vinnie.
"Aquila is the chariot-race champion," answered Varius. "Brutus hates Aquila because he cannot beat him. We must stop this wicked plan."
"But how?" asked Vinnie.
"Septimus will know what to do," said Varius. "He is a censor and my father’s good friend."
"A censor?" Mandy said.
"A censor protects Roman citizens and makes sure they obey the law."
"Do they protect horses too?" said Mandy, worried.
"Yes, they do," smiled Varius.
"Where do we find the censor?" asked Vinnie.
"At the forum," Varius replied.
Vinnie and Mandy followed Varius. They were walking down a road of large, flat stones.
"Where is the forum?" asked Mandy.
"On Palatine Hill, the oldest part of Rome," said Varius.
"What is the forum?" Vinnie asked.
"Look around," laughed Varius. "We’re here."
They were in an area filled with people and stalls. Everything seemed to be for sale.
"Would you like some figs?" asked one merchant.
"Look!" said Varius.
A toy seller held up a wooden horse with wings.
"What’s happening there?" Vinnie said, pointing.
People were standing in a big circle watching two men fight. The men held swords and shields.
"I can’t look!" said Mandy, covering her eyes.
Varius laughed. "They are gladiators!" he said.
"Gladiators?" asked Vinnie.
"Highly trained fighters," explained Varius. "They are just practicing now. But people pay to watch them fight."
"Do they get hurt?" asked Mandy.
Varius laughed louder and said, "Gladiators fight to the death."
Mandy’s face got very white.
Vinnie and Mandy followed Varius through the forum.
"Look at those buildings!" exclaimed Mandy. The forum was filled with temples and statues.
"Septimus will be in the main office building," Varius said. "Most Roman officials work there," he added.
They walked a little farther.
"Here it is," said Varius.
The children followed Varius into the building.
Varius walked over to some men. One man smiled when he saw Varius.
"Septimus, I am sorry to interrupt you," said Varius.
"No problem!" laughed Septimus. Then he saw Varius’ worried face. "What is the matter?"
Varius introduced the children and told him what Mandy had overheard.
"Brutus is so jealous," said Septimus. "We cannot allow him to carry out his plan."
"We’ll help," said Vinnie and Mandy at the same time.
Septimus nodded. "I will find Aquila and warn him."
Mandy’s cheeks grew red. "But what about the horses?" she yelled.
"Tell Aquila’s stable boy to guard them carefully," he said. "And find Master Antonius," he said to Varius. "He will be supervising the race. Tell him this news. Go quickly!"
Varius and the children headed to the stables. A boy carrying a bucket was hurrying by. Varius stopped him.
"Where is Aquila’s stable boy?" Varius asked.
"Young Melus?" replied the boy. "His mother became ill suddenly. He had to rush home."
"Oh no!" cried Mandy. "No one is watching the horses!"
"Where does Melus live?" said Vinnie.
"His father is a butcher. You know where to look." The boy hurried away.
"Come!" said Varius sharply. "Time is running out!"
Vinnie and Mandy quickly followed Varius through the city. The children were looking at everything around them.
"You are not familiar with our city," Varius said.
The children looked at each other.
"We are new here," Mandy said.
Varius nodded. "I understand. You will get to know the city very soon."
They passed a few buildings as they walked down a narrow street.
"This is where all the doctors live," Varius explained.
"All the doctors live together?" asked Vinnie.
"No, they have their own homes," Varius laughed. "But the city is divided up. The doctors all live in one area. The butchers live in another. It’s easier to find people."

A few minutes later, they arrived in the butchers’ area. People lived in apartments on top of their shops. Children were outside playing some kind of game. They had drawn squares in the dirt. Each square had a rock or a shell.
"It looks like tic-tac-toe!" said Vinnie.
"Sorry to interrupt your game," said Varius, leaning over the children. "Do you know where Melus the stable boy lives?"
"He is over there. His mother is sick," a girl said. She pointed to a house.
Varius and the children walked over and knocked on the door. Melus answered.
"We know about your mother, but your master Aquila is in danger," Varius said. He explained about Brutus.
"My mother is feeling better, praise the gods," Melus said. "My father is with her now, so I can return to the stables. What should I do about Brutus?"
"Don’t let anyone near Aquila’s horses," said Mandy, "or they will be poisoned."
"I will guard my master’s horses with my life!" Melus cried. He ran out the door.
Varius and the children left Melus’ house.
"Do you trust Melus?" Mandy asked.
"Yes, I do. Melus was chosen to look after Aquila’s horses. That is a very special job," explained Varius. "Melus knows this. So he will not betray his master."
"What should we do now?" asked Vinnie.
"We must speak with Master Antonius," said Varius. "He is responsible for our festivals and public buildings. As Septimus said, he is in charge of today’s race."
"When does the race begin?" asked Mandy.
Varius looked up at the sun.
"It will begin soon. We must hurry," he said.
Varius stopped in front of a large house with a stone fountain.
"Master Antonius lives here," said Varius.
A man with a hammer was bent close to the ground.
The man tapped the hammer gently on something small and blue. The children heard something breaking.
"Is he Master Antonius?" asked Vinnie.
"Oh no, this man is a mosaic artist," said Varius, pointing to the floor. It was a mosaic of animals and fish.
They examined the mosaic closer. Little pieces of pottery were stuck together to create a picture.
"That’s amazing!" cried Mandy.
A servant finally came and led them to a courtyard in the center of the house.
"This is different from Melus’ house," remarked Mandy.
A man appeared. He wore a large ring.
"Varius!" said the man. "What’s the matter? Be quick, boy. I must get to the games soon."
"Master Antonius, Aquila is in danger," warned Varius. "Today’s race will not be a fair one." He told Antonius what Mandy had overheard in the bathhouse.
"Poisoning the horses?" said Master Antonius. "Horrible! You are sure of this?"
"Brutus wants to win very badly," said Varius. "He should be watched carefully."
"I’ll have extra guards put near the stable," Master Antonius said.
"Thank you!" cried Varius, as he and the children left.
"Now what do we do, Varius?" asked Mandy.
"We’ll go to the Circus Maximus. The race will begin soon. We have done all that we can," Varius said.
They walked slowly down the road. A large crowd was walking ahead of them.
"Are they all going to the race?" asked Vinnie.
"Oh yes, people love the chariot races. Everyone comes to watch and bet on them," said Varius.
They followed the crowd into a large arena.
"Whoa!" Vinnie and Mandy cried together.

The Circus Maximus was a huge arena with many seats. In the middle of the track was a long stage. The stage had a huge tower in the middle. At both ends of the stage were posts. Metal objects were on a thick bar.
"Vinnie! The photo!" Mandy shouted. "The old man was here!"
Vinnie took out the photo. It was glowing blue.
"You're right!" he cried. "But what are they?" He pointed to the objects on the bar.
"There are seven of them . . . " Mandy counted. "I think they are dolphins! But what are they for, Varius?"
"One dolphin is turned up every time the racers go around the track," said Varius. "Each time around the track is a lap. The dolphins let the racers know how many laps they have to go."
Just then a tall man walked over to them. He looked down at Vinnie and Mandy.
"I am Aquila. Are you the children who saved my life?"
Aquila looked fierce but his eyes were kind.
"Septimus told me of your help," he said. "My victory will be in your honor."
"Aquila!" Another man came over to them. His smile wasn’t kind.
"How are your horses?" he said.
Aquila smiled too. "They are ready to race, Brutus. Melus brought them fresh water from his well."
Brutus’ face grew red. "What about the water I sent?"
"It was unfortunate," Aquila said coldly, "but Melus accidentally spilled it on the stable floor."
Brutus moved angrily toward Aquila. The two men seemed ready to fight.
"Take your places! The race is about to begin!" cried Master Antonius, stepping between the men. Varius held Aquila back too.
"I will have my revenge," said Brutus, walking away.
"Enjoy the race, children," said Aquila, and left.
"Are you okay?" Varius said to the children.
Vinnie and Mandy nodded nervously. They all found seats and watched Master Antonius walk onto the stage. He raised his arms and the audience grew quiet.
"Are you ready to start the race?" he asked the huge crowd.
The people cheered wildly.
Master Antonius pointed to the twelve gates at the end of the arena. Suddenly a horn blew loudly, and Antonius dropped a white cloth. The gates opened and the chariots came speeding out.
"There’s Aquila!" said Varius, pointing to a golden chariot. Aquila lashed his horses as he raced around the track.
"And Brutus!" yelled Vinnie. Brutus was close behind Aquila. His chariot was red and green. It had a spike sticking out from the middle of each wheel.
They raced once around the track. Men on the stage turned one dolphin up. Mandy noticed it right away.
"One lap!" she yelled.
"Go, Aquila!" Vinnie was yelling.
"Vinnie! Let me see the photo!" Mandy shouted. He handed her the photo.
"We’re getting closer to home!" she said.
"Aquila! Watch out!" cried Vinnie.
Brutus was trying to crash into Aquila’s chariot.
"If Brutus’ spike hits Aquila’s wheel, Aquila’s chariot could flip over," said Varius. "Then Aquila will be crushed under the horses’ feet!"
"Oh, I can’t look!" Mandy covered her eyes.
Aquila moved away just in time. Another dolphin was flipped to show a second lap was completed.
"Varius!" Mandy touched his arm. "Thank you!"
The two dolphins in the photo were glowing red as Aquila pulled ahead.
Vinnie was cheering loudly.
Mandy grabbed Vinnie’s hand.
"Go, Aqu . . . " Vinnie began to shout.
Then the children fell down the dark tunnel.
Jordan and Scarlet were screaming at the top of their lungs. "TV! TV! We want to watch TV!"
Vinnie and Mandy’s parents had gone shopping with Uncle Wilson and Aunt Leah. Before leaving, Aunt Leah had said: "No TV for Jordan and Scarlet."
"You’re not allowed," began Vinnie. The twins started screaming again.
"How about some ice cream!" Mandy said, clapping her hands.
"Ice cream?" cried Scarlet.
"We have chocolate and strawberry," said Mandy, walking toward the kitchen. The twins followed quietly.
Vinnie wiped his forehead. "Babysitting is hard. I need a break," he said to himself.
Vinnie started for his bedroom, and then changed his mind. He walked up to the attic.
"I wonder if I should . . . " thought Vinnie. "No, I can’t. Mandy will be mad. But she’s downstairs having ice cream . . . "
Vinnie found the album. "I’m only going to take a peek," he said to himself. "I’ll close it if I see a glowing picture."
He sat down and opened the album. At the same time, Mandy burst into the attic.
"I knew it!" she shouted. "I knew you would try to go without me!"
"But I . . . well . . . I . . . ," Vinnie stammered.
Mandy snatched the album from his hands. A photo was glowing.
"Oh, how strange!" she gasped.

Vinnie got up and looked over her shoulder. The old man stood between two statues of scary-looking animals. They had big eyes and huge mouths with many sharp teeth. Behind the statues was a tall structure. It was glowing brightly.
"It looks like rooftops stacked on top of each other," remarked Vinnie.
"I wonder where this could be?" said Mandy.
"I don’t know, but . . . ," Vinnie paused. "Where are the twins?"
Just as Vinnie asked that question, Jordan and Scarlet appeared at the door. And at that exact moment, Vinnie and Mandy fell down the dark tunnel.
"Hey!" cried Mandy.
"Whoa!" cried Vinnie.
"Hooray!" shouted people as they clapped loudly.
"Huh?" Vinnie opened his eyes. He was lying on a stage in front of lots of people. Mandy was next to him.
"What’s going on?" she whispered to her brother.
"Wasn’t that amazing?" A man stood in front of them. He was waving to the crowd. "Come back for our next show!"
The crowd moved away. Then the man turned and looked down at them.
"Who are you?" he said, stunned. "How did you do that?"
"Do what?" asked Vinnie.
"It looked as if you fell from the sky," he said, pointing up. "I am Samir the great magician. And yet, I cannot explain how you did that."
The children got up and looked around.
"Where are we?" asked Mandy. They were in a large square. Mandy could hear music and the sounds of animals.
Samir laughed. "You are at a celebration for Master Yuan—an important government official."
"Which government?" asked Vinnie.
Samir looked at him in surprise.
"Why, the Tang Dynasty of China, of course," he replied.
Vinnie and Mandy looked at each other.
"China?" they said together.
Samir looked at them with great interest. "Tell me the secret of that trick you just did," he said.
"We don’t know," Vinnie admitted.
"Ah, you do not wish to tell me?" Samir asked.
"No, we really don’t know," said Mandy.
Samir laughed loudly. "Well, see me if you ever need a job. That trick could make me—I mean you —a lot of money."
Samir walked behind a curtain at the back of the stage.
"Look at that!" said Mandy. She could see a group of houses outside a nearby gate.
"I count four buildings," said Vinnie.
"Is it a little village?" asked Mandy.
"Village?" said a laughing voice below them. The children looked down and saw a girl.
"That is Master Yuan’s courtyard house," the girl said. "Wealthy people live in such homes." She looked a bit older than Vinnie.
Vinnie and Mandy jumped down from the stage.
"You’re new to Chang’an," she remarked. "Everyone knows Master Yuan. You must be with the visiting performers. The acrobats are my favorite."
"Acrobats?" said Vinnie.
The girl led them through a noisy crowd of performers. Jugglers were lifting umbrellas with their feet.
"There they are!" cried Vinnie. Young girls were jumping and flipping in the air.
"What’s your name?" Mandy said to the girl.
"I’m Mei-Li," the girl replied. "My parents are bakers. They made two hundred buns for Master Yuan’s celebration."
Mandy introduced herself and pointed to Vinnie. "And he’s my brother Vinnie," she said. "What’s the celebration for?"
"Master Yuan’s son Jinying has passed the first level of the imperial exams," explained Mei-Li.
"What are they?" asked Mandy.

"They are very difficult tests. There are three levels of exams, and each level is harder than the one before," said Mei-Li. "If all levels are passed, the person becomes a mandarin. A mandarin is a very respected official."
"That’s a lot of work," said Mandy.
Mei-Li nodded. "It takes many years of study."
Vinnie rejoined his sister and Mei-Li. They walked past two monkeys dressed in red costumes. The children giggled.
"I have to go to the market," said Mei-Li. "It was nice meeting you."
"Can we come with you?" asked Vinnie.
"Sure," said Mei-Li. They walked toward a large gate.
Then Mandy noticed a monkey trainer beating one of the two monkeys.
"That’s not right!" Mandy thought to herself. She marched over to the trainer as Vinnie and Mei-Li walked on.
"You shouldn’t hurt your animals," said Mandy.
"Mind your own business!" yelled the trainer. He put the monkey in a cage and walked off.
Vinnie and Mei-Li were already out of sight, walking toward the market.
"Poor thing," said Mandy, as she walked over to the cage. "Don’t worry, I’ll save you."
Mandy opened the cage. The monkey jumped out and ran across the square.
"Wait! Come back!" Mandy shouted.
Vinnie followed Mei-Li through the city.
"Chang’an is so big!" said Vinnie.
Mei-Li nodded. "Chang’an is the capital of the Tang Dynasty. The famous Silk Road begins here. Almost all trade moves along the Silk Road."
"Oh, that’s why there are so many different people here," said Vinnie.
They passed a very high wall with a guarded gate.
"That’s the East Gate," said Mei-Li. "We have four gates, but we can use only three."
"Why?" asked Vinnie.
"The North Gate is only for the emperor," said Mei-Li. "Where is Mandy?"
"She’s wandered off again," sighed Vinnie. "Don’t worry, she does this all the time."
Meanwhile, the monkey ran fast out of the square. Then it climbed up on the roof of a building.
"Come here," she called to the animal. The monkey shyly moved down to a windowsill.
Mandy carefully climbed up some steps. She tried to grab the monkey. But she tripped and tumbled through a door.
"I’m terribly sorry," she apologized to a startled young man. He was sitting cross-legged on a low couch. In front of him was a low table covered with open books.
"May I help you?" he asked.
"Well, yes," Mandy said. "I’m looking for a monkey."
"Are you sure it’s here?" he laughed.
Mandy nodded. "I chased it here." She explained the trainer’s behavior.
The man nodded sadly. "We should treat all living things kindly. That’s Buddha’s way."
"Who are you?" asked Mandy.
"My name is Jinying. I am Master Yuan’s son," he replied.
"How come you aren’t at your party?" she asked.
"My father is a little too eager to celebrate. My exams are not over yet," laughed Jinying. "I still have many Chinese characters to memorize."
"How many do you have to know?" asked Mandy.
She glanced at his open book. She saw a vertical row of Chinese characters on one side of the page. Next to each character was a series of smaller characters.
"I memorize about two hundred a day," replied Jinying. "Each character has a different meaning."
"How many do you have to learn altogether?" Mandy asked.
"Over four hundred thousand." Jinying sighed.
Mandy was shocked. "I won’t disturb you then," she said.
"Wait!" Jinying stood up and stretched. "I need a break. I’ll help you find your monkey."
Meanwhile, Vinnie stopped and stared at the crowded streets.
"This is like New York!" he cried.
"Excuse me?" asked Mei-Li.
"Uh, nothing," he said.
Chang’an was busy and noisy with people, wagons, and animals. When he and Mei-Li reached the market, Vinnie was even more surprised. There were many lanes, and each lane sold only one product.
"Wow! There’s one lane for oil, and one lane for vegetables. And even one," Vinnie laughed, "for roast duck with the head still attached?"
"My favorite!" said Mei-Li.
"The duck seems to be looking at me!"
"But it’s delicious!" she replied. "Let’s try some."
Vinnie gulped. "Maybe I should go and find my sister."
Mandy and Jinying could not find the monkey.
"Maybe it left the property," said Jinying.
Outside, Mandy was amazed at Jinying’s courtyard house. It took up an entire block.
"Why do you have so many little buildings?" she asked.
"Each building has a different purpose," he replied. "We receive guests in the main house. My father and mother have their own buildings and so do I."
They walked past Jinying’s house. Mandy noticed that some people wore shiny silk, like Jinying. But others wore dark clothes made from rough material.
Some people on the street called out to Jinying. "Congratulations, Master Jinying," they said. Jinying nodded but kept walking.
"There it is!" Mandy suddenly caught sight of the monkey. It was climbing onto the roof of a strange building.
"What a funny house," giggled Mandy. "Why is it built so open to the outside?"
"It gets very hot here sometimes," replied Jinying. "People like to meet, relax, and keep cool in these places."
Jinying reached into his pocket. He had some sunflower seeds. He gave them to Mandy, and she held them out to the monkey. It came down from the roof and sniffed her hand. Mandy grabbed the monkey.
Suddenly a loud voice called out, "That’s my monkey!"
It was the trainer. He was on a horse and waving a large stick.
"What should we do?" Mandy asked. The monkey clung to her shirt.
"Come with me." Jinying took her arm. "I have an idea."
Vinnie, meanwhile, was trying to get back to the square. He walked to the end of a street and stared.
"I can’t believe it! This whole city is surrounded by a wall," he said aloud. Backing away, Vinnie bumped into someone. They both fell to the ground.
"I’m sorry," cried Vinnie. He turned and saw a bald man wearing a long robe. Next to him was a walking stick and book.
"Are you hurt?" asked Vinnie.
"I think I twisted my ankle. Would you mind helping me?" the man asked.
"Of course," Vinnie replied. He put the man’s arm around his shoulder.
"Where are we going?" Vinnie asked.
"To the monastery, over there," said the man, pointing.
On the other side of the city, Mandy and Jinying were running from the trainer. They tried to hide behind a wagon piled high with wheat.
"Thieves! I see you!" The monkey trainer had found them.
Vinnie helped the man to the monastery. When they arrived, Vinnie noticed a building in front. It looked like the one in the photo.
"Won’t you come inside?" asked the man.
"What are these things called?" Vinnie asked, pointing to the building.
"Pagodas," the man replied. "They are places to worship Buddha."
"Teacher Hu, you are hurt!" a young man cried. He walked quickly over to them.
"I am fine. My young friend helped me here, Sheng." Teacher Hu introduced his student to Vinnie and then said, "Let’s thank Vinnie by showing him around."
The monastery was very quiet and peaceful. Inside one temple was a very large statue of Buddha. There were candles burning around it.
"Ah, I must stop and rest," said Teacher Hu. "Sheng will answer all your questions, Vinnie." Teacher Hu spoke quietly to his student for a moment.
While the two men were talking, Vinnie took out the photo. The picture was not glowing blue.
"It’s not this place then," he said to himself.
"What are you looking at?" asked Sheng.
"Oh, nothing," Vinnie said. He shoved the photo back into his pocket. "Are there many pagodas in Chang’an?"
"Quite a few," replied Sheng.
"I’m looking for one with animal statues in front of it," Vinnie began.
Sheng stared at him, confused.
"The statues have sharp teeth and big eyes," said Vinnie.
"Oh, you mean the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda!" cried Sheng.
Back in the street, Mandy held on tightly to the monkey. The trainer was coming toward them on his horse.
"Jinying! He’s getting close!" Mandy cried.
Mandy and Jinying ran down the busy street. Several uniformed men joined the chase behind the monkey trainer.
"Stop—in the name of the Emperor!" shouted one guard, holding a club.
Mandy and Jinying slowed down, gasping for breath. The monkey trainer also pulled up his horse.
"Who are those men?" asked Mandy.
"The Gold Bird Guards," panted Jinying. "They control traffic on the streets."
"What is the problem here?" a guard asked Mandy.
"She’s a thief!" yelled the trainer. "She stole my monkey!"
"Is this true?" asked the guard.
"That man was speeding, sir," said Jinying, pointing to the trainer. "In Chang’an, there is a strict penalty for those who speed on the roads."
"You were going very fast," the guard said to the trainer.
"But . . . but . . . ," the trainer stuttered. "What about my monkey?"
The monkey was clinging to Mandy’s shirt.
"Does this man speak the truth?" the guard asked in a threatening voice.
Mandy’s eyes filled with tears. She could not imagine what would happen to her and to the monkey.
"Sir, I . . . ," she began.
Jinying suddenly stood tall. "This girl has broken no law!" he said in a strong voice.
Another guard rode up and recognized the young man. "It’s Master Yuan Jinying!" he cried.
The guards all bowed to Jinying.
Jinying told the guards that Mandy was only trying to save the monkey. The monkey was still in Mandy’s arms.
"We will be on our way," Jinying said gently.
She followed Jinying as he walked away.
"What will happen to him?" Mandy asked. She looked back at the guards and the monkey owner.
"Nothing. I explained his cruelty," replied Jinying. "The guards agreed he should give up the animal."
"Thank you so much," Mandy said. The monkey looked happy.
"I know a place where this monkey will be safe," said Jinying. "The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda."
Mandy didn’t know Vinnie was going to the same place.
Teacher Hu told his student, Sheng, to take Vinnie there.
"Why is this pagoda called the Giant Wild Goose?" asked Vinnie.
"There were some monks who lived in that temple," began Sheng.

"They had no meat to eat. They wanted meat so badly that they prayed every day to Buddha. Finally, one day, a group of geese flew above them. Suddenly, the biggest goose got tired and fell to earth. The monks believed Buddha was angry. Because of their greed for meat, an innocent animal died. So they decided never to eat meat again."
"Wow," said Vinnie.
They arrived at the pagoda. Vinnie counted five stories, just like in the photo. Then he heard a familiar voice.
"Vinnie!" Mandy ran over to her brother.
"What is that?" Vinnie pointed to the monkey on her shoulder.
"Isn’t he cute?" asked Mandy.
Vinnie rolled his eyes. "Mandy," he said, "I think this is the right building."
He took out the photo, and it was glowing blue.
