"But we’re not standing in the right place," said Mandy.
Jinying and Sheng were talking.
"Who is that?" Vinnie and Mandy asked at the same time. They looked at each other and laughed.
"Mandy?" Jinying walked over to her. "Sheng says the monkey will be safe here."
"Good-bye, little friend," said Mandy, sadly.
"I must return home now," Jinying said. "But before I leave, I will stop to touch the stone lions for luck."
"Lions?" asked Mandy.

"Long ago, nearby kings wanted permission to trade on the Silk Road. So they gave lions to our emperor as gifts. Our people had never seen lions before," explained Jinying. "Now we put two stone lions in front of important buildings. They protect the building and bring good luck and happiness."
The children followed Jinying.
"The picture is glowing brighter," Vinnie said excitedly.

Jinying led them to the statues in front of the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda. One of the lions was a male, and the other was a female. They both were guarding the entrance to the pagoda. The picture glowed red.
"Thank you, Jinying," Mandy called out. The children fell down the dark tunnel.
Vinnie and Mandy opened their eyes, and two pairs of eyes stared back at them. The twins dropped their ice cream and began screaming.
"Oh no!" gasped Mandy. "I think they saw us!"
When the grown-ups came back, the twins told them everything.
"It was really bright," said Jordan, covering his eyes with his little hands.
Vinnie and Mandy held their breath. Then Dad smiled at the twins.
"What an imagination!" he laughed.
Jordan looked at Vinnie and Mandy. "Tell them about your book!" he cried.
"Come on, kids," interrupted Aunt Leah. "It’s nap time." She led them upstairs.
"What about a game of catch?" asked Uncle Wilson.
"Okay! Let me get my mitt," answered Vinnie. Mandy followed her brother.
"Whew! That was close!" she said.
"We have to be more careful," agreed Vinnie, looking for his baseball mitt. "Do you want to play?"
"No, I’m going to read," said Mandy.
Vinnie stared at his sister. "Are you planning to go on a photo trip without me?" he said suspiciously.
"You tried to go without me—three times!" she yelled back.
"Only twice!" Vinnie shouted at her.
Mandy ran up to the attic.
"No!" yelled Vinnie as he ran after her.
When Vinnie got to the attic he saw Mandy with the photo album. Vinnie grabbed it.
"Let go!" cried Mandy, still holding on. The children pulled the album back and forth. Then Vinnie let go. Mandy fell to the floor and dropped the album. It lay open to another page.
"Hey, this photo is different," said Mandy. She picked up the photo.
The picture showed a sandy wilderness. The sun looked very hot. The old man was in front of a cave. Just inside the cave was a glowing object.
"I wonder what’s inside the cave?" Vinnie asked.
The photo glowed brighter.
"Looks like we’re going to find out," said Mandy.
The children fell down the dark tunnel and landed on warm sand. They could feel the heat right away.
"Oh, the sun is really hot," said Vinnie. He slowly opened his eyes.
"We’re in a sort of desert," she said, looking at the sandy ground.
All around them were short trees and small grassy areas too. It was very quiet.
"I’m not wearing much!" Vinnie cried. He was only wearing short pants made out of animal skin.
Mandy was wearing a top and a skirt made out of soft leather. She rubbed her hand against her skirt. "It feels very soft," she said.
Vinnie walked over to a tree and leaned against it. "Where do you think we are?"
"I don’t—" Mandy suddenly stopped. She covered her mouth.
"What is it?" Vinnie asked.
Mandy could not speak. She lifted a shaking finger at Vinnie. He heard a low growling noise.
Vinnie slowly turned his head.
"Argh!" he screamed as two growling hyenas ran toward him.
Vinnie was so scared he couldn’t move. Suddenly he felt a strong wind by his ear. An arrow flew by. One of the hyenas let out a cry, and the animals ran away.
"Vinnie!" Mandy ran to her brother.

"I’m okay," said Vinnie. "But who . . . ?" He stopped and stared at a young man holding a bow and arrow. He also wore an animal skin tied at his waist. He had six scars on his chest on his right side.
The man stared at the children for a long time. Then he said, "Where do you come from?"
"Our home is far away," replied Mandy. "We’re on a journey."
The man stared a bit longer. He seemed curious. "How long will your journey be?" he asked.
Vinnie and Mandy looked at each other.
"We don’t know," they answered.
The man motioned to them.
"Let us go to the village," he said. "You will be safe there." He walked away.
Mandy looked at her brother. "What do we do?" she said.
"Let’s follow him," replied Vinnie. "I don’t think he’ll hurt us. After all, he saved me from those scary wolves."
"They were hyenas," said Mandy.
The children ran after the man.
"Excuse me," said Vinnie, "where are we?"
"This is the Kalahari Desert, home of my people," he replied.
"Who are your people?" asked Mandy.
"We are the Ju/’hoansi," he said. "I am Kashe. What are your names?"
The children introduced themselves.
Kashe stopped in front of an open area. "Welcome to our village," he said, pointing to ten small huts. The huts were made out of sticks and grass.
"Kashe!" a woman called out. "You went hunting for food, but you bring us children."

The villagers all stopped what they were doing. They surrounded the children. The men were dressed like Kashe. The women also wore animal skins. Most of them had jewelry around their necks. Some wore brightly colored bands around their heads.
Kashe introduced the children to everyone. Then the crowd wandered away. But one curious young girl remained.
"Twi!" a woman called to the girl. "We have work to do."
"Yes, Mama," Twi called back. Then she turned to Mandy. "Will you come with us?" she asked.
"Where?" said Mandy.
"To gather mongongo nuts," said Twi. She looked up at the bright sun. "We should have left a while ago. I can tell it will be hot today."
"But it’s hot already!" cried Mandy.
Twi laughed. "This is not hot. It is still early in the day."
Mandy wiped her forehead. "It’s going to get hotter?" she thought.
"Come with me, Vinnie," Kashe said.
"Where are we going?" asked Vinnie.
Kashe gave Vinnie a bow. "We must return to the hunt," he replied.
"Cool!" yelled Vinnie.
Mandy and Twi joined some women, who greeted Mandy with smiles. Twi gave Mandy a cloth bag to hang over her shoulder.
"You put the nuts in here," said Twi.
The women headed off into the bushes. Mandy looked for Vinnie, but he had already left.
The women and girls reached some tall trees and then split up. Each woman worked under a tree, collecting the nuts on the ground.
"I’ll be over there," grinned Twi, pointing to a nearby tree.
"Wait! What do the nuts look like?" cried Mandy.
"Look," smiled Twi, as she picked up an egg-shaped nut. "This is the mongongo." Then Twi left Mandy to gather the strange nuts.
"Well," thought Mandy, "at least I’m not doing anything horrible like hunting."
Meanwhile, Vinnie was watching Kashe as he reached into a small cloth bag.
"Pay attention," said Kashe, holding up an arrow. "We will add the poison now."
"Poison?" asked Vinnie, nervously.
"Hold this arrow, Vinnie," said Kashe.
Vinnie held the arrow carefully.
"These are beetle larvae," explained Kashe, holding up some small yellow things. "They contain poison."
He squeezed some liquid from one larva. Then he put it on the arrow.
"We shoot the animal and the poison goes into the blood," said Kashe. "Soon, the animal dies."
Another man named Gau came running up. "We have spotted the birds," he said.
"Do you shoot birds?" asked Vinnie.
Kashe shook his head. "Birds circle in the sky above a dying animal. We are close to an animal we shot yesterday. We must go and carry it back to the village."
Meanwhile, Mandy was thinking that picking nuts wasn’t much fun.
"Mandy, how many have you got?" Twi walked over to her. Twi’s bag was overflowing with nuts. Mandy only had a few.
"How did you get so many so fast?" asked Mandy.
"We learn how to pick mongongo nuts when we are very young," said Twi, grinning. "Watch!"
She bent down. Her hands moved quickly back and forth on the ground. Then she stood up, smiled, and used only her toes to pick up a nut.
Mandy laughed and clapped her hands. "That’s amazing!"
The other women gathered together and emptied their bags on the ground.
"The nuts are heavy. So we crack the shells off here," explained Twi. "Then our bags are much lighter for the journey home."
"Good idea!" said Mandy.
"Oh, while we’re here," Twi said, "I want to show you something."
Mandy followed Twi to a small cave. At the opening, they found a rock with some paintings on it.
"These are drawings my ancestors made," said Twi. "They tell a story about our people."
Mandy could see animals and dancing men on the rock. The men had animal features too. Some had horns. Others had lion’s legs.
"This is the object in the photo!" shouted Mandy.
"What do you mean?" cried Twi.
"So why am I still here?" thought Mandy.
Vinnie and Kashe were walking through the desert shrubs with Gau. The other men were hunting in a different area.
"It is not good to hunt with too many people," explained Kashe. "Animals are very clever. They have good ears and can quickly smell hunters."
Vinnie was scared. Kashe had given him a bow and arrow. But Vinnie did not know how to use it. He remembered the hyenas.
"How often do you hunt?" asked Vinnie.

"When we need food," replied Kashe. "Usually we start early in the morning. But today I saw you and Mandy. I had to return to the village." Suddenly he stopped. On the ground was a pile of something that smelled bad.
"Is that what I think it is?" asked Vinnie. He pinched his nose at the smell.
Kashe and Gau looked at each other.
"The animal dung is fresh. They are close," Kashe said.
"Kashe, look here." Gau pointed to another pile of dung.
"This is also fresh," Kashe replied. "That is not good."
Vinnie was curious. "What is it?" he asked.
Kashe pointed to the first pile and said, "That dung is from antelope." Then he pointed to the second pile. "But this belongs to a rhino."
Kashe got his bow and arrow ready. "We must be very careful," he said, as he slowly walked on. "Rhinos are very dangerous."
Back at the village, Mandy and the women poured their shelled nuts into a big pile. Women brought out pots.
"Let’s get water," Twi said to Mandy. She held two white balls and gave one to Mandy. It had a funny smell.
"What’s this?" Mandy asked.
"It’s the shell of an ostrich egg," Twi said. "We use it to carry water for our meals."
Twi led Mandy to a water hole. It contained only a little bit of water.
"Is this all the water you have?" Mandy asked. She wondered how these people could live with so little water.
Twi nodded. "Our people are travelers, like you and Vinnie. We journey to find water." She bent down and scooped some water into the eggshell. "This water is almost gone, so we will be moving soon."
Mandy filled her eggshell and followed Twi to the village.
Vinnie was careful to stay close to Kashe. Suddenly Kashe and Gau ran behind a large bush. Vinnie joined them. Kashe pointed ahead.
"Oh!" Vinnie gasped.

He saw a peaceful herd of antelope and zebras. Just then Kashe and Gau stood up and aimed their arrows. The animals sensed the hunters and started to run. The men shot their poison arrows. One hit an antelope, which kept running. Kashe and Gau chased after it. So did Vinnie.
The women put the mongongo nuts into the pot with water and some roots. They used a long stick to mash everything together. As Mandy watched, her stomach began to growl.
"You can do this," said Twi. She gave Mandy the stick. Mandy stirred the dark red mixture.
"When the hunters return," said Twi, "we can all enjoy the meal."
Vinnie ran fast until he finally caught up with Kashe and Gau. They were standing in front of the fallen antelope and smiling.
"Good fortune!" Kashe said to Vinnie. "Usually antelopes can run for a whole day before the poison spreads. This one was weak."
Other hunters appeared from different directions.
"Did the boy get it?" asked a man.
Kashe turned to Vinnie and smiled. "Perhaps your arrow got this one, Vinnie."
Vinnie shook his head. "I was too scared to shoot." He showed them his arrow.
Kashe stuck his chest out. Vinnie noticed those six scars on his right side.
"In our tribe, you become a man after your first kill," said Kashe. "Look here." He pointed to one of his scars. "I got this when I was your age."
"Did an animal attack you?" asked Vinnie.
Kashe laughed. "No, I killed a male antelope. That’s why I have scars on my right side. If it had been a female, I would have scars on my left side."
Kashe then pointed to his eyes. "These scars make me see clearer. The ones on my arms help me shoot better. The scars on my chest help me to stay calm when hunting."
"Didn’t it hurt?" asked Vinnie. He shivered at what might have made those scars.
Kashe laughed again. "Pain is part of growing up."
Suddenly Gau shouted loudly. He pointed toward the trees. Two large black rhinos were stamping their feet.
"We must leave," warned Kashe. "We have disturbed them."
Gau and Kashe began to slowly walk backward. But the angry animals charged the group.
"I didn’t know rhinos ran so fast!" cried Vinnie as he ran with the men. Vinnie’s heart was racing too. Suddenly he heard a scream.
"Gau!" shouted Kashe, looking around. Gau lay on the ground. A rhino had slashed Gau’s leg with his horn.
"We must get him to the village," said Kashe.
"Where are the rhinos?" Vinnie asked.
"They’re gone for now," said Kashe. "Quick, help me."
They carried Gau to the village. Kashe explained to everyone what had happened.
Gau was placed near a fire in front of one hut. He was in a lot of pain.
"Call the healer," ordered Kashe.
Frightened, Mandy ran to Vinnie.
"Did he say healer?" gulped Vinnie.
Vinnie remembered the healers from their Iroquois travels.

The villagers gathered around Gau. He groaned in pain. Suddenly some women appeared, howling and screaming. The villagers began to clap loudly and chant. A man wearing bracelets on his wrists and ankles jumped into the fire.
"Wow!" said Vinnie.

The man began dancing and jumped in and out of the fire. He waved his arms above his head and then moved over to Gau. The healer placed his hands on Gau’s leg. The villagers clapped harder, and the women screamed louder.
"Oh, Twi, I’m scared!" cried Mandy.
"Shh, Mandy," whispered Twi.
"Yeah, Mandy, cool it," said Vinnie.
Soon, everything got quiet. Gau sat up, and Kashe walked over to him. The other villagers gathered around.
An old man was sitting close by. He was holding a rock and dipping his fingers into some kind of paint. He started drawing something on the rock.
"What’s he doing?" Mandy asked Twi.
"He is recording the healing on a rock," explained Twi. "His picture proves our healers have great power. We use these rocks to tell the story to our children."
"Stories?" asked Vinnie.
"Yes," said Twi. "Sometimes we have bigger stories to tell. So we put them on bigger rocks."
"Come," Twi’s mother called. "We have delicious mongongo!" Everyone cheered. Twi brought over two bowls for Vinnie and Mandy.
Mandy took a sip. "It’s wonderful!" she said.
Kashe came over and sat beside Vinnie and Mandy. They all watched some boys playing a game. They were throwing long wooden sticks at a round target made out of woven grass.
"The little ones are already practicing to be good hunters," said Kashe. "One day you’ll be a fine hunter too, Vinnie."
"Vinnie," said Mandy, "I think I know what the glowing thing is."
"What is it?" asked Vinnie. He didn’t want to take the photo out. All the villagers would see it.
"It’s a rock. I saw it when I was gathering mongongo nuts with Twi," Mandy said.
"But you didn’t return home," Vinnie pointed out.
She thought for a moment. "I know. It’s strange."
"You should get some rest," said Kashe, turning to the children. "We are moving our village tomorrow."
"Where?" asked Vinnie.
"To a place with fresh water," Kashe answered, and went inside a hut.
"Vinnie," Mandy whispered, "We can’t go with them—we have to get home!"
The children quietly left the village and went toward the cave. Nobody saw them leave. Vinnie took out the photo. It was glowing blue.
"We’re close," said Mandy. They walked over to the painted rock just inside the cave.
"This is it!" she said. She could see animals and dancing men.
Vinnie looked at the photo. "But why weren’t you sent home when you were here with Twi?"
"I don’t . . ." Mandy began. "Wait—maybe because we always have to go photo traveling together!" she cried.
The photo was glowing red.
"That’s it!" shouted Vinnie.
The children fell down the dark tunnel.
Vinnie and Mandy were glad when the twins left. But two minutes later, Mom brought bad news.
"Get changed," Mom said excitedly. "We’re going to an art gallery!"
"What?" Vinnie and Mandy said together.
"It’s at the college," said Mom. "It’ll be a good experience for you."
"But, Mom . . . ," Mandy cried.
"I don’t want to go," said Vinnie.
Mom gave them a long stare. The children knew what that meant. Vinnie and Mandy went up the stairs, dragging their feet.
"I can’t believe this. I don’t want to go to a boring art gallery," said Vinnie.
"Well, it might be fun," said Mandy, trying to sound cheerful.
The children reluctantly went to their bedrooms to get dressed. Vinnie was combing his hair in front of the mirror when Mandy knocked on his door.
"Are you ready?" she asked when he opened the door.
Vinnie quickly pulled her into his room. "Hey, we have some time," he said. "Why don’t we go on a trip before leaving?"
"Okay, then at least something exciting will happen this afternoon," agreed Mandy.
The children ran up to the attic. The album was still on the bookshelf.
"Open it!" urged Vinnie.
"Kids! We’re leaving in one minute!" shouted Mom.

Mandy opened the album. In the next photo, the old man was standing with some people beside a table. On the table was an object that looked like a little tree. But all the branches formed a perfect egg shape. Light glowed from inside an opening at the top.
"What’s that? Is it a tree or an egg?" whispered Mandy.
"I’m not going to call you again!" They heard Mom’s footsteps on the stairs. She did not sound happy.

Vinnie and Mandy looked at each other. Mom’s footsteps got closer. Just as she flung open the attic door, Vinnie and Mandy started down the dark tunnel. The last thing they saw was their mom standing in the doorway, looking stunned.

Mandy fell first. She landed hard on a wooden surface. Vinnie fell nearby. They were in a large space with thick, dark curtains in front of them. Behind them was beautifully painted scenery. Through a small opening where the curtains met, the children could see bright lights. They heard loud clapping.
"It’s so noisy!" shouted Vinnie. He peeked between the curtains. "Uh-oh!" he cried.

The applause got louder, and suddenly, the curtain began to open. Vinnie and Mandy were on a stage! Vinnie grabbed his sister’s hand and quickly dragged her to the side of the stage. Loud applause broke out.
"Bravo! Bravo!" the audience cheered.

Vinnie and Mandy watched the opening curtain. The crowd was standing up, shouting and clapping. A beautiful dancer was at the front of the stage, bowing and blowing kisses. The audience was throwing roses at their favorite ballerina.
The beautiful ballerina gracefully stepped back from the front of the stage. She took one last bow as the curtain closed again and hid her from the audience.
Immediately, the children were surrounded by a swarm of people—dancers, costumers, and stagehands. Everyone ignored Vinnie and Mandy.
"Anna! Bravo! You were magical!" cried a nearby gentleman. He smiled at the ballerina as she walked toward him. She held an armful of roses. More flowers lay scattered on the stage.
"Bring them to my dressing room," ordered the ballerina, throwing the bundle of roses to Mandy.
"But I . . . ," Mandy began.
The dancer brushed past her.
A man shouted at Vinnie: "You! Collect all of Miss Pavlova’s flowers!" He shoved Vinnie out onto the stage. Someone pushed Mandy toward the dancer.
"Hurry up!" the ballerina ordered. Mandy followed her. She couldn’t see where Vinnie had gone.
In the ballerina’s dressing room, Mandy stood nervously by the door. Anna and the gentleman were arguing.
"You are my manager, Victor! I wanted to dance in my other ballet shoes!" she cried, stamping her feet.
"I’m sorry, Anna. Next time, I will bring all your shoes," Victor apologized.
They talked loudly and with so much passion. Mandy watched them fascinated. "Where had Vinnie and I landed?" she wondered.
"Girl! What are you staring at?" Anna was speaking to her.
"Oh, I’m sorry, ma’am," she apologized. "Your flowers . . ." Mandy held them out.
"Take them to my carriage and wait. You’re the new girl, right? Sergei said Tatiana was sick tonight." Then Anna waved her arm in a way that told Mandy to leave.
After collecting the flowers from the stage, Vinnie was given a broom.
"Are you new here?" asked a young boy. He was about Vinnie’s age and was already sweeping.
"I guess," replied Vinnie, wondering where "here" was.
"I’m Mikhail. What’s your name?" asked the boy.
Vinnie introduced himself. Both he and the boy were dressed in dark trousers and shirts.
"She’s a beautiful dancer," said Vinnie, starting up a conversation. He hoped Mikhail would reveal where they were.
"Anna Pavlova is Russia’s most famous ballerina," Mikhail said proudly. "She just came back from a tour of Europe and the United States."
"Russia!" Vinnie said to himself.
Meanwhile, Mandy was riding away in a carriage with Anna and Victor. As she looked back, Mandy gasped at the grand building. "What a gorgeous theater!" cried Mandy.
"The Mariinsky Theater has brought me much success," Anna said softly. She seemed happier now. She blew the theater a kiss.
"For your next tour," began Victor, "we will travel on the Trans-Siberian Railway to Vladivostok, and then we’ll go . . ."
Anna grew angry again. "What? I just got back! I need to rest!"
"But, Anna," Victor said calmly. "Your fans all across the motherland want to see you dance!"
Mandy looked out the window, amazed. "Vladivostok? We’re in Russia!" she thought.
Anna cried, "I will stay in St. Petersburg. I am tired, Victor! I will not discuss this anymore!"
Vinnie’s back felt stiff. He stretched and followed the other cleaners out of the theater.
"Good night, Vinnie!" Mikhail called out.
"Wait!" Vinnie cried. "Uh, I’m looking for a place to stay tonight. I have nowhere to sleep."
Mikhail looked at him kindly. "Let me ask Papa." He spoke to a man smoking a pipe nearby.
"We live simply, Vinnie," Mikhail’s father said, "but you are welcome. The czar does not care about his people. So we must take care of one another."
"Thank you," Vinnie said with relief. He hoped Mandy had a place to sleep too.
Mikhail’s home was very small, but clean. It was three rooms in an apartment building near the marketplace. Mikhail’s mother welcomed them with soup and some bread.
"This isn’t much," Mikhail’s mother said, handing Vinnie a thin blanket, "but it will keep you warm." Vinnie soon fell asleep next to Mikhail.
The next day, they ate hot cereal called kasha for breakfast. Afterward, Mikhail’s mother poured tea into three glasses and one cup."Have some tea," she said.
Vinnie reached for the cup, but Mikhail’s mother stopped him.
"Drinking tea from cups is only for women," she laughed. "Russian men drink from glasses."
"Today is a big day!" said Mikhail’s father. "We’re going into the Imperial Palace of the czar."
"Why are you going there?" Vinnie asked.
"We have a special delivery to make," Mikhail replied. "Today is the presentation of the Easter gift. Papa and Uncle Anton are in charge of the flowers."
"What gift?" asked Vinnie.
Mikhail chuckled, "Why, the same gift that is given to the royal family every Easter!"
Vinnie had no idea what the gift was, but he pretended to know: "Oh, that is exciting. I can’t wait to see it."
"I’ll need help," said Mikhail’s father. "Anton and I can’t carry all the baskets of flowers."
Mikhail and Vinnie were eager to help. They wanted to see inside the palace too.
Meanwhile, Mandy had slept in a small servant’s room in Anna Pavlova’s house. First thing in the morning, Mandy had to take Anna her breakfast. Then Mandy helped the ballerina dress.
"I’m going to have lunch at the palace," she told Mandy. "You will come with me. Make sure the ruffle at the bottom of my dress stays clean." Anna pointed to the hem of her long dress.
When Mandy and Anna arrived at the palace, Mandy was speechless. It wasn’t just the size of the palace. It was how luxurious it was! The palace reminded her of Versailles in France.
Four palace guards came out to meet the carriage. Anna gracefully got out. Mandy was close behind, but she wasn’t so graceful. Mandy tripped on the hem of the ballerina’s dress.

Vinnie and Mikhail rode down the streets of St. Petersburg. The buildings were grand but old, and birds had built nests in the stone cracks. Vinnie saw that many people were poor. Children with sad, hungry eyes were in the streets. The old people sitting in front of the buildings looked tired and sick.
"People don’t look very happy," Vinnie said to Mikhail.
Mikhail nodded sadly. "Many people are angry at the royal family. The czar does not know how people really live."
"Mikhail," his father said, sharply. "Keep silent."
"But, Papa, even you said that change must happen!" Mikhail cried.
"We do not speak of these matters in the street," Mikhail’s father said nervously. "The czar’s spies are everywhere."
Inside the palace, Mandy was in trouble. The ruffle of Anna’s dress was muddy and stained.

"Clean this up now!" said Anna. She pulled the ruffle off her dress and handed it to Mandy. Then a servant led the ballerina down a hallway. As she walked off, Anna’s dress looked shorter and very plain.
Another servant motioned to Mandy: "Come to the kitchen! We’ll clean it there."
In the halls and rooms of the palace, everything shone. It was as if gold had been poured on the walls. The furniture was covered in thick purple and red velvet. Crystal lights sparkled.
"First time in the Winter Palace?" asked the servant.
"Yes, it’s beautiful," Mandy exclaimed.
"The royal family is usually here only in winter. But this year, the Romanovs are staying longer," explained the servant.
"Romanov . . . that name sounds familiar," Mandy thought.
Outside the kitchen, they passed delivery men carrying baskets of flowers.
A little while earlier, Vinnie had arrived at the palace. In the square outside, he unloaded baskets of flowers from a wagon.
"Wow! Look at how big the palace is!" he cried, staring.
"Come, we have work to do," said Mikhail’s father.
Inside, Vinnie passed a servant and a little girl carrying some wrinkled fabric. The tall basket of flowers blocked his vision, and he didn’t see that it was Mandy.

Mandy cleaned the ruffle as best as she could. Then she left the kitchen to take it to Miss Pavlova. She paused in a hall to look at a royal family portrait. In the painting, there were five children—four girls and a young boy."Romanov . . . ," Mandy said aloud, looking more closely at the picture.
"Awful, isn’t it?" said a girl a bit older than Mandy who was standing nearby. She wore a pink dress with matching ribbons in her hair.
"I think it’s a fine picture," Mandy said nervously.
"It doesn’t look like me at all," the girl complained playfully.
Mandy looked at the picture again. This girl must be the one sitting to the right of the boy. "You do look better in real life," admitted Mandy.
The girl looked curiously at Mandy. Then she said, "I like you. You’re very honest."
Mandy smiled. "I’m Mandy. I need to find Miss Pavlova. Do you know where she is?"
"Yes. She is with my parents," replied the girl. "My name is Anastasia."

73.title: Princess Anastasia and the Royal Family

paragraphs.text: Vinnie was tired from unloading so many flowers. As he rested in the empty wagon, he saw a side door of the palace open. A bearded man in dark clothes stepped out. He was speaking with another man. Vinnie sank down in the wagon, hiding.
"Rasputin, the Russian people are angry," said the bearded man’s companion. "They want the czar to pay attention to them!"
"I agree," said Rasputin. "But what can I do?"
"The people are desperate," the other man said sadly. "I’m afraid they will rise up and hurt the royal family."
The men walked away, and Vinnie got out of the wagon.
"Who is Rasputin?" Vinnie wondered, heading back into the palace.

Inside, Anastasia was telling Mandy about her older sisters. "They’re so annoying, really. All they care about is their powder and lipstick. I think they look like clowns," she said. "Do you have any sisters?"
"No, only a brother," Mandy replied. Suddenly, she missed Vinnie.
"I have a brother too. Alexei," Anastasia’s voice softened. "He’s a joy. Have you seen our piano room?"
"No, but Miss Pavlova . . . ," Mandy began, holding the ruffle.
Anastasia took the ruffle and stopped a servant passing by. "Take this to Miss Pavlova. Tell her I needed Mandy’s assistance," she said.
Anastasia linked her arm through Mandy’s. "Now, for the piano room!"
Meanwhile, Vinnie had found Mikhail in the kitchen drinking a glass of water.
"What are these flowers for again?" asked Vinnie.
"Today the royal family will receive another Fabergé egg. They get one every Easter," explained Mikhail. "The czar has a big feast to celebrate the new egg."
"What’s so great about an egg?" asked Vinnie.
"This is not an ordinary egg," laughed Mikhail. "It is a work of art made of jewels and gold. You have to see it to believe it."
At that moment, Anastasia was showing Mandy a cabinet filled with Fabergé eggs. Each egg was decorated according to a different theme.
"This egg was special," Anastasia said, pointing to a gold egg with a miniature golden carriage beside it. "My father gave this to my mother in 1897. That was the year he became the czar of Russia."
Mandy was fascinated. She looked at some other eggs. One had a crown on top that was covered in rubies and diamonds.
"Turn the pearl button on the side," ordered Anastasia.
Mandy obeyed. The crown rose and three small picture frames popped out.
"Here’s Papa, and Olga and Tatiana, my two eldest sisters," explained Anastasia.
"So each egg has a surprise in it," remarked Mandy.
Anastasia nodded. "We are getting a new egg today!"
Suddenly, Mandy remembered the egg-shaped object in the photo. "I must be in the right place," she thought.
Anastasia led Mandy to another room in the palace. Suddenly, Mandy noticed a familiar figure holding some flowers.
"Vinnie!" she shouted. He turned around and smiled.
"Mandy!" called Vinnie. He ran over to his sister.
Mandy introduced Vinnie to her new friend.
"You’re Princess Anastasia?" asked Vinnie.
"Yes, but just call me Anya," she said.
Vinnie turned white. But before Mandy could say anything, a voice interrupted. "Your highness, the Fabergé egg is here. We will begin the celebration soon."
"Rasputin!" thought Vinnie.
"Go about your duties," ordered Rasputin, pointing to Vinnie and Mandy. Then in a kinder voice, to Anastasia he said, "Go to your parents, Princess."
"Rasputin, you can’t tell me what to do!" cried Anastasia.
"You will listen, little one," he said. "I am your mother’s closest advisor. Obey me!"
Anastasia stamped her feet and walked off with Rasputin.
"Something bad is going to happen," Vinnie whispered to Mandy.
"How do you know?" asked Mandy. "What are you talking about?"
"I can’t believe you don’t get it!" Vinnie nearly shouted. "She’s Princess Anastasia! Don’t you remember the movie we saw?"
Mandy grabbed Vinnie’s arm. "The Romanovs!" she said. "Now I remember. The whole family gets murdered. We have to do something!" The horror of it made Mandy cry.
Vinnie held his sister’s hands. "Mandy, we can’t change history," he said sadly.
At that moment, two men in military uniforms walked by. They were carrying a gold box on a red cushion. Nearby, some servants whispered in excitement.
"That must be the new egg," said Vinnie.
The men carried the box into the palace reception room. They left the door slightly open. Vinnie and Mandy peered through.
In the reception room, the royal family stood near a small table. Anna Pavlova was there too. Rasputin stood next to the czarina. The czar took the box and pulled out a green colored egg.
"It looks like a tree!" cried Anastasia. The egg was supported by a short stick and covered in leaves made of jade. The tree’s fruit were colorful jewels.
Vinnie took out the photo: it was glowing blue.
"What’s this?" said the czarina, touching a lever on the side of the egg. Suddenly, the top of the tree opened. A little bird popped out as a melody filled the room. Everyone clapped.
"The photo!" Mandy whispered. The object in the photo was the bird. It was glowing red. Just as Mandy closed her eyes, she saw Anastasia wink at her.
The children fell down the dark tunnel. The next thing they knew, they were home in the attic again.
Mom stood in the doorway.
"My eyes! What was that light?" she shouted.
Vinnie and Mandy looked at each other. They were in trouble.
After the art gallery, Mom wanted some answers. "What’s going on in the attic?" she demanded.
The children looked at each other.
"What was that light?" asked Mom. "And that book?"
"We found some old books and a photo album," Mandy started to explain, but Vinnie glared at her.
"Hmmm," said Mom, suspiciously. "Well, that attic does have to be cleaned out."
"We can do it," said Vinnie, hoping to change the subject.
"Okay, put everything into boxes," said Mom. "Who knows? Something valuable might be up there."
Mom went into the kitchen.
"That was close!" Mandy sighed.
"Why did you tell her about the album?" Vinnie asked, annoyed.
"I wasn’t going to lie," protested Mandy.
Vinnie shrugged. "Well, let’s start cleaning the attic."
The children took some empty boxes upstairs. But the minute they got to the attic, they forgot about packing. Vinnie picked up the album and opened it.
"It’s beautiful," gasped Mandy at the photo.
The old man was sitting in a room. There was only a low table in the center of the floor. A vase of flowers was glowing on top of the table.
"It looks like . . . ," said Mandy.
Before she could finish her sentence, the children fell down the dark tunnel.
They landed inside a box of some kind. Red silk curtains covered the openings on either side. Whatever they were in, it was moving.
"Ouch!" Mandy slid and bumped against one side. Vinnie slammed into her. Then they both slid to the other side. Vinnie tried to stand up, but he banged his head against the low ceiling.
"We’re trapped in a moving box," cried Vinnie. He poked his head between the silk curtains. "Whoa!" he gasped.
Mandy looked too. "Wow!" she cried. "No wonder we’re bouncing around!"
The children were in a kind of little house on long poles. Two men were carrying them. Fancier and bigger houses on poles were behind and in front of them. Men with swords rode on horses everywhere.
"We’re in some kind of parade," cried Vinnie. "Look at that, Mandy!"
Vinnie pointed to two horsemen. They carried a flag with a symbol of two birds on it. People in the street bowed their heads as they passed.
Mandy ducked her head back inside and noticed their clothes.
"Look at what we’re wearing!" she cried.
They wore robes with wide belts around their waists.
"What’s this backpack thing?" Vinnie pointed to some folded fabric on Mandy’s back.
"I don’t know. But my legs feel crushed," complained Mandy. "I can’t move them around." Mandy tried to kick her legs, but her skirt was too tight.
"These look like Japanese kimono," said Vinnie.
"That’s it! We’re in Japan!" she exclaimed excitedly.
A little while later, the parade stopped.
"Let’s stay in here," whispered Mandy.

Vinnie nodded. The children hid behind the silk curtain and peeked outside. They were stopped in front of a large open gate. The same symbol of two birds was mounted above the gate. They heard someone walk up to their box.
"Uh-oh," whispered Vinnie. Between the curtains he saw a long skirt and a huge sword.
A man stuck his face through the curtains. "Come out," he ordered.
Outside, the children noticed the man was only about seventeen. His hair was pulled back and tied up. People carrying bundles stared at the children.
"Who are you?" the young man asked. The children introduced themselves.
At that moment, an older man in a dark purple kimono appeared. People bowed to him and backed away respectfully.
"What is the trouble, Haruki?" the man called out.
"Daimyo Masamune," Haruki said, bowing deeply. "These children were riding in one of your palanquins."
Daimyo Masamune stared at the children. Vinnie and Mandy gasped. He had only one eye!
"Is your father a missionary?" he asked. "A Dutch trader?"
Vinnie and Mandy were too scared to say anything.

"You’re afraid of me, aren’t you?" He touched his missing eye and laughed. "But it’s clear, you have traveled to Sendai on one of my palanquins. No one saw you. No one stopped you. You have courage, like a samurai."
"A samurai?" Vinnie finally spoke. "Cool!"
Daimyo Masamune said to Haruki, "You will look after them until I return. I must pay a visit to Shogun Ieyasu." Then he added, "Do not let them leave my castle."
"Come this way," said Haruki to the children, leading them through the gate.
"Are you a samurai?" asked Vinnie excitedly.
"I am being trained as a samurai," Haruki replied.
"What is a daimyo?" asked Mandy.
"A daimyo is the master of the samurai. Each daimyo is given a district by the shogun. The samurai living in that district serve the daimyo."
Then Mandy asked, "What is a shogun?"
"The shogun is what you Europeans call a general," explained Haruki.

Vinnie and Mandy walked along a high stone wall. The castle was huge with many houses and courtyards of different sizes. Haruki climbed two low steps that led into the first house. Vinnie and Mandy did the same. Sliding doors separated the different rooms. Vinnie peeked inside one of the rooms as they passed.
"Hey!" he shouted, staying behind.
"What is it?" asked Mandy.
"It’s a dragon!" Vinnie cried, pointing into the room.
Mandy’s eyes grew big. A large frightening creature stood there wearing a suit of armor.
Vinnie and Mandy stared at the scary creature.
"This is Master Masamune’s private room," snapped Haruki.
"What is that?" Vinnie pointed.
"It’s his armor," said Haruki.
The helmet was made of iron, and it had a scary mask. A big curved moon was on top.
"Do samurai wear that all the time?" asked Vinnie.
"Samurai only wear their armor during battle," explained Haruki. "But we always carry our swords." Haruki showed the children his sword. "Now follow me," he said, walking away quickly.
"Please go slower," Mandy cried. "I can only take small steps."
Haruki slowed down. His kimono was not tight around the legs like Mandy’s.
"Why is my kimono so tight?" Mandy asked.
"The kimono trains women not to step too fast or too far," explained Haruki.
Haruki slid open a door to a room.
"Stay here until I return," he said, closing the door.
Mandy admired a hanging scroll on the wall. Vinnie played with the sliding door.
"I wish we had doors like this at home," he remarked, opening the door wide.
Outside, three men walked by in silence. They walked to another house and crawled through a small door.
"I’ll bet they’re samurai too!" said Vinnie, excited. "Let’s see what’s going on."
"Bowing to enter is a sign of respect," said one samurai, as the children crawled through the door too.
In the room, the samurai were sitting very still on straw mats. There was a space beside one of the samurai close to the door.
"Let’s sit there," whispered Vinnie, pointing.
A man greeted everyone, and the samurai bowed to the floor. Then the man took a cloth and began slowly wiping a small teacup.
"It looks like he’s going to serve tea," said Mandy.
"It sure takes a long time," said Vinnie, yawning.
The man cleaned each teacup and spoon. Next he opened a small bowl and took some tea from it. Then he put the tea into a cup. His movements were graceful and slow.
"My legs hurt," complained Vinnie. He stretched his leg and accidentally kicked the samurai next to him. The samurai did not even notice.
The man serving the tea now poured water into the cup. Then he quickly stirred the tea. Vinnie began to massage his legs. Another samurai gave Vinnie a stern look.
"Be still, Vinnie," whispered Mandy.
"Let’s get out of here," said Vinnie. He quietly slid the small door open and Mandy crawled out. When it was Vinnie’s turn, his kimono got stuck in the door.
"Help!" he cried.
Everyone in the room turned and stared.
Smiling nervously, Mandy pulled her brother free and slid the door shut.
The children stood outside the door and looked around.
"Which house did Haruki put us in?" asked Vinnie.
"The doors all look the same," said Mandy.

The children walked around trying to find their way back. But they were lost. Soon the smell of cooking led the children to a kitchen. Servants were busily preparing a meal. One woman saw them. She was standing over a large pot of steaming rice on a stone stove.
"Is the tea ceremony over already?" she asked.
Mandy shook her head and asked, "How long does it usually last?"
"Two to four hours," the woman replied.
"Two hours? I’m glad we got out of there," said Vinnie.
Mandy was looking out a small window. "A path leads around the kitchen. It might take us to the front entrance. We can find the house from there."
The children stepped outside and walked down the path. But it led them away from the kitchen and into a forest.
"We’re really lost now," said Vinnie, realizing how far they had walked.
"My feet hurt," said Mandy. They had taken their shoes off at the house. Mandy sat down on a rock and rubbed her bare feet.
"What should we do?" asked Vinnie.
He sat beside her. A tree branch cracked nearby.
"Who’s there?" Vinnie said.
A young girl stepped out of the trees. She was not wearing a kimono but a gray colored top, pants, and straw sandals. She was holding a basket full of flowers.
"That outfit looks much more comfortable," Mandy said to herself. She looked at her tight kimono.
"I am Seiko," the girl said shyly. "Where did you come from?"
"From Daimyo Masamune’s house," answered Vinnie.
"Excuse me," Mandy interrupted. "Where can we get some shoes?"
"Come with me," she said. She giggled and covered her mouth.
The children followed Seiko and soon they came to a busy street. Farmers pushed their carts down the road. Women in colorful kimonos tiptoed by, whispering and giggling.
"Is this your first time in Sendai?" asked Seiko.
"Yes," replied the children. They stared at everything around them. One side of the street had only bookstores. Shops on the other side sold only things made of straw.
"This is like China! It’s easy to find what you want," said Vinnie.
Seiko took them to a shop selling straw hats, mats, and shoes.
"This is my aunt’s shop," said Seiko, handing the children two pairs of straw sandals. "Do they fit your feet?"
The sandals fit perfectly, but they looked funny with the children’s silk kimono.
After they put on their sandals, Mandy realized something. "Seiko, we have no money to buy these," she said.
"It is a gift," said Seiko. She said good-bye to her aunt and picked up her basket of flowers. They went back onto the street.
"Did you come to Sendai with Shogun Ieyasu?" asked Seiko.
"Who’s he?" asked Vinnie, forgetting about the general.
Seiko looked at him strangely and said, "You do not know Shogun Ieyasu?"
"Well, oh sure," said Vinnie nervously.
"The shogun has come a long way to see Daimyo Masamune," said Seiko.
"Why?" asked Mandy.
"The shogun likes to visit all the daimyos in every district," she said, "to make sure they are obeying his orders."
"What’s going on over there?" Vinnie pointed to a crowd buying colorful strips of paper.
"People are getting ready for the Star Festival," Seiko said. "Sendai celebrates the festival better than any other town!"
"Why are they decorating those trees?" Mandy noticed bamboo trees along the street with shiny pieces of paper hanging from their branches.
"People write their wishes on paper and then tie them to the trees," explained Seiko. "The wind carries their wishes away and makes them come true."
Seiko turned into a small street off the main road. The children followed. They finally came to a narrow road with two-story buildings on each side.
"This is where I live," said Seiko.
Bright and colorful fabrics hung from poles along the rooftops. They swayed with each gentle breeze.
"What is this place?" asked Vinnie.
"It’s my home and a dye factory. My family and another family all work together. We make the most beautiful kimono in all of Sendai," Seiko said proudly.
She took them inside her home. Seiko’s parents and her brother were stirring the dyed cloth in large wooden vats.
"The flowers I picked will be used to dye the fabric," said Seiko. She handed the flowers to her father.
"What kind of flowers are they?" asked Mandy.
"They are called safflowers," said Seiko.
Mandy touched the dyed fabric. It felt soft and smooth. Seiko’s mother spoke to her daughter.
"My mother will bring you some food and drink," said Seiko.
"Thank you," said Vinnie. He remembered the rice at Master Masamune’s house. It had looked very good.
A few minutes later Seiko’s mother appeared with two bowls on a tray.
"Is that rice?" Vinnie asked eagerly.
Seiko’s mother bowed to them. "I apologize. Only samurai are allowed to have rice. I can only offer porridge."
Vinnie felt embarrassed for wanting rice. He took the bowls and bowed to Seiko’s mother. "This looks delicious!" he said. "Thank you very much."
Vinnie and Mandy stayed awhile to watch Seiko’s parents dye the fabrics.
"I’ll take you to Daimyo Masamune’s home now," said Seiko.
When they reached the daimyo’s house, Seiko said good-bye at the front gate.
"Thanks for everything," said Vinnie, pointing to his sandals.
"Come and visit again," said Seiko. Then she bowed and left.
"Do you think Haruki will be looking for us?" asked Vinnie.
"I hope he doesn’t get in trouble," said Mandy.
As they walked up to the house, the children heard metal clanging. The noise was coming from the other side of the house.
"Let’s have a look," said Vinnie. Sighing loudly, Mandy followed.
The children came to a courtyard filled with samurai, old and young. Some were teaching; others were training. A few samurai practiced with swords. Another group was learning to use a bow and arrow.
"There you are!" a familiar voice called out. It was Haruki. "I was looking everywhere for you."
"We’re sorry," the children apologized. Mandy explained what happened.
Haruki bowed his head and said, "Thank you for coming back. Daimyo Masamune would have been very angry with me."
The samurai suddenly stopped their training at the sound of horses. Daimyo Masamune had returned home.
"Haruki, did you take good care of our guests?" he asked, approaching them.
Haruki bowed his head.
"We were watching the samurai training," said Vinnie enthusiastically.
Daimyo Masamune motioned for Vinnie and Mandy to follow him.
"A samurai’s training is not only about weapons," he said. He took them to a smaller courtyard full of red maple trees.
"It’s beautiful!" cried Mandy.
Then Daimyo Masamune led them into a room next to the courtyard.
"Isn’t this in the photo?" asked Vinnie. He took out the photo and looked at it.
Daimyo Masamune stood in front of a vase on a small table. In the vase were three stems that formed a triangle. Two were flowers. He gently picked up a flower lying on the table.
"A true warrior must have perfect control," he said, putting the flower in the vase.
"We must have peace in our heart." Then Daimyo Masamune picked up a pine stem.
"Mandy, the photo is glowing blue!" Vinnie whispered.

Daimyo Masamune’s flower arrangement was very lovely. He pointed to one flower and said, "This stands for the sacred mountain." Pointing to another, he said, "And this is the river." Then he pointed to a white flower in the middle. "And this is the mist that unites the river and the mountain. Nature is one." Daimyo Masamune closed his eyes.
The flower arrangement in the photo glowed red.
"We’re going home," whispered Vinnie, grabbing his sister’s hand.
The children fell down the tunnel and were back in the attic.
Vinnie and Mandy were in the attic putting old books into boxes. Their father popped his head in the door.
"How’s it going?" he asked cheerfully. He stepped into the room and began to measure a wall.
"Dad, what are you doing?" asked Vinnie.
"Just planning some changes," he replied, writing in a notebook.
"Changes?" Mandy asked, worried.
"The attic is going to become my new den," said Dad.
"Your den? Why?" the children cried.
"Oh, I just need a little space to myself," he explained.
"Can’t you use the basement?" said Vinnie, a bit rudely.
"It’s too damp down there," Dad said. "What’s wrong with the attic? You’re not hiding something up here, are you?"
"Of course not, Dad," laughed Mandy.
Dad put his notebook in his pocket. "Once you clear this space out, I’ll start moving in," he said. He went downstairs, whistling happily.
"What are we going to do?" asked Mandy.
"We still have some time," said Vinnie. "But let’s not waste another moment."
He went and got the photo album.
"Look, Mandy," he said.
In the picture, the old man was standing in front of a large elm tree by a building. Something was sticking out of its branches on a long pole. It was glowing.
"What do you think this is?" asked Mandy.
"We’re about to find out!" said Vinnie, closing his eyes.
The children fell down the dark tunnel.
"Ow!" cried Vinnie.
"Oh!" yelled Mandy.
Vinnie landed on a damp surface. Mandy landed nearby. The air smelled of the ocean. They were on a long, wide pier.
"Are you okay?" Vinnie asked, opening his eyes.
"Yes," Mandy answered. She sat up and looked around, rubbing her arm.
The pier was in the harbor of a city. Brick and wooden buildings lined narrow streets. She could see a white church tower in the distance.
"It looks like we’re in a seaport," she said. "I wonder where?"
Several tall-masted ships were tied to the pier with heavy rope. One ship was just coming in to dock.
"I can see the ship’s name," Mandy said. " The Liberty. "
Vinnie pointed. "It looks like the men over there are waiting for the ship."
Suddenly, the children heard marching feet. They turned around. Soldiers wearing red coats and black hats were heading toward the ship in a line. They held long guns.
"The Redcoats!" shouted a man on the dock. Everyone turned to watch the soldiers approach.
"Who are they?" asked Vinnie nervously. "They look angry."
The Redcoats stopped and held their weapons in front of them. The leader stepped forward and spoke to one of the men on the dock.
"Vinnie! I think I know where we are!" Mandy almost shouted. "The Redcoats! Aren’t they the British Army?"
Vinnie stared at the soldiers.
"Their uniforms do look familiar . . ." He paused. "We’re still in America!"

Carefully, Vinnie and Mandy moved closer to the ship being tied to the dock. The Redcoat captain was speaking to a tall man in a black hat. He wore a long coat, pants that ended just below his knees, white stockings, and black shoes.
"Mr. John Hancock," the captain read from a paper, "by order of His Royal Highness, King George III of England, you are under arrest."
"What have I done?" John Hancock asked calmly.
"Your ship, The Liberty , is carrying illegal tea into Boston Harbor," said the captain.
Before John Hancock could say anything, the soldiers took him away. The men on the dock followed angrily. One of them saw Vinnie and Mandy and quickly walked over.
"What are your names?" he asked when he got close.
"I’m Vinnie, and this is my sister Mandy," said Vinnie bravely.
"Are you American patriots?" the man asked.
"Yes, sir!" Vinnie said proudly.
"Good," the man said. He took out a piece of paper and wrote something on it. "You must find John Adams and give this to him. Go quickly. No one will suspect you."
"Yes, sir." Vinnie saluted, but the man didn’t see. He had already moved away to rejoin the others.
"Vinnie! Why did you say that?" Mandy said. "We don’t even know who those men are!"
"John Hancock? John Adams? Come on, Mandy. We are in Boston. These are the founders of our country!" Vinnie said passionately. "Right now, America is under British rule. We must help."
"So what can we do?" she asked.
"Just as the man said, we must find John Adams," explained Vinnie.

The children walked down the busy Boston streets. Horses, carriages, and wagons were everywhere. Women were in simple cotton dresses. Men wore three-cornered hats. As they approached an intersection, Vinnie and Mandy heard shouting and clapping.
"What’s going on?" Vinnie wondered.
On the next street, a crowd was gathered in front of a man standing on a barrel. He looked excited and angry.
"Should we pay taxes to the British?" he shouted.
"No!" the crowd cheered.
"We have no vote! We have no one to speak for us in England!" the man continued.
People shouted loudly.
"The Redcoats take over our homes! We pay too much for our tea! We even pay too much to mail our letters!" cried the man.
"Who is he?" Mandy asked a boy standing nearby.
"That’s Mr. Keith, the grocer," said the boy.
"Why is he shouting?" asked Vinnie.

The boy stared at them. "You aren’t from Boston, are you?" he said. "King George signed the Stamp Act. The law makes us pay extra money, a tax, for everything we buy. Everyone is very angry about it."
"I never knew America was like this once," Mandy whispered to Vinnie.
The children introduced themselves to the boy.
"I’m Will," he said. "I’m going to my father’s workshop."
"Workshop?" asked Mandy.
"He’s a cooper," said Will. "I help him build barrels. What does your father do?"
"Well, right now he’s building a den," said Vinnie.
"A den?" asked Will, confused.
"Forget it, Will. Vinnie’s just joking," said Mandy.
The grocer had stepped down, and the crowd was breaking up.
"Well, the speech is over," said Vinnie.
"Will, we need your help," said Mandy. "We must find John Adams."
Will stopped smiling and stared at them. "Who sent you?" he asked suspiciously.
Vinnie explained what happened on the docks.
"You must see my father," said Will. "He knows where Mr. Adams is."
Vinnie and Mandy walked to Will’s father’s workshop.
It was in a large house where Will’s family lived. Strips of wood were stacked high outside the shop. Inside, a man was sitting on a bench. He was scraping a strip of wood with a two-handled knife.
"What’s he doing?" asked Mandy.
"That’s my dad. He’s shaping a strip of wood to fit a barrel," Will explained. "Next he’ll arrange all the strips inside metal hoops that will hold them together."
"Will! Are you ready to help your tired father?" laughed the man.
"These are my new friends, Vinnie and Mandy," said Will.
"Hello, children!" cried Will’s father. "Welcome to our home and shop."
"Father, Vinnie and Mandy have a special message for Mr. Adams," said Will.
Suddenly serious, his father looked at the children. "Let me see it," he said.
Vinnie shook his head. "I’m sorry, sir, but only Mr. Adams can see it."
Mandy looked at Vinnie proudly. He was taking his responsibility seriously.
"Will, take the children inside," said his father. "Then go to the silversmith and find Mr. Revere. He will help."

Will led Vinnie and Mandy through the house to a warm kitchen. In a large fireplace, a black pot was bubbling. The children saw more pots and pans hanging above the fireplace. Two little girls sat on the floor playing with cloth dolls and little teacups.
"These are my twin sisters, Margaret and Jane," said Will.
"Who are your friends, Will?" asked Will’s mother. She sat at a table peeling potatoes.
Will introduced Mandy and Vinnie, and then Mandy spoke to the girls.
"What are your dolls doing?" she asked.
"They are having a tea party," explained Margaret.
"But this tea is not from England," said Jane.
"British tea is very bad," said Margaret.
"Didn’t John Hancock get arrested for smuggling tea?" Vinnie whispered to Mandy.
Will interrupted them. "Stay here. I will be right back," he said. "My mother will look after you."
"Would you like some tea?" asked Jane, holding up a tiny teacup.

Will left to get Paul Revere, and Vinnie and Mandy stayed to help his mother pick apples. Several large apple trees grew in the backyard. Will’s mother gave them each a basket, and they all filled them with apples. As they worked, the children asked about England.
"A while ago, the British passed the Stamp Act," Will’s mother said.
"We heard something about that," said Vinnie.

"Everything we read—newspapers, magazines, books, even playing cards—must have a stamp. The stamp shows that a tax has been paid for it. Americans shouldn’t have to pay taxes to the British," she said with feeling.
"That’s not fair," said Mandy.
"Many people are upset," Will’s mother continued. "And many of us spoke up. Some Boston men formed a group called the Sons of Liberty."
"Are Mr. Adams and Mr. Hancock members?" asked Vinnie.
Will’s mother did not answer. She said, "It is a secret group. No one knows for sure who is a member. But we know they are fighting for America’s freedom."
"Is that why Mr. Hancock was arrested?" asked Mandy.
"I want to show you something," Will’s mother said in a direct way.
She carried her basket into the house and down to the basement. The children followed. The basement was filled with barrels of apples.
"Wow! What are you going to do with all these apples?" asked Vinnie.
"We make apple cider," she explained. "Our Boston apple cider is very popular in Europe. We ship it everywhere."
She proudly showed them a stack of clothes, neatly folded.

"See these clothes?" said Will’s mother. "Some women and I belong to our own group. We are called the Daughters of Liberty. We make all of our own clothes. We don’t buy any dresses from Britain. Boston families don’t want or need anything from Britain."
Just then, Will returned. "We need to go now," he said simply.
Vinnie and Mandy said good-bye to Will’s mother and his sisters. They followed Will to the center of town. Beautiful brick homes with stone steps lined the streets. Some houses also had offices.
They walked up to one office with a sign that read, "John Adams, Attorney." A servant opened the door.
"Will Coats to see Mr. Adams," Will told the servant.
They followed the servant into an office. It was beautifully decorated with polished wooden furniture. Portraits hung on the walls.
"Is Mr. Adams a famous attorney?" asked Mandy.
Will nodded and added, "He is also a fighter for freedom."
"And the second president of the United States," whispered Vinnie to his sister. Mandy giggled.
The servant led them to two men talking before a fireplace. They turned when the children walked in.
"Come in!" A man with a sharp, thin nose walked toward them. "I’m John Adams," he said, "and this is Paul Revere."
Vinnie and Mandy looked in awe at the men. They were two of the most famous figures in American history.

John Adams would become the second president of the United States. And Paul Revere would make a famous midnight ride from Boston to Lexington. He’d ride to warn of the first British attack in the American Revolution.
"I am told you have a message for me," said John Adams to Vinnie.
Vinnie trembled nervously as he gave him the paper. Both men read the note and spoke in low voices.
"Thank you for delivering this. John Hancock needs our help," said Paul Revere.
"Can I help?" asked Vinnie.
Adams patted Vinnie on the shoulder.
"You are very brave," he said. "In a few years, we hope you can enjoy the freedom we are fighting for."

Just then, there was excitement in the street. Vinnie and Mandy ran to a window and looked out. A man was calling out in a loud voice as he walked down the street. Another man was beating a drum. People were coming out of their houses and following them.
"Who is he?" asked Mandy.
"The town crier," explained Paul Revere. "He is announcing a town meeting."
"I think we should all attend," said John Adams.
The children followed the men out of the house.
Vinnie turned to Mandy. "I can’t believe we just met these famous people!" he said.

The townspeople gathered at a church and went inside. The place filled up quickly as people sat on the long, wooden benches. John Adams and Paul Revere walked to the front of the church. Will’s father had just arrived. Vinnie, Mandy, and Will sat with him.
"Welcome," said Adams. "We have many things to discuss. But first, most of you know what happened this morning."
"They had no right to arrest John Hancock!" someone shouted.
"We must do something, now!" yelled another.
Vinnie and Mandy listened and watched closely. Everyone was allowed to say what he or she felt.
"I say we should just pay the taxes," said one well-dressed man.
Angry voices burst out. "Are you loyal to the British?" shouted an old man.
"Let’s not question each other’s loyalty," said a young man. "We are all patriots!"
"Please, please!" cried John Adams, raising both arms. The room quieted down. "Americans believe in freedom of speech," he said.
People shouted in agreement.
"But the British have no right to treat us this way!" yelled a man in a red vest.
The room exploded in cheers.
"There will be a war soon," said Will’s father, shaking his head.
"Maybe not, Father," said Will. "The British might allow us to have our freedom."
Vinnie shook his head. "Your father is right, Will. There will be a war. Very soon."
Mandy looked all around. The faces in the room were angry. Everyone was ready to fight for freedom.
When the town hall meeting ended, people returned to their homes. Paul Revere and John Adams stayed behind speaking together. The children stayed close by.
"Paul, you know what to do," said John Adams.
Revere nodded and put on his hat. "It was nice meeting you," he said to the children and then left.
"Where is he going?" asked Vinnie.
"Mr. Revere takes important messages to New York and Philadelphia," explained Will. "That’s what I want to do someday."
"To be a messenger?" asked Vinnie.
"To be one of the Sons of Liberty," said Will seriously.
"Good-bye, children," said John Adams. "Never forget the value of freedom."
They all shook hands, and the children left.
As they walked down Boston’s streets, the daylight was fading.
"Come for supper. Mother is making meat stew," said Will.
"You have been so kind to us," said Mandy. "But we should go now."
"Where are we going?" Vinnie whispered to her.
"Thank you for everything," said Mandy to Will.
"Well, you know where I live," he said. "Visit some time. You can try our apple cider."
Waving good-bye, the children watched Will disappear down the street.
"That’s just great!" Vinnie sighed. "Without Will, how are we supposed to find this tree?" He took the photo out of his pocket.
Mandy was looking up the street. Two familiar figures were walking ahead of them.
"Vinnie, let me see the photo," said Mandy.
He showed it to her. The flag in the photo was glowing blue.
"There’s a big tree over there. It looks like this one," said Mandy.
Mandy followed the two figures, walking just behind them. Vinnie followed her. When they got to the corner, the children noticed a sign on the nearby elm tree.
"Can you read it?" asked Mandy.
Vinnie shook his head. "It’s too far."
The two figures walked into a grocery store. Vinnie ran up to the tree and quickly read the sign. Then he ran back to Mandy.
"It says, ‘The Tree of Liberty’," he gasped.

The two men reappeared. One of the men was Mr. Keith, the grocer. He held a long pole. The other man carried a red and white, bundled cloth. At the tree, they tied the cloth at the top of the pole; it was a flag! They lifted the flag high enough in the tree so it stuck out from the branches.
The grocer said, "The Sons of Liberty will meet tonight."
"Action will be taken," said the other man. Then he turned around. It was John Hancock.
"He’s been released!" Mandy nearly shouted.
"Mandy! The photo!" Vinnie pointed to the picture. Sticking out of the tree, the red and white flag was glowing brightly. It was time to go home.
The children’s eyes closed as they fell into the familiar dark tunnel.
Vinnie and Mandy sat talking in the living room. The children were nervous about Dad’s idea for his den.
"We have to go on as many photo trips as possible," said Mandy urgently. "After the attic becomes Dad’s den, we won’t be able to go anymore."
"I know," Vinnie said. "But now Dad is always in the attic. If only he would leave for a while . . ."
Loud barking interrupted the children. "Look who’s visiting," said Mom, walking through the front door. A black dog rushed in after her.
"Corky!" cried Vinnie, rubbing the dog’s head. Corky was the neighbor’s dog and very friendly.
"I thought I heard Corky’s bark!" said Dad, coming down the stairs. Corky jumped into his arms. "Good boy! Good Corky!" Dad patted the dog affectionately.
"We’ve been asked to watch Corky for a few hours," said Mom. "Our neighbor has a doctor’s appointment."
Dad loved dogs and wanted to get one, but Mom always said no.
"I have an idea," Dad said brightly. "Let’s take Corky to the park."
"Sounds good," agreed Vinnie. "I can take my bike."
Mandy stared hard at her brother. "Vinnie!" she said through clenched teeth.
"Mandy? Do you want to go too?" asked Mom.
"Uh, yes," Mandy said slowly. "But I have to get something from upstairs. Vinnie does too."
"I do?" Vinnie looked puzzled. Then he realized what Mandy meant. "That’s right! We’ll be right back."
Vinnie followed Mandy up to the attic.
"Sorry about that," he said, reaching for the album. "I didn’t catch on to your plan."
"We can go on a photo trip," said Mandy. "And still be back in time to play with Corky."
Vinnie opened the album to the next page. "Look at this one, Mandy," he said.
The old man was on a ship at sea. He stood near a large coil of rope. Three small round things rested on top of the coil.
"They look like rocks," said Mandy, examining the picture. Next to them, a wooden object glowed. "What could this be?"
"We’ll soon find out!" said Vinnie.
The children’s eyes closed, and they fell down the dark tunnel.
The children landed hard, and their fall echoed loudly. They were in a building with a high ceiling and large windows. The children lay between some wooden benches.
"I think we’re in a church," whispered Vinnie. He pointed to a large cross on the wall. There were statues of angels too.
"Look," said Mandy quietly. She pointed at two men standing together and talking. One man held a book close to his chest.
"Finally!" the man said. "The king and queen have provided the money for my journey. With your powerful family behind me, we’ll sail west to the Indies."
"My brothers and I support you fully, Master Columbus," said the other man.
"Columbus?" whispered Vinnie. "Is he Christopher Columbus?"
Vinnie and Mandy hid behind the church benches and watched the two men.
Columbus put his book down and hugged the other man. "Thank you, Martin Alonzo," he said. "We have much to do before sailing."
"The Pinzon family is with you! The sailors are ready too," said Martin Alonzo. The two men hurried out of the church. They never noticed the children.
"Do you think he’s really Christopher Columbus?" asked Vinnie excitedly.
"Hey, he left his book!" cried Mandy, running to pick it up.
" The Travels of Marco Polo, " Mandy read on the cover. She flipped through the pages. "Whoever he is, he must love this book. He’s written in it and underlined some parts."
Mandy stopped. She thought she heard a noise. "What was that?" she said.
"What was what?" asked Vinnie.
A young man stepped out from behind a stone column. Vinnie screamed.
"Shh! Quiet!" said the young man. He seemed as scared as the children.
"Who are you?" asked Mandy.
"My name is Julio," he said. "That man, Martin Alonzo, is my uncle. I didn’t want him to see me."
Julio looked about 18 years old. The children introduced themselves.
"Why were you hiding?" asked Vinnie.
Julio looked embarrassed. "Today we sail and . . . I was scared."
"Are you sailing with someone named Christopher Columbus?" asked Vinnie.
Julio nodded.
"Wow!" cried Vinnie. "He’s a great explorer!"
"He is crazy!" said Julio. "He thinks we can find the Indies by sailing west."
"Columbus knows what he’s doing," said Vinnie.

Julio shook his head. "Columbus planned this journey many years ago. But nobody wanted to support him, not even Queen Isabella. But now that Spain is a powerful nation again, the queen and King Ferdinand said yes."
"What if Columbus discovers something great? There’s only one way to find out," Mandy said.
"He DID discover something great. America!" Vinnie said.
"The Portuguese travel around Africa. They reach the Indies going east without any problems," said Julio. "When people heard of Columbus’ crazy plan, no one wanted to sail with him."
"So why are you going on the voyage?" asked Vinnie.
Julio’s face softened.
"My uncles are the Pinzon brothers. Everybody here in the port of Palos respects them. When they decided to support Columbus, the sailors decided to go. I couldn’t be the only one to say no."
"How many uncles do you have?" asked Vinnie.

"Three," replied Julio. "They are all very capable seamen. I came to the church today to pray for a safe voyage. I didn’t expect my uncle to be here. If he knew I was scared, he would call me a baby."
"So when are you leaving?" asked Mandy.
"In a few hours," replied Julio. "I am ready now. I must get to my ship."
The children followed Julio out of the church and into the street.
The streets of Palos were busy with people carrying goods. They were carrying supplies in their hands, in wagons, and on animals. Everyone was heading in the same direction: to the docks.
Julio led the children in that direction as well. Mandy could smell the ocean before she saw it.
"Mandy, look!" cried Vinnie.
At the end of the street was the harbor. Vinnie pointed to three ships tied up at the pier. One was bigger than the other two.
"The biggest one is—," began Julio.
"The Santa Maria . And the others are the Pinta and Niña ," said Vinnie.
Julio looked impressed.
"You’d better return that book to Columbus," Julio said to Mandy. "He won’t sail without it."
"Where can I find him?" asked Mandy.
"Aboard the Santa Maria , of course," replied Julio.
"Can you take us there?" said Mandy.
"Sure, come on," Julio said, waving his hand.
They walked down the street to the pier. The harbor was busy. Men were loading all kinds of equipment onto the ships. Seagulls circled above the waves. Along the way, they asked Julio more questions.
"Why are the sailors afraid of sailing west?" Mandy asked.

Julio took a breath. He was still nervous about the trip. "It is said that sea monsters live in those waters. Even if you somehow sail past them, well . . . ," Julio paused. "The ocean ends at some point. Then what happens?"
"Oh, don’t worry. The world is round. Your ship won’t fall," laughed Vinnie.
"How do you know what is out there?" Julio said angrily. "I bet you haven’t been on an adventure in your life!"
Vinnie and Mandy smiled at each other and thought of their photo trips.
"Julio!" someone called. A middle-aged woman approached them. She was carrying a wool blanket.
"Señora Molina! What a pleasant surprise!" Julio cried happily. He introduced the children to her. "Señora Molina owns a wool shop. Her wool is the softest and warmest in all of Spain."
"Here, take this," said Señora Molina, handing the blanket to Julio. "This will keep you warm on cold nights."
"Thank you so much," Julio said. He hugged her.
"Be careful, Julio," she whispered, wiping her eyes.
Julio waved good-bye, then he and Mandy and Vinnie continued onto the pier.
"One day I will make Spanish wool famous," said Julio, holding the soft blanket close to him.
"How?" asked Vinnie.
"When I have my own ship, I will sell wool at every port on earth," Julio said proudly.
"Maybe you’ll become an explorer like Columbus," said Mandy.
"Who wants to be like him?" replied Julio. "He’s a dreamer with some crazy ideas."
"But look at him now!" exclaimed Mandy.
"Look at what?" Julio laughed. "He hasn’t discovered anything yet!"
As they approached Columbus’ three ships, Vinnie noticed a few sickly men. They were very thin and pale. One man had dark spots on his legs.
"Julio," Vinnie whispered. "Those men look very ill."
Julio nodded sadly. "They have just gotten back from a long journey. They have scurvy."
"Scurvy?" asked Vinnie.
"It’s a disease some sailors get," said Julio. "The ship’s doctor thinks it’s because sailors don’t eat enough fruit."
"But fruit is good for you!" exclaimed Mandy.
Julio smiled at her.
"You’re right, Mandy. But, aboard ship, fruit rots very quickly. On long voyages, it’s impossible to keep fruit fresh."
Vinnie and Mandy looked at the sick men.
"That’s sad," said Mandy.
Suddenly, a high-pitched whistle blew and the pier buzzed with excitement.
"Time to sail," said Julio.
"But what about the book?" Mandy asked.
Julio looked around. Sailors were rushing past him and boarding the ships. "Look!" he shouted. "There’s Columbus on the Santa Maria . Come on!"
Julio ran onto the ship, and the children followed. On deck, a man stood by the ship’s rail. He was holding several sheets of paper.
"Julio, get to your post," ordered the man.
"Diego, these children must see Columbus," said Julio. "Can you take them to him?"
Diego looked at the children impatiently. "He has no time for children," he said. "Go away."
"Please," pleaded Julio. "It’s important that they see the captain. This little girl found his book and wants to give it back to him."
"Since you are Martin Alonzo’s nephew, I will do as you ask," said Diego.
"Good-bye, Vinnie and Mandy. It was nice meeting you," said Julio. He waved before running off to another part of the ship.
"Thank you, Julio!" cried the children.
"Come on, we’re sailing in a few minutes," said Diego. He led them past sailors getting the ship ready.
"I can’t believe we’re on the Santa Maria !" gasped Vinnie. He looked around excitedly.
Mandy noticed some men carrying big sacks to an opening in the deck. A ladder led down into the cargo hold. With a loud crash, one of the men dropped a sack. Potatoes spilled out, all over the deck.
"Watch out!" shouted Diego. "Grab those potatoes!"
Everyone stopped to catch the rolling potatoes.
"I got one!" Mandy shouted.
"I’ll get that one," Vinnie called, running after a potato that rolled a long way down the deck.
Soon the potatoes were collected in the sack again. A young boy stepped forward and tied the sack tight.
Mandy wiped her hands on her skirt. "That was fun," she said, laughing. Then she stopped. "Vinnie! The ship is moving!"
Mandy looked around, but could not see her brother. Vinnie had disappeared into the crowd of sailors. The Santa Maria was pulling slowly away from the pier.
"Oh no! What am I going to do?" she said to herself.
Mandy could not believe it. She was aboard the Santa Maria . And it was sailing away from the dock.
"Where is Vinnie?" she wondered. Diego had disappeared too. Then Mandy spotted a familiar figure. It was Christopher Columbus, and he was speaking with some sailors.
"Excuse me, sir!" she called out. Mandy took the book out of her pocket.
A sailor grabbed her arm. "How did you get on the ship?" he asked, surprised. "You’re a little girl!"
"Wait a minute!" Christopher Columbus interrupted. "What do you have in your hand?"
"This is why I’m here, sir," explained Mandy. "I found your book in the church. I knew it was important to you."
"I thought it was lost," Columbus said. "This must be a sign from God. You have brought good luck for our journey."

On another part of the ship, Vinnie was looking around. After he helped gather the spilled potatoes, Vinnie had somehow lost Mandy. The ship was full of activity. The Santa Maria was long and narrow. Vinnie counted more than 35 sailors aboard. They were uncoiling ropes, connecting equipment, and opening the large, white sails. Before he knew it, the ship was in open water.
"I wonder what Mandy’s doing," he thought.
He looked behind him. The Niña and Pinta were following closely. They were smaller ships with fewer sailors.
"Don’t just stand there," said a young boy about Vinnie’s age. He was holding a mop. "You’ll get in trouble. Here, take this."
"But, I’m not—," Vinnie began.
The boy gave Vinnie an odd look.
A big sailor walked over to them. "Why are you just standing there?" he demanded. "Get to work!"
"Yes, sir!" cried Vinnie. He started mopping the deck quickly.
The sailor walked away.
"Thanks for the warning," Vinnie said to the boy.
"I’m Manuel," the boy said. "This is my first time sailing. How about you?"
"My first time too," said Vinnie.
Together, the boys mopped the deck. It was wet from the mist of the ocean waves.

Meanwhile, Mandy stood listening as Christopher Columbus spoke to some of his crew. She realized that each of them had a different job. One man was a carpenter. Another was a cook. A silversmith and a doctor were on board too.
"Unexpected things happen at sea," Columbus was saying. "Each of you has a duty to make sure this voyage is successful."
"Any wood that needs repair, the men can see me," said the carpenter.
"I’ll keep the meat well salted," said the cook.
"Captain, I’ll make sure your instruments are working perfectly," said the silversmith.
"If any men get sick or break their bones, I will take care of them," said the doctor.
"Good. And every day, I expect a report from each of you," said Columbus.
"Yes, Captain," the men said.
Columbus took Mandy to his cabin. "You will be safe here," he said.
Curious, Mandy picked up a round metal object. Its pointy, moving hands were like a clock’s.
"What’s this?" asked Mandy.
"It’s an astrolabe," explained Columbus. "It measures the height of the sun from the horizon. It helps us know where we are on the ocean."
Columbus took the astrolabe and said, "I have to go now. Stay here."
Meanwhile, Vinnie was getting hungry. A sailor’s life wasn’t much fun.
"We’re all going to starve," said an old sailor nearby.
"Monsters will eat us before we starve!" screamed another.
"I want to go home!" thought Vinnie.

Manuel was tying a knot in a rope. Another boy was standing by a large coil of rope, holding an hourglass. When the sand emptied into the bottom, the boy cried: "One glass is gone. Now the second begins!"
"What’s he doing?" Vinnie asked Manuel.
"We take turns turning over the hourglass. Each time it empties, a half hour has gone by," explained Manuel. "After eight turns, or four hours, another boy takes over."
The boy called to Vinnie, "Hey, take over a minute, will you?"
He put the hourglass into Vinnie’s hands.
"It’s the second half of the hour," said the boy. He ran off before Vinnie could protest.
"Here," said Manuel. He took a biscuit out of his pocket and gave it to Vinnie. Biscuits were used to mark the time after each turn of the hourglass. Vinnie thought he was supposed to eat it.
"Ow!" cried Vinnie, after he tried to bite it. The biscuit was so hard that Vinnie put it down on the ropes.
Meanwhile, Mandy sat alone in the captain’s cabin. The cabin boy had left her a biscuit to eat. She put it in her pocket.
Suddenly, there was a loud boom.
Mandy, ran out onto the deck. "What was that?" she shouted.
"It’s the Pinta! " cried someone. "The ship needs help!"
At that moment, she heard a familiar voice shouting, "One glass is gone, and now the second begins!"
"Vinnie!" she cried happily.
"Mandy! Am I glad to see you!" he exclaimed when she ran up. He put the hourglass on top of the ropes.
"What are you doing?" she asked.
"Every thirty minutes, I turn this hourglass over. Each time, Manuel brings a biscuit. They’re so hard I can’t eat them," said Vinnie.
