"Don’t eat them!" Mandy shouted, pulling out the photo. "We need them! See?"
The photo was glowing blue.
"But there are only two biscuits!" cried Vinnie. "We need three to go home."
"Don’t worry," said Mandy, pulling the biscuit from her pocket.
Mandy placed it next to the other biscuits. In the photo, the hourglass glowed red.
"I’m so glad we’re leaving!" cried Vinnie.
The children closed their eyes and fell down the dark tunnel.
Summer was almost over. Soon, Vinnie and Mandy would be starting school. Right now, they were folding laundry.
"Dad has almost finished moving into the attic," said Vinnie. "We don’t have a lot of time left for photo trips!"
"And when school starts, we won’t have any time at all," Mandy sighed.
The children looked at each other.
"We shouldn’t waste a single moment," said Vinnie. He tossed a sock into the laundry basket.
"Mom and Dad are in the kitchen," Mandy said in a low voice. "Maybe we can sneak upstairs."
"Let’s go," said Vinnie, and they ran up the steps.
Once they were inside the attic, Mandy grabbed the photo album.
"Look, Vinnie!" exclaimed Mandy. "We’re almost at the end of the album." She showed him how many pages were left.
"I can’t believe how many trips we’ve done," said Vinnie.
"This is interesting," said Mandy, pointing to the new photo.
The old man stood in a boat by a river. The sun was setting behind him. Something glowing leaped out of the water.
"Can you tell where this is?" asked Mandy.
Vinnie shook his head.
"Well, we’re about to find out!" Mandy cried.
The picture glowed brighter, and the children’s eyes closed. Soon they were spinning down the dark tunnel.
Mandy and Vinnie fell onto soft soil. They could hear shouts and laughter.
"Where are we?" asked Mandy, standing up.
They were in a small village. People were running around laughing. Two women hurried over to the children, holding small cups. They splashed Vinnie with colored water.
"Gross! What is this?" screamed Vinnie. The front of his shirt was soaked bright red. He rubbed at the wet stain.
"Everyone is splashing each other," Mandy said, looking around.
The street was filled with people holding cups. Laughing loudly, they chased each other, throwing colored water.
"What’s going on?" asked Vinnie.
A boy splashed Mandy.
"Hey!" cried Mandy. Her sleeve and part of her arm were stained purple.
The boy set down his cup and put his hands together in front of his chest.
"Hello," he said, bowing slightly. His face, arms, and clothes were soaked in many bright colors.
The children imitated the boy’s greeting. Vinnie introduced himself and Mandy.
"I’m Rishi," said the boy. "Is this your first time here?"
Vinnie and Mandy nodded.
"What’s going on?" asked Vinnie.
"It’s the spring festival!" shouted Rishi, picking up his cup. He splashed someone running by.
Everyone was soaked with different colors. Mandy noticed a cup someone had dropped. She picked it up. There was still some colored water inside.
"Oh well, if you can’t beat them, join them," she said. Mandy laughed and quickly splashed Rishi and her brother.
The splashing ended and the laughter quieted down. People were returning home.
"What happens now?" Mandy asked Rishi.
"We wash," said Rishi. "And life continues."
Vinnie and Mandy looked around. They still did not know where they were.
"Rishi, we’re new here," said Vinnie. "What is this place?"
"The city of Patna," Rishi said. He noticed Vinnie and Mandy still looked confused.
"India!" he shouted.
"Wow!" cried Vinnie and Mandy.
Rishi stared at them curiously. "Where are you from?" he asked.
"America," said Mandy.
"America?" repeated Rishi. "I’ve never heard of it."
Suddenly, a young girl ran up.
"Rishi! Mother says to come and wash," said the girl.
"This is Rima, my sister," Rishi said. He introduced Vinnie and Mandy. "Would you like to meet my parents?" he asked.
"We’d love to," said Mandy.

Rishi and Rima’s house was made of mud and bamboo. The roof was made of palm leaves. A small clay stove was in a porch area. Rishi’s mother was stirring rice in a pot. His father was standing next to her wearing a white turban. Rishi introduced the children to his parents.
"Hello," Vinnie and Mandy said, putting their hands together and bowing. Rishi’s father did the same and smiled.
"The boys will wash first," said his father.
Vinnie followed Rishi outside to a large jug of water. With a cup, Rishi scooped up some water. He handed it to Vinnie.
"You wash first," said Rishi.
"Thanks," replied Vinnie. He emptied the cup over his head.
Shocked, Rishi stared at him. Then he said: "Do not waste water."
"I’m sorry," said Vinnie, his face turning red.
"We have a short rainy season," explained Rishi. "So we collect rainwater in a well outside the village."
Rishi filled the cup again. He dipped his fingers in the cup and rubbed water on his arms.
"Water is very valuable," Rishi continued. "We must not waste one drop."
Embarrassed, Vinnie looked at the puddle at his feet.
Inside the house, Mandy was looking at a row of statues on a low table.
"What’s this?" Mandy asked. She pointed to a statue of a four-headed person with four arms.
"Brahma," explained Rima. "He is the creator of the universe. Brahma is one of our three main gods."
"Who are the others?" asked Mandy. There was a dark blue statue with four arms. Each of its arms held an object.
"That is Vishnu, the preserver of the universe," said Rima. "And this is Shiva." The statue of Shiva sat with its legs crossed and eyes closed. "The destroyer of the universe."
Mandy looked at the smaller statues on the table.
"Are all of these gods?" she asked.
Rima nodded. "We worship many gods."
Vinnie and Rishi returned. They looked cleaner.
"It’s your turn," Vinnie said to Mandy. "Oh, and don’t waste water."
Mandy gave him a puzzled look and headed outside with Rima.

After washing, Mandy put on clothes Rima gave her. She wore loose pants and a shirt that almost came to her knees. Vinnie also dressed in a long shirt. But he wore a skirt that went all the way to his ankles!
"Time to eat," Rishi’s father announced.

The family gathered around the stove. Vinnie and Mandy joined them. Rishi’s family closed their eyes and began to chant quietly. They put their hands together. Then, the family threw rice grains into the fire.
"They’re praying," whispered Mandy to Vinnie.
After the prayer, Rishi brought out a bowl of water. He and Rima sat beside their father and washed his feet.
"I guess this is a sign of respect," whispered Vinnie. "Maybe we should wash Dad’s feet too," he joked.
Mandy giggled.
Finally, the food was served. Rishi’s father sat on a mat, cross-legged on the floor. His wife put rice onto a large banana leaf for him.
"Does your mother always serve your father food?" Vinnie asked Rishi.
"Of course," he replied. "It is our custom. Now we must serve our mother."
The children washed their hands, and their mother sat beside their father. Then Rishi and Rima served rice to their mother.
"Children eat last," said Rishi. He gave rice to Vinnie and Mandy and they sat on a mat.
"How do I eat this?" Mandy asked. She had no spoon or fork.
"Like this," said Rima, picking up the rice with her hand.
Vinnie and Mandy tried to copy her, but most of the rice ended up on the floor. Everyone laughed.
Then, without warning, a large cow walked right into the porch!
"Hey!" cried Mandy. She dropped her rice and hid behind her brother.
"Get away! Move!" Vinnie got up and waved his arms at the cow. The cow looked at him with big, bored eyes.
"You mustn’t . . . ," Rishi cried.
Vinnie slapped the cow’s back, and it mooed loudly.
Mandy wondered why Rishi’s family wasn’t doing anything.
"Get away! Shoo!" Vinnie grabbed a stick lying against the wall and poked the cow.
Suddenly, a man ran into the porch. He saw Vinnie poke the animal. "What are you doing to my cow?" he shouted.
"Please, Babu Yadav," Rishi’s father said, trying to calm the man.
Rishi grabbed the stick from Vinnie. "Stop!" cried Rishi.
"What’s the matter?" asked Vinnie.
"That boy! He hit my cow! I’m telling the king!" Babu Yadav shouted.
"What is he talking about?" asked Vinnie, confused.
"Vinnie! Cows are sacred animals. We never treat them badly," said Rishi.
"Even if they come into your house?" asked Vinnie.
"There is great punishment for those who harm cows," Rishi said seriously.
"The king will hear about this!" Babu Yadav cried.
Rishi’s dad tried to calm Babu Yadav, but he was still upset.
"He tried to hurt my cow," Babu Yadav said. "It is wrong."
"What did I do?" cried Vinnie, worried.
"Babu Yadav, I give you my word," said Rishi’s father. "I will bring the boy to the king myself."
"You’d better take him to the king!" Babu Yadav threatened. He left with the cow.
"Why are cows so important?" asked Mandy.
"The cow is like our mother," began Rishi’s father.
"I don’t understand," said Mandy.
"Cows are gentle creatures and provide milk to feed the world," Rishi’s father continued. "It would be wrong to harm your mother."
"Why do I have to see the king?" asked Vinnie.
"Babu Yadav insists," said Rishi’s father. "We have to go to the palace. The king will decide what is best."
Rima and her mother stayed home. Vinnie and Mandy left with Rishi and his father. They walked down the muddy roads. Vinnie noticed many cows walking around freely.
"Do you believe in karma?" asked Rishi.
"What’s karma?" asked Vinnie.

"Our bodies die, but our souls do not. We live many lives," said Rishi. "If we hurt an animal or a person, we will be hurt in our next life." Rishi continued, "This is why all living things should be treated kindly."
Suddenly, they heard a loud clapping noise. People on the road moved to the side. Everyone stood still covering their eyes.
"What’s up?" asked Vinnie.
"Do not look!" Rishi said urgently.
An old man in torn clothes walked up the road. He was clapping two wooden boards together.
"Hello," Mandy called out to him softly.
The man turned away from Mandy and kept walking. After he left, Rishi and the others started on their way again.
"Why didn’t anyone look at him?" Mandy asked Rishi.
"He’s an untouchable," explained Rishi.
"Why was he clapping those wooden things?" asked Vinnie.
"It’s the law. Untouchables must alert everyone that they are coming," Rishi replied. "No one is supposed to even look at them. They are the lowest kind of people. Untouchables do the dirtiest jobs."
"Why?" said Mandy.
"We have castes in our society," Rishi began. He pointed to two men with their hair knotted on top of their heads.
"They are the highest caste, the Brahmans. They are our religious teachers."
A large elephant with bells came in the opposite direction. On its back was a colorful rug and carriage. A young man in white sat on top.
"The nobles are the next highest caste. Like him," said Rishi.
"The next caste is made up of farmers and merchants. My family belongs to this caste," Rishi said proudly. "Below us are the servants’ caste and finally the untouchables."
Mandy and Vinnie just looked at each other.
Mandy was very upset. Rishi was explaining the caste system, but she didn’t think it was right.
"It’s cruel!" she said angrily. "You treat cows better than humans."
"The untouchables did something wrong in a past life," explained Rishi. "The gods are punishing them."
"But you don’t even look at them," said Mandy.
Vinnie poked Mandy to keep quiet.
"If we look at them, we will be unclean for the whole day," said Rishi.
"Well, I think—," Mandy began.
Vinnie interrupted: "I think we’re at the palace."
They looked ahead and saw a spectacular view. Flowers decorated the road to the palace entrance. The children passed through an arch with fountains on either side.
"It’s wonderful!" Mandy gasped, forgetting her anger.
"Look at the elephants and monkeys!" Vinnie laughed.
Trainers were putting gold paint on two elephants. Monkeys sat in the trees above, watching. Golden statues stood along the way to the palace door.
A male servant led them inside.
"The palace has over a hundred rooms," whispered Rishi. "This one is for chess." He pointed to an open door. "There are many bedrooms. The king can sleep in a different bed every night."
They waited behind two women. One woman held a live chicken in her arm. She was yelling at a woman holding a baby.
"There you are!" a familiar voice said sharply. It was Babu Yadav waiting by a doorway. Music floated out of the room as the women ahead of them went in.
"Babu Yadav, have pity. These children are strangers," began Rishi’s father. "They did not know . . ."
"I don’t care," said Babu Yadav. "He must be punished."
The women quickly came out through the door.
"It’s our turn. The king is waiting!" exclaimed Babu Yadav, as he walked into the king’s hall.
Rishi’s father and the children followed.
"Whoa!" gasped Vinnie when he stepped inside.
A tiger tied to a post was licking a huge bone. A small distance away, musicians were playing. One plucked a harp.

Two women stood beside a short, fat, man sitting on a soft couch. They gently waved fans made of animal hair over his head. The man wore a long robe and tight pants. The turban on his head was decorated with jewels.
"What is your problem?" the man asked.
"My king, I come before you with a troubled heart," Babu Yadav began, bowing low.
The king nodded for Babu Yadav to continue. The man told about the cow and Vinnie, and the king’s eyes opened wide. He stared at Vinnie and Mandy.
"You are not from India," he pointed out.
"No, sir, I mean, your majesty," Vinnie stuttered.
"If I may go on, my king," Babu Yadav interrupted.
The king held up his hand. "Your cow was not harmed. So we can overlook this matter," yawned the king. He clapped his hands. "Next!"
Vinnie was relieved that he wasn’t punished.
"I’m glad everything worked out," said Rishi’s father, as they passed out of the arch and onto the street again. "What will you children do now?"
Mandy remembered the photo. "Is there a river or lake nearby?" she asked.
"You must mean the Ganges, the holy river," said Rishi. "I will take you there."

They said good-bye to Rishi’s father, and the children walked down the road. Soon, they heard music. By the road, an elderly man sat on a straw mat playing a flute. In front of him was a round basket.
"What is that man doing?" asked Vinnie.
Suddenly, a snake appeared. It swayed to the music.
"He’s a snake charmer," explained Rishi.
The children watched the snake weave back and forth, hissing.
"Come, here is the River Ganges," said Rishi.
The children joined some people waiting for a boat on the riverbank. Once they were aboard, Mandy noticed pictures hanging everywhere.
"Wow!" Mandy exclaimed.
"This is a floating art gallery," explained Rishi. "People ride down the Ganges while they enjoy the drawings and paintings."
"This one looks like a man with an elephant head," Vinnie said, pointing to a picture.
"That’s Ganesha," said Rishi. "He is our god of wisdom, science, and the arts."
Vinnie and Mandy calmly watched the peaceful river. Along the shore, cattle were drinking lazily. Women filled jugs and then walked away, balancing them on their heads.
"Mandy, the picture is glowing blue," whispered Vinnie.
"Can you tell us about this river, Rishi?" asked Mandy.
"This river is named for the goddess Ganga. She came to Earth and blessed these waters," began Rishi. "We believe that if we bathe in the river, our sins will be forgiven."
The sun was about to set. A sudden splash caught their attention.
"Rishi! What’s that?" asked Mandy, pointing.
"Oh, those are the sacred dolphins of the Ganges," cried Rishi.
"Why are they sacred?" asked Vinnie.
"The dolphins are special friends of the goddess Ganga," said Rishi. "We don’t see them very often now. This is a special moment."
Vinnie and Mandy watched as a dolphin swam closer. The photo was still glowing blue.
"Thank you, Rishi," Vinnie said. "It’s been a wonderful journey."
"Are you going home?" asked Rishi.
The dolphin jumped out of the water, and the photo glowed red.
"Yes, we are," replied Vinnie.
The children fell down the dark tunnel and landed with a thump on the attic floor.
"Where are you kids? I thought I told you to fold the laundry!" Mom shouted from downstairs.
Grinning, Vinnie and Mandy went downstairs to finish their job.
Vinnie and Mandy stood by the front door with their parents. Mom was taking them shopping for new school clothes.
"What will you do, honey?" Mom asked Dad.
"Don’t worry about me." He smiled. "I’ll be working on my den."
Vinnie and Mandy looked at each other.
"Do you have to do it now, Dad?" Mandy asked. She had left the album on a shelf. He would certainly see it.
"Why shouldn’t I? You’ll be out," replied Dad. He opened the front door for them.
"But . . . ," whined Mandy.
"What’s the matter?" asked Mom. "You love to go shopping."
"I know, but . . . ," said Mandy.
"We need a miracle," Vinnie whispered.
"What did you say?" asked Mom.
The phone suddenly rang, and Dad answered it. "It’s your mother," he said to Mom.
"I’ll just be a minute, kids. Wait in the car," Mom said.
"Well, okay," said Mandy, feeling a bit uncertain.
Vinnie winked at Mandy and said, "Uh, I left something upstairs. I’ll be right back."
"Me too!" Mandy added quickly. They both ran upstairs.
"I think those kids are hiding something," Dad muttered to himself.
When they got to the attic, the children let out a long sigh.
"I was so scared he’d find this," Mandy said as she took the album from the shelf.
"We don’t have a lot of time," Vinnie said. "Do you want to go on a trip now?"
Mandy nodded. "But hurry! Mom won’t be on the phone long."
Vinnie opened the album. The old man was standing by a table with a small black machine on it. A woman was holding something and it was glowing.
"It looks like a sewing machine," remarked Mandy. "But what’s glowing?"
Vinnie looked at the photo. "Some kind of curtain, I think." Before he could look more closely, the children fell down the dark tunnel.
Mandy landed on soft grass, and Vinnie fell beside her. A crowd was gathered nearby.
"Where are we?" Mandy asked, dusting off her clothes. She wore a pretty pink dress with ribbons.
Vinnie looked down at his pants. They came just to his knees. He wore long socks and black shoes.
"I don’t know," Vinnie began, but he was interrupted by music.
The children ran to join the crowd. Everyone was standing in front of a very large, carved marble arch. Behind the arch was a huge building with many columns.
"The flag on that arch looks familiar," said Mandy.
"Mandy!" Vinnie cried excitedly. "I think we’re in—"
Before Vinnie could finish, someone grabbed Mandy.
"There you are!" a young woman shouted. "I’ve been looking everywhere for you!"
The young woman held Mandy’s arm tightly. "Miss Charlotte, you must not run away like that again," she said.
"Excuse me," Mandy said, turning to look at the woman. "I’m not Charlotte."
"Oh, you’re not," the woman said, letting go. She started to cry.
"Please don’t cry," Mandy said kindly. "Can I help you?"
The woman shook her head. She wore a long black skirt and a black shawl over a long-sleeved blouse. A bonnet was on her head.
"I’m Florence, Miss Charlotte’s new nanny," she said. "We came here to watch the royal foot guards."
"Look at that!" Vinnie interrupted them.

Soldiers in red jackets and bearskin hats marched in front of the building. They were stepping very slowly, in perfect time with each other. Another group of soldiers marched just as slowly toward them.
"It’s the changing of the guards," Vinnie cried excitedly. "We’re back in England, Mandy, and this must be Buckingham Palace!"
"Quiet, Vinnie," whispered Mandy. "Florence is upset."

Florence looked at Vinnie strangely, but continued. "Sometimes, Miss Charlotte likes to play tricks on me. She saw the crowd and ran off. I’ve been looking and looking . . . ," cried Florence. She blew her nose into a handkerchief. "She was wearing a pink dress like you."
The ceremony was over. Now, new guards stood in front of the palace, and the old guards were marching away.
Florence wiped her eyes. "I must not give up. Miss Charlotte is probably close by."
"We’ll help you find her," said Mandy.
"We will?" said Vinnie.
"By the way, I’m Mandy, and this is my brother Vinnie," said Mandy.
"Oh, thank you, Miss Mandy. But where is your nanny?" asked Florence.
Mandy looked around. She and Vinnie were dressed very nicely. Some other children were dressed nicely too. They all walked with young women dressed like Florence.
"We’re just visiting," Mandy said quickly.
"Is your family new to London?" she asked.
The children looked at each other. They remembered their earlier photo trip to London.
"It’s only our second visit," Vinnie said truthfully. "We don’t live here."
"Well, I’m glad you’re here," said Florence. "I would appreciate your help, thank you."
The children followed Florence down the street.
"Where do you think Charlotte would go?" asked Mandy.
Florence thought for a moment. "Miss Charlotte has always wanted to see the Crystal Palace," she said. "That’s where the Great Exhibition is."
"That sounds interesting," said Mandy. "What kind of exhibition is it?"
Florence smiled at her. "Let’s start looking for Miss Charlotte there," she said. "It’s not far."
The children followed Florence, who headed quickly down the street.
Florence led the children through a park of tall trees and green lawns. They passed fountains and statues.
Women in long, full dresses strolled by. Men in top hats and long coats accompanied them.
"All the men seem to like hats," remarked Vinnie.
Florence looked at Vinnie strangely again.

"What game are they playing?" Mandy asked, pointing to a group of young men and women. Each held a stick with a round wooden head on the end. The sticks looked like big hammers and the players used them to hit balls through hoops.
"That’s croquet," explained Florence. "People love to play games in Hyde Park."
Mandy stopped suddenly and let out a loud gasp. They stood in front of a large glass building. Many people were walking through the doors.
"Wow!" cried Mandy.
"This is the Crystal Palace," explained Florence. "The Great Exhibition is inside."
They followed the crowd into the building. Mandy covered her mouth in shock. The sunlight shone through the glass roof onto many exhibits.
"Whoa!" Vinnie cried, glancing from side to side.
The Crystal Palace was divided into areas, and each had a special theme. In one area, the children saw different kinds of machines. In another, women gathered around collections of jewelry.
"There are over 13,000 exhibits," said Florence.
Vinnie saw all kinds of things on display: art, tools, kitchen devices, and even animals.
"I can see why Charlotte wanted to come here," said Mandy. She looked up. Above an amazed crowd, a man walked on a tightrope.
"What’s that?" Vinnie cried.
He ran over to a tall structure with a marble statue inside. A big crowd was gathered around it.
"The statue in this iron structure is―," said a man wearing a top hat.
"Shakespeare!" Vinnie shouted.
"The young man is right!" shouted the man. "This is indeed England’s own William Shakespeare."
Mandy and Florence caught up with Vinnie.
"Queen Victoria’s husband, Prince Albert, is the one who planned the exhibition. It just opened in May. The Crystal Palace was built in only nine months," said Florence.
"Florence, where do you think Charlotte is?" asked Mandy.
"Miss Charlotte loves music. I heard they have the world’s largest organ here," replied Florence. She stopped to speak to a man who had a map.
"This way, Miss Mandy and Master Vinnie," called Florence.
The children followed Florence. They passed exhibits from countries in Asia and Europe.
"It feels like we’re in a giant shopping mall," said Mandy.
They reached an area where an orchestra was playing.
"I don’t see her anywhere," said Florence, worried. The children looked around too. But they did not see anyone wearing a pink dress like Mandy’s.
Vinnie wanted to stay longer at the Crystal Palace, but Florence wanted to leave.
"I didn’t get to see everything," Vinnie complained.
"Hush, Florence needs our help," Mandy whispered as the children followed Florence outside.
Suddenly, Florence cried out, "Miss Charlotte!"
A girl about Mandy’s age was walking on the other side of the street. She stopped when she saw Florence.
"Miss Charlotte!" cried Florence again.
Charlotte crossed the street looking very sorry.
"This is most upsetting," Florence said to her.
"Don’t be angry," Charlotte said. "I just wanted to have some fun by myself."
"Well, it wasn’t fun for me!" Florence said.
"Who are you?" asked Charlotte, looking at Vinnie and Mandy.
Florence introduced the children to her.
"You’re visiting London?" Charlotte said excitedly. "Florence, we must show them around. We can go to father’s factory!"
"A factory?" asked Mandy. After the Crystal Palace, a factory didn’t sound very interesting.
"Your father wouldn’t like it," began Florence.
"Would you like to go?" Charlotte asked the children.
"Well," replied Vinnie.
"We can take that cab!" Charlotte exclaimed. She ran to a nearby carriage and got in before Florence could object.
"This is a cab?" whispered Vinnie, climbing into the horse-drawn carriage. "Cool!"
The carriage rolled through the London streets. The children listened to the pleasant clip-clop of the horse’s hooves.
As they rode through the city, Mandy noticed the streets changing. The colorful streets, alive with people and shops, became dark and empty.
"Where is everyone?" asked Mandy. She looked out the carriage window. Poorly dressed children were playing outside. A few older people sat on doorsteps.
"Most people are in the factories," explained Florence. Then she pointed to some big, brick buildings. Their tall chimneys poured dark smoke into the sky.
"Are all these buildings factories?" asked Mandy, looking at the gloomy buildings.
"Yes," said Florence.
"Here we are!" Charlotte called out cheerfully.
They stopped at a factory door. Charlotte jumped out of the carriage and ran inside. Florence asked the cab driver to wait for them. Then Vinnie, Mandy, and Florence followed Charlotte inside.
They walked into a large room filled with long tables. Ten women sat at each table, among piles of pieces of cloth. The women were sewing the pieces by hand.
Mandy looked around. "Vinnie, look!" she said in a shocked voice.
Many of the people working in the factory were children.
Vinnie and Mandy could not believe their eyes. They followed Charlotte through the factory. Every room was filled with factory workers: men, women, and children.
"Florence, why are children working in the factory?" asked Mandy.
Florence’s face was serious. "For their families, Miss Mandy," she said. "People want British products, so our factories must stay busy. That means everyone, including poor children, must work."
It didn’t seem fair to Mandy, but she kept quiet. Loud noises came from a nearby room. They went in and saw huge machines with big metal rollers moving back and forth.
"They look like mechanical weaving machines!" Mandy cried, but no one heard her. The sound was so loud that she had to put her fingers in her ears.
"Miss Charlotte!" yelled a man carrying a stack of paper under one arm.
"Mr. Geoffrey! I want to see my father," Charlotte yelled over the noise. The man turned and led them out of the noisy room.
"He is very busy, Miss Charlotte," said Mr. Geoffrey. "He can’t see you now."
Charlotte looked very sad. "I want him to meet Vinnie and Mandy."
Mr. Geoffrey shook his head.
"Please," pleaded Charlotte.
"I’m sorry, no," said Mr. Geoffrey.
"What are you making here?" Vinnie asked.
"This is a textile factory. We weave cloth and make clothes," replied Mr. Geoffrey.
"Do all the factories here make clothes?" asked Mandy.
"No, across the street, they make parts for the railroad," he said.
"Why are there so many factories?" Mandy wanted to know.
Mr. Geoffrey laughed. "The world is changing. Industry is the future! If you need something, England can make it."

Since Charlotte was not allowed to see her father, she wanted to leave. So they left the factory and found the cab driver waiting. Suddenly, church bells rang. Vinnie turned to see a large bell tower in the distance.
"That is St. Katherine’s, an old church that escaped the Great Fire in 1666," Florence said proudly. "The fire destroyed over 87 churches in London, but not St. Katherine’s!"
"Let’s go. It’s teatime!" demanded Charlotte. She turned to Vinnie and Mandy. "Would you like to come to my home for tea?"
"We’d love to," they replied.
They got into the carriage and rode toward Charlotte’s house. As they passed through the streets, the city changed again.
"How clean and pretty the streets are," Mandy thought.
The houses here were bigger and nicer too. Charlotte’s house was on a square with several other homes. A pretty garden was in the middle of the square. Little children were playing outside.
"What a difference from the other side of London," Mandy said to herself.
Charlotte’s home was beautiful. The entrance hall had a stone floor covered by a large rug. The furniture was made of rich wood and leather.
"We’ll have tea in the parlor," Charlotte said to Florence.
She led Vinnie and Mandy to a lovely room with a piano. Charlotte sat on the velvet-covered piano bench and began to play.
"I’ve been playing since I was four," Charlotte bragged. "I love music. Mother says she’ll take me to see Johann Strauss. His orchestra plays at Buckingham Palace sometimes."
"Mandy!" Vinnie whispered. He had taken the photo out of his pocket. "The picture is glowing blue."
"We have to find the sewing machine," whispered Mandy. Then she suddenly called out to Charlotte, "May we have a tour of your house?"
Charlotte stopped playing, shrugged, and rang a bell. Florence walked back in.
"Florence can show you around," said Charlotte.
"Certainly," smiled Florence. "Right this way. This house has twelve rooms, including a library, four bedrooms, and the parlor."
"Does Charlotte go to school?" asked Mandy.
"She has a private teacher. Miss Charlotte also takes ballet, piano, and art lessons," said Florence.
"What about the poor children in London?" asked Vinnie.
"Most of them leave home and go to school until they are ten. Then they work at the factory where their parents work," said Florence. "You saw some women and their children at the factory."
"Yes, the women were sewing by hand," said Mandy. "That’s hard work."
Florence nodded and said, "And it takes a lot of time. But Charlotte’s father just brought home something special."
"What is it?" asked Mandy.
"I will show you," Florence said with a smile.
Upstairs, Florence stood before a closed door. "Mr. Singer, an inventor, came up with a great idea," she said.
Florence quietly opened the door.
"It’s a sewing machine," said Vinnie.
"You already know about this?" asked Florence, shocked.
"Vinnie thinks it’s amazing!" Mandy said quickly. "Charlotte’s father should put these in his factory."
Florence shook her head. "No, there are only a few machines, and they’re expensive."
"Do you know how to use the sewing machine, Florence?" asked Mandy.
"Oh yes, I make play dresses for Charlotte and . . . ," said Florence.
"Curtains?" asked Vinnie, looking at the photo again. It was starting to turn red.
"Oh no, Master Vinnie," explained Florence. "Charlotte’s father would never have homemade curtains."
"Well, then what?" asked Mandy.
"Just something for me to wear," replied Florence, giggling. She shyly took something from a nearby chair and held it up.
"Underpants!" shouted Mandy. The children’s eyes closed as they fell down the dark tunnel. They were back home.
Dad moved his desk into the attic. He filled the bookcase with his books. When Dad wasn’t looking, Vinnie and Mandy hid the photo album. They put it in a bag and stuffed it far under his desk.
"Dad’s feet will never reach it," said Mandy.
"Hopefully he won’t look under there," Vinnie added.
But a week later something terrible happened.
"The bag is gone!" Mandy exclaimed as they stood alone in the attic.
The children looked everywhere, but the bag wasn’t in the room. Suddenly Mandy heard a loud bang outside and looked out the window.
"Look, Vinnie," cried Mandy. "Dad’s putting out the trash."
Dad had just put a big box of junk by the street.
"So?" asked Vinnie.
"Silly, I’ll bet the album’s in there!" cried Mandy as they watched their father walk into the backyard.
The children ran downstairs and outside to the trash. Vinnie dove into the box of junk and began to search. "Here it is!" he shouted, lifting the bag.
The album was still inside, and they hugged and danced around. Vinnie and Mandy happily went back into the house.
"That was really close," said Mandy. "We have to find a better hiding place."
"Let’s take it back upstairs," said Vinnie.
Once in the attic, Vinnie asked, "Hey, do you want to . . . ?" And before Mandy could answer, he opened the album. "Now this is cool!" he exclaimed.

The old man was standing on a dusty road. Two men were standing before him. One was much younger than the other. The older man wore a long coat and was firing two guns. In the air were five glowing objects.
"Is he a cowboy?" asked Mandy.
"We’re about to find out," answered Vinnie.
The children felt their eyes closing and fell down the long, dark tunnel. They landed on something soft. Vinnie opened his eyes.
"Where are we?" he asked.
They lay in a covered wagon among sacks of potatoes, beans, and dried meat.
"This stuff looks like someone is going on a long camping trip," remarked Mandy.
The children had landed on a pile of rolled up blankets. Mandy noticed some clothing in one corner too. The wagon was moving slowly, but the ride was bumpy.
"I’m hungry," said Vinnie, opening a sack. Inside were strips of hard meat. He picked one up.
"Vinnie! Don’t eat that!" Mandy whispered.
"It looks like beef jerky," Vinnie said. He smelled it.
Suddenly the wagon stopped. Then, someone opened part of the heavy cloth covering the wagon. A man wearing a cowboy hat looked in.
"Well, look what I found in my wagon, boys," he called out, staring at the children.
Vinnie dropped the jerky.
The cowboy leaned toward them. A little afraid, Vinnie and Mandy moved to the other side of the wagon.
"Come on out of there," he said in a firm but friendly voice.
The children crawled forward and looked out.
"Wow!" Vinnie said loudly. A large herd of cattle was nearby. Vinnie counted about ten cowboys riding horses.
The children started to climb out of the wagon.
"Where are we? Oops!" cried Mandy, almost falling off the wagon.
"Careful now, little one," the cowboy laughed. "We left Texas quite a while ago. We’re in Kansas, on the Chisholm Trail."
"Kansas?" cried Vinnie.
"How did you two get in my wagon?" asked the cowboy.
"Actually, we . . . ," stuttered Vinnie.
"We wanted to go on an adventure!" Mandy interrupted.
The cowboy smiled and shook his head. "You’ll get adventure, all right. But this trail can be dangerous."
The children introduced themselves, and Mandy said, "We promise not to bother you. Can we stay?"
"Hey, Cookie! When’s supper?" a young cowboy called to the man.
"Wait a minute, my friend," Cookie shouted back. Then he turned to the children. "I’ll talk to the boss to see if you can stay. Meanwhile, you can help me cook."
Cookie asked the children to unload a frying pan and a large pot. Then, as Cookie picked up a sack of beans, another cowboy walked over.
"Who are these kids?" he said.
"They’re Vinnie and Mandy, and they’re on a big adventure," chuckled Cookie. He winked at the other man. "This is Frank, children. He’s the trail boss."
"That’s right," said Frank sternly. "Come with me, Vinnie. I can use your help."
Vinnie followed Frank. Mandy stayed behind to help Cookie.
"What are we going to do?" asked Vinnie.
Frank untied two horses from a nearby bush.
"We need to move the herd," explained Frank, getting on one horse. "Just follow me."
Frank made a clicking noise with his tongue and then rode off. Nervously, Vinnie climbed onto the other horse.
"Good horse," he said softly. The horse didn’t move. Vinnie tried making the clicking noise like Frank. But his horse just lowered its head and ate some grass.
Vinnie watched Frank circle the cattle, going in and out of the herd. He shouted and snapped a whip in the air.
"Please, do something," Vinnie said to his horse.
"First time on a horse?" asked Frank, riding over.
"Yes, sir," said Vinnie.
"Our horses know their job," said Frank. "But you need to show them who’s boss."
Frank showed Vinnie how to hold the reins and lightly kick with his heels.
"Now, give it a try," ordered Frank.
"Come on, horse!" Vinnie shouted in a strong voice. The horse moved slowly forward. Vinnie held on as tight as he could.
"Come and get it!" called Cookie.
Frank and the other cowboys came up to Cookie’s wagon. The children served the hungry men and everyone sat around a big fire to eat.
"Frank says you can stay," Cookie said to Vinnie and Mandy. "But you’d better keep out of trouble."
"We promise!" exclaimed the children.
Mandy listened to the cowboys tell stories, and said, "I wish I had a cowboy hat and boots."
"I wish I had a gun!" Vinnie cried.
"Hey, kids," a cowboy called out. He held up a harmonica. "Sing something."
"I can’t sing," said Vinnie shyly.
"He’s right! He can’t sing!" giggled Mandy.
"Come on," the cowboy said. "Singing calms the cattle, so they can sleep."
"Like a lullaby?" asked Vinnie.
"Yep. We all sing, so don’t be shy," said the cowboy, and he began to play."Oh, give me a home where the buffalo roam," sang Vinnie as the cattle mooed happily.
Meanwhile, Mandy was helping Cookie clean up. "What is the Chisholm Trail?" she asked.
"Well, we take the cattle from Texas along the trail to Kansas. The cattle end up at the market where they are sold," explained Cookie.
"How long does it take?" asked Mandy.
"Depends on the weather and the Indians," said Cookie. "It can take from two to three months."
Later some cowboys unrolled their beds and went to sleep. Others just leaned back, covered their eyes with their hats, and slept on the ground. Cookie gave Mandy and Vinnie bedrolls. Vinnie yawned.
A few men were walking around, staring at the herd.
"Why aren’t those men sleeping?" Vinnie asked Frank.
"They’re guarding the cattle," Frank replied.
"From what?" asked Mandy.
"Wild animals, cattle thieves, and Indians," said Frank.
The children heard howling in the distance. Mandy moved closer to her brother.
The next morning, the children woke to a sunny day. Everyone was already up and ready to go. The wagon was loaded, and the cattle were starting to move again.
"Good morning, kids," Cookie called. "You missed breakfast, but I saved you some biscuits. We have to get going."
"Where?" asked Vinnie, munching on his biscuit.
"It’s time to get back on the trail," said Frank as he brought over Vinnie’s horse from the previous day. The horse sniffed Vinnie’s biscuit. "You come with me."
"And Mandy can ride with me," said Cookie. He picked her up and helped her climb onto the wagon seat.
The horses followed the cattle at an easy pace. They rode over dry, flat prairies of tall grass. The sun was hot, and the sky was bright blue. There was a soft wind.
Vinnie wiped his face with his sleeve and thought: "This is the life of a cowboy!"

Hours passed as Vinnie and Mandy rode along the trail with the cowboys and cattle. But then, another group of cowboys approached. As they passed each other, the cowboys nodded silently to one another. Some said a simple "Howdy," but none of them waved.
"Those cowboys are dressed differently," remarked Mandy to Cookie.
"They are Spanish cowboys from California. They know horses better than anyone in the West," explained Cookie. "On this trail, we meet cowboys from all over."
"Why don’t you wave at each other?" Vinnie asked Frank. They were riding next to Cookie’s wagon.
"That’s a cowboy rule," said Frank. "You see, if we raise our hand, the horses might get scared. So we nod instead."
"What other cowboy rules are there?" asked Vinnie.
Frank thought for a moment. "We don’t ride another man’s horse. And we never wear another cowboy’s hat."
The cowboys continued along the trail. Vinnie was beginning to get bored when his horse began to whinny. Other horses shook their heads and snorted nervously.
"What’s the matter?" asked Vinnie.
"Something or someone is coming," said Frank.
He put a hand on his gun and looked around. Suddenly, six men on horses appeared. Vinnie could tell immediately that they were not cowboys.
"It’s a Cherokee hunting party," explained Frank.
The cowboys lined up their horses in front of the cattle. They pulled out their guns.
The Cherokee slowed down and stopped. Their leader called out, "We come in peace."
"What can we do for you?" asked Frank, motioning his men to put down their guns.
Mandy noticed that the Cherokee dressed differently from the Iroquois. Vinnie and Mandy had met the Iroquois on an earlier trip.
"We wish to speak with you," said the Cherokee man, getting off his horse.
Frank and another cowboy went to speak with him.
Vinnie noticed a young boy in the hunting party. Vinnie got off his horse and smiled at the boy. "Hello," Vinnie said.
"Hello," the boy answered without smiling.
Vinnie introduced himself. The Cherokee boy, still on his horse, moved closer to Vinnie.
"Tell your father to give us some of his cattle," he said in a threatening voice.
"Who? Frank? He’s not my father," Vinnie said. "And why should he give you anything?"
Still on his horse, the boy circled Vinnie slowly. Vinnie felt frightened.
"Your people have taken everything from us," he said angrily. "Those animals belong to the people of this land. That’s us!"
Vinnie thought about Magua, his Mohawk friend. His people were angry with whites too. Vinnie did not know what to say.
"And besides," continued the Cherokee boy. "If you don’t give us cattle, we will attack. We will kill all of you."
A man from the hunting party turned to Vinnie and the young boy. "Sequoia, we are leaving," he said.
"Will they give us cattle?" asked Sequoia.
The man nodded and turned his horse around. The boy followed.
"What are you doing, Frank?" Vinnie asked.
The cowboys were taking some of the cows from the herd.
"We’re giving cattle to the Cherokee," replied Frank. "They are very hungry. These cattle will keep them alive. Plus, we must have peace between us."
Vinnie watched the Cherokee ride off with the cattle.
"What if you didn’t give them anything?" Vinnie asked.
Frank got back on his horse and said, "They probably would have attacked."
Vinnie shivered.
Cookie got back onto the wagon beside Mandy.
"Is everything okay?" she asked.
"There’s nothing to worry about," said Cookie.
The cowboys continued along the Chisholm Trail. They rode for hours, and Mandy was getting tired.
"We’re at the end of the trail now," Cookie said to Mandy. He pointed ahead. Mandy could see some buildings and men on horses.
"What is that place called?" she asked.
"That’s Dodge City," Cookie answered.
Frank rode up to the wagon. "Why don’t you take the kids to the hotel, Cookie? We’ll get the cattle to the market."
Cookie urged the wagon’s horses forward, and Vinnie followed close behind.
"See you at the hotel!" called Frank as he led the cowboys in another direction. Cookie and the kids went to the center of town.

Dodge City was muddy and noisy, and cowboys were everywhere. Their faces were different colors. They were dressed in different ways. But they were alike in one way—they all were dusty and dirty.The men laughed loudly and seemed to be having a good time.
Cookie stopped his horses in front of a large wooden building. The entrance had swinging wooden doors. The children could hear a piano and lots of shouting.
"What’s this place?" asked Vinnie, patting his horse’s neck.
Suddenly, a man stumbled backward through the swinging doors. He landed in the muddy street. Another man came out shaking his fist.
"This is the saloon," said Cookie. "Not a place for children."
Cookie took them across the street to the hotel. Inside, families were eating at tables and people were playing cards.
"Nellie?" Cookie called to a pretty young woman wearing an apron.
"Howdy," she said in a friendly voice. "Glad to see you’re back from the trail safely."
"Thanks, Nellie," said Cookie. He introduced the children. "Keep an eye on them for me. I’m going to the saloon for a little drink."
"Hey, kids, we’re about to have a square dance in the back room," said Nellie. "Do you want to dance?"
Vinnie and Mandy had never seen a square dance before. Four musicians stood in a corner of the room. Each one held a different instrument: a violin, a banjo, a bass fiddle, and a guitar.
"Everybody, grab your partners!" shouted the man with the violin, and the band began to play.
"Let's try it," said Vinnie, taking Mandy's hand.
The dancers smiled and laughed as they whirled around the floor.
"This is hard!" gasped Mandy, trying to do the dance steps.
"Just don't step on my feet!" shouted Vinnie.
Suddenly an old man ran onto the dance floor, shouting. "There's going to be a shootout!"
The music stopped, and Nellie ran to the children.
"What's a shootout?" Mandy asked.
"It's when two men fight with guns," explained Nellie.
"Young Foster and Wild Bill Hickok are outside!" yelled the old man.
Hearing this, people ran into the street. Everyone wanted to watch the shootout.
"Who's Wild Bill?" Vinnie asked Nellie.
"He's the famous sheriff from Abilene," she replied. "And the best shot in the West. He comes to Dodge City to play cards. He's good at that too."
"Come on, Mandy," said Vinnie, grabbing her hand.
"Vinnie, I don't like guns!" cried Mandy, but he pulled her along.
People had gathered along the street. They watched the two men in the middle of the road. Standing about fifty meters apart, the men faced each other.
"You're a cheat, Foster," said one of the men. He had long hair and wore two guns.
"You can't prove it, Wild Bill," shouted the other. He wiggled his fingers and seemed ready to draw his guns.
"Now gentlemen, you know the rules." Another man walked over and stood between the gunfighters.
"Hey, Mandy, there's Cookie and Frank!" Vinnie pointed. The cowboys were watching the shootout too.
"Vinnie! Doesn't this remind you of the photo?" asked Mandy.
She pulled the photo out of her pocket, and it was glowing blue. She saw that the two men in the street were the same as in the photo.

"Calm down, Wild Bill," said a woman in a red dress. She came out of the saloon holding some coins in her hand. "Foster is just a kid—" Suddenly, she tripped and the coins flew high into the air. Wild Bill drew his guns as fast as lightning and shot the five coins one after the other. The coins never hit the ground. The crowd cheered.
"Vinnie! This is it!" Mandy said excitedly as the photo glowed red.
The children shut their eyes and fell down the dark tunnel. They landed back in the attic.
"We didn't get to see the shootout," said Vinnie, disappointed.
Dad was spending more time in the attic. Vinnie and Mandy were getting anxious. The attic was looking more like a tidy office. The children were running out of places to hide the album.
"We have to do something," Mandy said as she sat in the kitchen.
Dad was in the attic, setting up his computer. Suddenly they heard a familiar bark.
"Corky!" yelled Vinnie. He ran to the front door and opened it. The next door neighbor stood there with his dog.
"Hey, Vinnie," said the neighbor, smiling. "Is your dad home? He promised to drive me to the auto repair shop to pick up my car."
"Dad! Corky’s here!" yelled Mandy excitedly. The children knew how much Dad loved dogs.
"Hey, Corky!" Dad said, coming down the stairs. He petted Corky, and the dog wagged its tail happily. "Tell your mom I’ll be right back," he said to the children, grabbing his car keys.
"Take your time!" Vinnie and Mandy exclaimed.
As soon as Dad was gone, they ran up to the attic. Last time, the children had hid the album behind a large plant.
"Whew! It’s still here," Vinnie said with relief. He opened the album. "Mandy, look!" They were almost at the end of the album.
"What happens when we get to the last page?" Mandy asked sadly.
"Let’s think about that later," Vinnie said quickly. He turned the page.
"Wow! What is that?" Mandy cried.
The photo showed a large temple. People were walking up its steep steps. They held glowing objects. The old man stood watching them nearby.
"It looks like some kind of a parade," Vinnie said. "I wonder where this is."
Before the children could say another word, they fell down the dark tunnel.
Mandy landed first in some soft dirt. She took a deep breath. "Stinky!" she cried, holding her nose.
"Hey! Ow!" Vinnie cried. He had hit something hard after his fall down the tunnel.
The children opened their eyes. Two pairs of big brown eyes looked down at them.
"Uh, hello?" Mandy said softly to two large oxen.
Vinnie had bounced off an ox!
"This must be some kind of farm," said Vinnie, still rubbing his back.
The children stood up. They were next to a barn with no walls. Its straw roof was held up by wooden poles.
Suddenly the ox Vinnie had hit let out an angry snort. The animal shook its head and began to dig at the ground with one hoof. The children froze.
Vinnie gulped. "I think he’s getting ready to attack."
The angry ox lowered its head and snorted.
"Let’s run!" shouted Mandy.
"Where?" Vinnie cried.
"What’s going on?" a voice said suddenly.
A young boy about Mandy’s age appeared. He spoke softly to the angry ox and patted its neck.
"Well, we . . . ," stuttered Vinnie.
"Did you come to see Budi? The fastest ox in the village?" the boy asked proudly. He tied a ribbon around the calm ox’s head.
"What’s your name?" asked Mandy.
"I’m Wayan, and these are my oxen, Budi and Gede," he replied. "Who are you?"
The children introduced themselves. Wayan had black hair and eyes. He wore a long, layered skirt but no shirt.
"Are you here for the races?" Wayan asked, tying a ribbon on the other ox. "Races?" asked Vinnie.
Just then a girl walked up. She stopped when she saw Vinnie and Mandy.
"Wayan!" she exclaimed. "Here are some flowers."
Mandy introduced herself and Vinnie to the girl.
"I am Wayan’s younger sister, Nyoman," she said.
"Why are you decorating the oxen?" asked Vinnie. The two animals were now decorated with ribbons and flowers.
"So people know who owns them," explained Nyoman. "And it makes them look handsome."
"What kind of race is it?" asked Mandy.

"It’s a race of the fastest oxen," Nyoman said. "It is a tradition. Long ago, farmers needed to plant the rice seed quickly. They needed to plant several crops a year. So they made their oxen plow faster and faster. Soon it became a contest."
Nyoman and Wayan’s parents walked up.
"Are these your friends?" their father asked, smiling kindly.
"Yes. Can they come to the race with us?" asked Wayan.
"Of course, but we must hurry," replied his father.
Wayan and his father led the oxen down the road. Vinnie and Mandy followed with Nyoman and her mother.
"Wow! What is that?" Mandy pointed to a hill that looked like a tall, grassy staircase.
"Those are rice fields," explained Nyoman.
"They look like giant steps!" Vinnie said.
"The farmers specially shape the land like that," said Nyoman.
"Why?" asked Vinnie.
"It helps them send water evenly to all the fields. Water is very important to rice fields. The rice farmers must work together to keep all these fields alive," explained Nyoman.
The children saw narrow streams of water here and there.
Nyoman shook her head at them. "How can you live in Bali and not know about rice fields or the races?"
"Bali?" cried Mandy. She turned to Vinnie. "We’re in Indonesia!"
Vinnie, Mandy, and Wayan’s family passed farmers in the fields that surrounded the village.
When they arrived in the center of the village, Vinnie and Mandy stopped to watch two men with swords.
"Are they fighting?" Vinnie asked.
"Long ago, warriors used to fight with those weapons. But now they use them for this dance," explained Nyoman.
They all watched the men’s careful movements. Their dance was smooth and graceful.
Finally they reached a large field. There were many wooden carts on the field.
"We’re here!" Wayan exclaimed.
"Help me tie the bar," his father instructed.
Wayan and Vinnie placed a long bar on the oxen’s necks. The bar connected two long sticks to a small cart.
"Let’s take them to the starting line," said Wayan’s father.
They joined a group of other men with their oxen. Wayan’s father climbed onto the cart and stood up. He grabbed the rope reins to steer the team.
"Ready!" shouted an elderly man with a red flag. He swung the flag down. All the oxen took off, pulling the carts.
"Go, Budi! Go, Gede!" shouted Wayan.
The crowd cheered as the oxen ran down the field. The race was only 100 meters long, but it was very exciting.
"We won!" Wayan was jumping up and down with joy.
"Congratulations!" Vinnie yelled.
The other men congratulated Wayan’s father. Wayan and Vinnie went to pet Budi and Gede.
"Help me take this bar off, Vinnie," Wayan asked. "Let’s take the oxen for a walk."
The boys walked through the crowd. Some villagers stopped to congratulate Wayan.
Meanwhile, Mandy and Nyoman walked among the crowd in the village.
"What happens now?" asked Mandy.
"Some people will go home and prepare for the Iron Fence festival," explained Nyoman. "It is being celebrated now. But my parents will attend a village meeting first."
"What is the meeting about?" asked Mandy.
"Today it will be about water for the rice fields," said Nyoman. "But they discuss lots of things at village meetings."
Mandy suddenly realized Vinnie wasn’t around. "Where are the boys?" she asked.
"Wayan is probably showing off his oxen to his friends," laughed Nyoman.
Soon the girls reached a large, open building.
"What’s this place?" asked Mandy.
"This is the village community hall," replied Nyoman. "You don’t know much about Bali, do you?"
"No," said Mandy. "This is my first time here. So I really want to learn about your people."
Nyoman smiled at her and said, "We are very friendly people, Mandy."

114.title: In the Village and on the Mountain

paragraphs.text: Vinnie and Wayan left the racing field. They tied the oxen to a tree and walked up the mountain.
"Where are we going?" Vinnie asked as they went higher.
"To my favorite spot," said Wayan.
The boys stopped to rest.
"Wow!" Vinnie gasped. "I can see everything from up here!" He was looking down at the village and ocean.
Wayan laughed. "From here, everything—the mountains, the sea, the village—looks connected. In Bali, everything we build and do is based on this idea of connection," he said.
"I don’t understand," said Vinnie.
"To be happy, people should live in harmony with nature, the gods, and each other. My father says that harmony with those three things is necessary for a good life," continued Wayan.
Back at the village, the adults were ready to hold their meeting.
"Mandy, come home with me," said Nyoman. "We can get ready for the festival."
"Sure," replied Mandy, walking with her new friend.
The homes reminded Mandy of the courtyard houses she had seen in China.

Nyoman pointed out that every family had separate areas for different activities. "We sleep and eat in different places. There’s also a building for ceremonies and a guest house. The wall is to keep out evil forces." Then Nyoman asked, "Are you hungry?"
"Yes," said Mandy.
Suddenly Nyoman climbed up a tall tree. "Watch your head!" she called, and she dropped a coconut. It broke in half. Nyoman climbed down, and the girls shared the delicious fruit.
"I love climbing trees," giggled Nyoman.
"Can I try?" asked Mandy.
Nyoman led her to a smaller tree with green bananas and said, "Climb this one."

Mandy was about to climb when she heard loud screeching. A few monkeys scrambled down a tree and started chasing the girls. Laughing, Nyoman and Mandy ran until they reached the rice field behind Nyoman’s house. There Mandy noticed a miniature house on a pole. Grains of rice were sprinkled inside.
"What is this?" she asked.
"A rice field temple," explained Nyoman. "Rice farmers give rice grains to the Rice Mother. She is the most loved goddess in Bali."
"Wow," said Mandy. "There are a lot of temples in Bali!"
"Every family has one. Every village has one too," said Nyoman. "There are mountain temples and river temples . . . Bali is called the island of a thousand temples."
Back on the mountain, Vinnie and Wayan were ready to return to the village. Suddenly Vinnie felt the ground shake.
"Whoa! What’s that?" he shouted. A low sound rumbled like thunder.
"The mountain is not happy," said Wayan worriedly.
"What do you mean?" asked Vinnie.
"The god who lives in the mountain is upset," said Wayan.
The ground shook harder.
"Let’s get out of here!" shouted Vinnie.
The girls headed toward a large, open structure. It was one of seven buildings that made up Nyoman’s family’s home.
"Now we can prepare the offerings," said Nyoman.
"What offerings?" asked Mandy.
"To give to the temple," she explained. Nyoman held up some coconut leaves and different kinds of flowers. "I will show you how to make it."
Meanwhile the boys were running down the mountain.
"I think the rumbling stopped," gasped Vinnie, out of breath.
When they finally reached the village, the mountain was quiet again. In fact, no one in the village seemed to know that the ground had shook. They were all getting ready for the Iron Fence festival.
"That mountain is a volcano," said Wayan. "According to our ancestors, it has erupted several times. Who knows when it will happen again?"
"Well, I’m glad it didn’t erupt today!" cried Vinnie.
Meanwhile Nyoman and Mandy finished making three offerings. Then Nyoman wove some flowers through a bamboo comb. She put it on her head.
"That looks so pretty," remarked Mandy.
"I will make you one too, Mandy," said Nyoman, "since we will be going to the temple."
"Oh, thank you!" said Mandy.
Nyoman began to weave flowers into a comb for Mandy.
"Why is it called the Iron Fence festival?" Mandy asked as Nyoman put the comb in Mandy’s hair.

"It is a time when we imagine an iron fence around our minds. The fence protects us from evil spirits and bad thoughts. We try to think only good thoughts so we can be better people. We celebrate by making offerings at the temple, like these. There will be music and a special dance too!" she added.
"That’s so interesting!" Mandy said.
"You look wonderful, Mandy!" said Nyoman. "Now let’s go see the dance."
The girls went to meet Nyoman’s parents in the center of the village. The area was already filling up with people who wanted to see the performance. Everyone was smiling and looked happy.
"The dance is about to begin!" cried Nyoman as she led Mandy close to the stage.
"Who are those men?" asked Mandy. A large group of musicians were sitting on the ground. Some of them had drums and gongs. Mandy did not recognize the other instruments.
"That’s the band," explained Nyoman. "They will play music for the dance."
One of the musicians began to beat a drum. Soon the others joined in. Mandy liked the music a lot.
"I wish Vinnie could hear this," she thought to herself.
The band played as two large, masked creatures jumped onto the stage. One looked like a scary lion made of straw. The other had long hair, bulging eyes, and pointy fingernails.
"What is this dance about?" asked Mandy.
"This is a story of good and evil," explained Nyoman. "The lion protects his people and land from an evil spirit." She pointed to the two dancers in strange costumes.
Mandy clapped her hands excitedly. She was scared and amazed at the same time.
On the other side of the crowd, Vinnie was watching the dance too.
"Cool!" he kept saying. "Look at that mask!"
"Watch the lion’s helpers," said Wayan as men in checkered clothes jumped out.
"They have knives!" shouted Vinnie.
"Yes. The evil spirit will soon put a spell on them," said Wayan.
Vinnie noticed Mandy in the crowd with Nyoman and her family. "Hey! There’s my sister!" he shouted and ran over.
"Where have you been?" she asked.
"It’s a long story," said Vinnie. He told her about the rumbling volcano.
The dance ended. People began to leave the village center, walking in happy groups. Wayan came over to Vinnie and Mandy.
"We’ll make our offerings now," said Wayan.
"Where is the temple?" asked Mandy.
"It’s on the slopes of that mountain," said Nyoman. "It is the most important temple in all of Bali. We call it the Mother Temple."
"It’s the only temple anyone can enter," added Wayan.
"What do you mean?" asked Mandy.
"You have to belong to a special group to worship at other temples," explained Nyoman. "At Mother Temple, everyone is welcome."
"I don’t know if it’s a good idea to go there," said Vinnie, remembering the shaking ground.
"We are not afraid of the mountain god," said Wayan. "The Mother Temple protects us from his rumblings."
Vinnie stopped. "I don’t want to go up there again, Mandy," he whispered, grabbing his sister’s arm. "It’s a volcano!"
Mandy suddenly gasped as she stared ahead. On the slope of the mountain was a large temple. The village people were all heading toward it.
"Vinnie, look!" Mandy pulled the photo out. It was glowing blue.
"We’re in the right place," Vinnie said. "But what’s everyone holding?"
"Mandy! Vinnie! Come on," Nyoman called to them. "We must take our offerings to the gods." She quickly walked on ahead.
"What’s in their hands?" Vinnie asked again. As they got closer, they saw people walking up the steps. Everyone held something in their hands.
Mandy looked at the photo and smiled. The offerings in the photo were glowing red. "Flowers," Mandy said, pointing.
Everyone was holding flowers wrapped in coconut leaves.
Suddenly the children were blinded by the bright light. They fell down the dark tunnel and landed with a thump in the attic.
When Mandy woke up, the house was very quiet. Vinnie was already awake and eating breakfast. Mom was in the kitchen reading the newspaper.
Mandy grabbed a banana. "Where's Dad?" she asked.
"He had a business meeting," said Mom. "He went to the city early this morning."
Mandy barely heard what Mom was saying. All she could think about was the attic. If Dad was out, then it was empty!
Mandy looked over at Vinnie.
He was looking back at her, grinning. "Let's go!" he whispered.

A minute later the two kids ran up the stairs. Vinnie pulled the photo album from its hiding spot. They flipped toward the end and noticed there were just two pages left. But neither one said anything about it.

"There he is!" Mandy spotted the old man in the photo. He stood in front of a building with three large, glowing gates. Vinnie and Mandy stared at the photo. Seconds later they tumbled into the dark tunnel.
Mandy and Vinnie landed on their backs. They lay on the floor of a small room.
Mandy sat up and then looked at Vinnie. "Does this floor feel warm?" she asked.
"Yes," said Vinnie. He sat up too.
"I hope there isn't a fire," said Mandy. She leaped to her feet and looked around.
Suddenly the door opened, and a boy entered the room. He jumped back when he saw Mandy and Vinnie.
"Who are you?" the boy demanded. "What are you doing here?"
"Uh, well, I, uh…" stuttered Vinnie.
"Uh . . . I'm Mandy, and this is my brother, Vinnie," said Mandy. "The floor is very warm!" she added. "Is . . . is your house on fire?"
The boy stared at Mandy for a moment, confused. Then he burst out laughing.
"My home is not on fire! Our floors are heated!" He shook his head, still laughing. "Don't you have heated floors in your house?"
Mandy blushed and shook her head. She felt silly for saying something.
"Follow me, and I will show you how it works," the boy continued. "My name is Gildong, by the way."
He led them to the kitchen. "Heat from the stove warms stones under the floor," he explained. "That is how the floor stays hot."
"Wow," said Vinnie.
"That's cool!" Mandy added. "I mean warm," she joked.

"Come," Gildong said. They followed him to the porch. He reached for a bamboo basket and began wrapping it in cloth. "I have an important errand," he explained. "I must bring these bowls to a nobleman's house. His family is having a special ceremony tonight. Would you like to come with me?"
"Yes!" cried Vinnie and Mandy together.
Vinnie and Mandy followed Gildong to the nobleman's house. He led them through a busy street.
Suddenly Mandy noticed something strange. "Why are so many people wearing white?" she asked.
Gildong laughed. "You must be from very far away," he said. "In Korea poor people usually wear white. Only nobles and royalty can wear colors."
"So that's where we are!" thought Mandy. "Korea!"
Soon the children reached a large house. In the courtyard people looked very busy. "They are getting ready for a special ceremony," said Gildong.
Vinnie watched a woman pounding something with a thick stick.
"She's pounding rice," explained Gildong.
The children saw a room with a big table. A girl was placing food there.
"I'm hungry," Mandy said.
"Sorry, but the food is for the ceremony," said Gildong. "Tonight they are remembering the nobleman's grandfather. He died on this day many years ago."
"I don't understand," said Mandy. "Why are they making food for someone who died?"
"The family honors their grandfather by offering wine and food," said Gildong.
Mandy nodded.
Vinnie asked where the food would go after the ceremony.
"The nobleman's family will share it with others," Gildong said. "That's an important part of the ceremony."
"Gildong!" a voice shouted.
The children turned to see an old woman waving at them.
"Finally!" she said to Gildong. "You have come with the bowls! We are thankful your father could make these for us."
Gildong unwrapped the basket and gave the bowls to the woman.
"May I look at one?" asked Mandy.
"Yes." The woman handed one to her.
"It's so smooth," Mandy said.
"One day I will make bowls like that too," said Gildong proudly.
The woman thanked the children for bringing the bowls."You must have a snack before you leave," she said. "Have a seat and wait here. I will be back in a few minutes."
The woman soon returned. She was carrying a tray of snacks for the children.
"Mmm . . . These are so sweet! What are they?" Mandy asked, chewing on an orange fruit.
"They are dried persimmons," Gildong answered. "And these are rice cakes." He popped a soft white rice cake into his mouth.
When they were finished, Gildong stood and bowed to the woman. "Thank you," he said.
Vinnie and Mandy hopped up too and bowed. "Thank you!" they said. "Good-bye!"
The children left the house. Suddenly Gildong stopped. "Hmm," he said. "Do you hear something?"
Mandy's face lit up. "Yes!" she said. "I hear music!"
Mandy, Vinnie, and Gildong stood outside the nobleman's house, listening.
"Where is the music coming from?" wondered Mandy.
She pointed toward a group of houses. "Maybe it's coming from over there."
"No." Gildong shook his head. "It's coming from over there."
Just then a girl raced toward them. She slammed into Gildong, knocking him down.
"Oh!" cried the girl, falling too.
Gildong stood and rubbed his arm. "Aren't you going to say sorry?" he snapped.
"For what?" The girl dusted off her skirt. "You were in my way."
Mandy stepped in between them. "My name is Mandy," she said to the girl. "What's yours?"
"I'm . . . uh . . . well . . ." The girl's cheeks turned pink. "It's a secret," she said finally.
At that Gildong finally smiled. "That's your name—'a secret'?" he said with a grin.
"No!" said the girl. But she was smiling too.
"What's that?" she asked suddenly. She could also hear music now. "I've never heard anything like that before."
Gildong looked at her strangely. "Well, then let's go!" he said, running toward the sound.
The others raced after him.
"Look!" cried Mandy. A group of men were playing instruments and dancing in a large circle.
The girl was amazed. "What is this?" she asked.
"You don't know?" Gildong looked at her, surprised. "It's a peasant band!" he said. "They are celebrating the harvest."
"Everyone is having so much fun," said Mandy.
"Wow!" said Vinnie when one man began twirling wildly. "Look at that!"
Some people danced to the beat while the crowd cheered for the performers.
Mandy listened to a musician play a small horn. "Oh! He's really good!" she said.
The girl watched with a huge smile. But when the band stopped playing, she stepped away from the crowd. There was an odd look on her face.
"What's wrong?" Mandy asked her.
"I think I’m lost . . . ," the girl said. "My home is far from here." Then she looked nervously at Gildong. "Do you know how to get to the palace?"
"The palace!" Gildong burst out. "Why do you need to go to the palace?"
The girl stepped closer to them. "Can you keep a secret?" she whispered.
"Yes," said Vinnie.
"Of course!" answered Mandy.
"The palace is my home," the girl said. "I am a princess."
The children stared at the girl in surprise.
"What?" cried Mandy. "You're a princess?"
"What are you doing here?" asked Gildong.
"I wanted to see the world outside the palace," the girl explained. "So I put on my servant's clothing and I escaped."
"You left the palace?" Gildong said. He stared at the princess, looking worried. "You had better go back," he said. "When your servants learn that you are missing . . ."
"I know." The princess nodded. "I must get back. But I do not know the way."
"I do," said Gildong. "Please follow me, Your Highness."
The children walked for a while and soon they could see the palace walls.
"Wow!" Vinnie whispered.
The princess stopped and looked at her new friends. "Would you like to come inside?" she asked.
"Yes!" cried Vinnie.
"But we are not royalty, Your Highness," Gildong reminded her. "This is not allowed."
"You are my friends," said the princess firmly. "So you are welcome here. But there are guards everywhere," she added. "We must be careful that you are not seen."
They followed the princess. "You can enter there," she said, pointing to the gate. "I will distract the guards."
The princess went over to the guards and began talking to them. When the guards turned around, Mandy slipped through the gate. Vinnie was next, followed by Gildong.
A moment later the princess joined them. "Welcome to the palace!" she said happily. "I will show you around."
They walked past a long wall.
Gildong stopped to look at a grand building with two roofs. "That building must be very important," he said.
"Yes," the princess said. "That's the throne hall. My father met with noblemen there."
"Is your father the king of Korea?" asked Mandy.
"No, not anymore . . ." The princess looked away as they walked on. "He died not long ago, and now there is a new king."
"How sad . . . ," murmured Mandy.

"Yes," the princess said with a sigh. "But my father, King Sejong, did many wonderful things for our people. During his time there were lots of new inventions." She stopped beside something on the ground. "For example, this is a rain gauge. It was invented by scientists. They worked for my father."
"What does it do?" asked Mandy.
"It measures how much rain falls. People can tell if the harvest will be good or bad."
They continued walking. Then Vinnie spotted something shaped like a bowl. "What is that?"
"A sundial. The famous scientist Jang Youngsil invented that type of sundial. It works like a clock," the princess said.
Mandy studied the sundial. "What time is it now?" she asked the princess.
"It is . . ." The princess bent closer. "Oh no!" She gasped. "It is time to go back to my room!"
"Hurry!" the princess cried to the children. "I have been gone too long! By now the servants will be looking for me!"
When they reached a courtyard, several servants rushed toward the princess.
"Where have you been, Your Highness?" cried one woman.
"Your Highness!" Another servant gasped. "Who are these strangers? Did they kidnap you?"
"No, they did not kidnap me!" the princess replied. "They helped me," she added. "And now they are my honored guests."
The servants did not look happy to hear this. But they bowed quietly and then stepped aside.
The children followed the princess into a small building. She invited them to sit around a low table. Then she left for a moment to change her clothing.
Mandy noticed a sheet of paper with unusual writing. "Are these Chinese characters?" she asked when the princess returned.
"No," said the princess. "That is Hangeul, the alphabet that my father invented."
"Your father invented an alphabet?" said Mandy.

"Yes," said the princess. "Our people have always spoken in Korean. But they used Chinese characters to read and write. Chinese characters were very difficult to learn. And only nobles could go to school to learn them."
"That's not fair!" Mandy said.

"I agree," said the princess. "My father didn't think it was fair either. That is why he worked with scholars to invent a simple alphabet. Hangeul is very easy to learn. And now the Korean people have their own alphabet."
"It sounds like your father was a great king," said Mandy.

"He was. And he loved his people very much," replied the princess. "But Hangeul has not spread to everyone yet. Some people are upset by Hangeul. They say that learning is only for nobles and royalty."
The princess pulled out a clean sheet of paper. "Now I will show you just how beautiful Hangeul is!"
The princess poured water into the inkstone. Then she made ink, dipped a brush into it, and wrote two Hangeul letters.
"Here you are." She gave the paper to Vinnie. "This says Vi-nnie. For your name!"
"Thank you!" said Vinnie.
Next the princess wrote Mandy's and Gildong's names in Hangeul too.
Gildong was very pleased by the gift. "Thank you, Princess. I will remember this. I hope I get to learn Hangeul soon."
"I think you will, Gildong," she said with a smile.
Just then there was a sound at the door. A servant spoke in a worried voice.
"Your Highness! The guards are coming! And they are looking for your friends!"
"The guards are coming!" the servant repeated.
"Uh-oh," said Vinnie.
"Someone must have seen us sneak into the palace," cried Mandy.
Gildong's face was pale. "We will go to jail if they find us here," he said.
The princess stood. "Don't worry! I have a plan," she said. "I will hide you in my palanquin. Then my servants will carry you out of the palace."
"Prepare my palanquin at the backdoor!" the princess ordered a servant.
"Yes, Your Highness," the servant replied and then hurried off. Soon the children were following the princess.
Mandy stopped when she heard something. "Is that a guitar?" she asked.
Gildong stopped too. "I think it's a string instrument, a geomungo, " he said. "Only rich people play it."
"Come on!" The princess waved for them to catch up. Then she led them to a small courtyard. Four servants stood waiting there beside a beautiful palanquin.
"They will carry you outside the palace," said the princess. "So I must say good-bye now."
"Good-bye," said Mandy. "And thank you!"
Vinnie and Gildong said thanks too. Then the three of them ducked into the palanquin.
A moment later Mandy felt the palanquin start to move. "We're off!" she thought.
Then Vinnie nudged her and showed her the photo. "Mandy, the photo is glowing blue!" he whispered.
"But where are the three gates?" she whispered back.
Soon the palanquin stopped. When they climbed out, they saw they were outside the palace gates.
The four men bowed and went back to the palace.
"I must go home to do my chores," Gildong said. "Good-bye!"
"Thank you for everything!" said Vinnie, waving to their new friend.
"Good-bye!" Mandy added.
She turned and grabbed Vinnie's arm. "Come on! Let's see if these are the right gates."
But Vinnie already knew that they were. He looked at the photo. It was glowing red.
"We're going home!" he whispered.
The children fell into the tunnel. When they opened their eyes again, they were back in the attic.
Mandy put the photo back inside the album. "That palanquin ride reminded me of our Japan trip," she said.
"Yes," Vinnie said, nodding.
"There's only one more page in the album," she said slowly.
"I know," he answered.
"That means there's just one more photo trip left," Mandy added.
Vinnie didn't say anything. He just nodded. Then he turned away to hide the sad look on his face.
The family was in the kitchen, planning to shop for school supplies. Vinnie and Mandy were about to start at a new school. But they weren’t very excited.
"Come on, you’ll make new friends!" said Dad.
"Yeah, I know," Vinnie sighed.
"But they won’t be the same friends," said Mandy unhappily.
The children were sad because their photo trips were almost over. Only one page was left in the album. Just then the phone rang. It was Dad’s boss.
"Sorry, but I need some privacy," said Dad.
"No problem, Dad," said Vinnie.
"We’ll talk later about school, kids," said Mom.
Vinnie and Mandy ran up to the attic.
"Can you believe it? Our last photo trip," said Mandy. She hugged the album.
"Well, let’s do it!" cried Vinnie.
Mandy opened the album to the last page. The old man stood in a beautiful cathedral with tall columns. The old man held a glowing object in his hands.
"A book?" asked Mandy, looking at the glowing object. "What do you think, Vinnie?"
"No use guessing," he said. "We’ll find out soon!"
The children’s eyes closed, and they fell down the dark tunnel.
Vinnie and Mandy landed on a stone floor and opened their eyes. Mandy was wearing a long dress with long sleeves. Vinnie wore stockings and a short tunic.
"We’re in some kind of storage room," said Vinnie.
Stacks of paper, brushes, and rags were piled around them. Hammers and other tools were scattered about. Large, flat panels of wood leaned against the wall.
"It must be a painter’s storage room," said Mandy, picking up a paint brush.
The door opened, and a boy a little older than Vinnie walked in. He was thin with curly hair. He stared at Vinnie and Mandy.
"Oh, hello," Mandy said nervously.
"What are you guys doing here?" the boy asked.
"We were just . . . ," stammered Vinnie.
"You are not from here," the boy said.
"How did you know?" asked Mandy.
"No one would come into Master Verrocchio’s workshop uninvited," the boy said.
The children looked embarrassed. "We don’t know our way around," Vinnie said.
The boy smiled warmly. "I can show you the city," he said. "But I must see the master first." The boy picked up a stack of rags and some brushes.
"Have you worked for your master long?" asked Vinnie, thinking the boy was a servant.
"He is not my master. He is the master of this workshop. I am his student," said the boy.
"Student?" asked Vinnie.
The boy looked at him and replied, "I am studying to become the greatest artist in the world."
Vinnie and Mandy followed the boy out of the storage room and through another door.
"Whoa!" Vinnie exclaimed.

They were in a large, spacious room with a high ceiling. In one corner, sunlight poured into the room through big windows. Young artists sat looking at a woman posing in a red robe. They made sketches of her in their notebooks.
In another part of the room, some boys were painting shields. Others were painting chests. The workshop was busy with activity.
"Hey, Leo, who are your friends?" asked a boy with dark hair. He came up to them. He had some blue paint on his cheek.
Vinnie and Mandy introduced themselves.

"My name is Sandro," said the boy. Then he turned to his friend. "You know the rules, Leo," said Sandro. "Work to create and create to work. That means no visitors. If Master Verrocchio finds out, you’re in trouble."
"They are new to Florence," replied Leo. "I promised to show them around. I’m sure the master won’t mind."
"Florence?" Mandy shouted, clapping her hands loudly. She had always wanted to visit Italy. Several people stopped and looked at her.
"Mandy, people are staring at you," Vinnie whispered.
Suddenly everyone turned to look at the door. A tall, older man came in. He was dressed in a black robe that covered a blue tunic. He wore a black hat.
"Why am I hearing talking and not creating?" he asked loudly.
