"Master Verrocchio? Our new student here has brought some friends to visit," said Sandro.
"Is that so?" Master Verrochhio said. He walked over to them. "I was just outside the workshop. I didn’t see anyone come in. How did you get inside?" He glared at the children.
Before they could answer, Leo said, "Sir, I take full responsibility for them. They were lost. I thought I could help them."
Master Verrocchio’s face softened as he looked at Leo. "Did you finish the drafts I wanted?" he asked.
Leo handed him a stack of paper.
Master Verrocchio studied the drawings. To Vinnie, they looked like computer drawings. The lines were so straight and precise. Master Verrocchio nodded with approval.

"You have a gift," he said. "Your talent is already being noticed." Master Verrocchio handed Leo a soft leather folder. "Inside are plans for work at the Medici Palace. The lord’s son has requested you to bring them to him."
"But, sir," Sandro protested. "I was supposed to deliver them."
"Young Lorenzo wants Leo," Master Verrocchio said. Nodding to Leo, he said, "Return here after delivering the plans."
"Yes, sir," Leo replied respectfully, taking his notebook and pencil.
Leo bowed and left the workshop with Vinnie and Mandy.
Vinnie and Mandy followed Leo out of the workshop and into the streets of Florence.
"Wow!" gasped Mandy.
Women dressed in long gowns passed by. Silver and gold nets held their hair away from their faces. Men wearing leather shoes and hats bowed as the women passed.
"What a beautiful building!" Mandy pointed across the street.
"That was designed by one of Florence’s most famous architects," began Leo. Then he described everything about the building.
"You sure do know a lot about architecture," said Vinnie.
"I like to learn about everything," Leo replied.
"By the way, thank you for helping us in there," said Mandy. "Your teacher looked a little angry."
Leo shrugged. "No need to thank me. You guys were just lucky I found you first."
They walked down the street in silence. Mandy noticed two men arguing with a young woman. She asked Leo what was going on.
"Those men are angry about her dress," he said. "Clothing is very important in Florence. Her dress has stripes on the sleeves. Women of her lower class are not allowed to wear stripes by law."
"What?" asked Mandy, shocked.
"There are strict rules about what people can and cannot wear," continued Leo.
"Do you mean poor people cannot wear certain clothing?" asked Mandy, getting upset about the unfairness.
"Naturally," replied Leo. "For example, only the wealthy can wear velvet and use gold thread."
"But—," began Mandy.
Vinnie interrupted. "Hey Mandy, everyone is singing as they work," he said.
Sure enough, in almost every shop, people were singing or humming.
"Yes. It is our custom to sing as much as possible!" said Leo.
As they passed a barber shop, the owner came out. He was a bald man with a big stomach. He smiled when he saw Leo.
"How are you?" he cried. He patted the boy on the back. "Is your back tooth bothering you again? I can pull it for you!"
"I’m fine, Signori Fontana," replied Leo.
"When are you coming for a trim?" asked Mr. Fontana.
Mandy looked inside. A man was sitting in a big wooden chair, waiting to get his hair cut.
"Soon, I promise," said Leo.
"Bring me one of your magnificent drawings when you come, will you?" the man laughed. He waved and went back inside the shop.
"Your barber pulls teeth?" asked Mandy, surprised.
"Of course, Signori Fontana also is the best surgeon in Florence," Leo replied.
They stopped on top of a bridge. "This is the Ponte Vecchio, or the old bridge," explained Leo. "It’s one of six bridges in Florence."
The bridge was supported by three wide arches. Shops selling meat, fruits, and flowers lined the road over the bridge. Below, the river flowed calmly.
"It is one of the most beautiful places in Florence," said Leo.
The children agreed.
Vinnie and Mandy walked down the streets of Florence with Leo. As they walked, Mandy thought there must be something special about the boy. Everyone seemed to like him.
Vinnie said, "Mandy, look up!"
Mandy lifted her head. People were looking down at them from open windows and balconies.
"Why is everyone staring at us?" Vinnie asked.
Leo laughed. "They’re not staring at you. They’re just enjoying the view from their balconies."
"Enjoying the view of the street?" asked Mandy.
"Yes! Watching people is fun! Look!" Leo opened his notebook. The pages were filled with extraordinary pictures of people and animals.
"Leo! You’re amazing!" Mandy gasped.
"No wonder your teacher says you’re gifted!" exclaimed Vinnie.
Leo shrugged and closed his notebook.
"Tell us about the Medici family," asked Mandy.
"They are the most powerful family in Florence," said Leo.
"What do they want you to do?" asked Vinnie.

"All artists need supporters. Powerful families such as the Medici hire artists. Master Verrocchio’s workshop does a lot of work for them," said Leo. "We make furniture and portraits of their family. We even make their kitchen utensils."
Leo stopped in front of a large estate. "Here we are!" he said. Leo led them through a gate and into a courtyard with a lovely garden.
"My lord Lorenzo is expecting you, sir," said a servant by the door. He took them inside the palace and into a large courtyard.
"Whoa!" Vinnie said loudly. "It looks like a museum!" The stone walls were decorated with carvings.
"The family must really love art," remarked Mandy.
"Leo!" called a young man about seventeen years old.
He came toward them and smiled. He wore a shirt with puffy sleeves and a high lace collar.
"Welcome," he said. "Please have a seat."
"These are my friends," Leo said, introducing Vinnie and Mandy.
A servant brought in some cakes.
"I am a great admirer of you, Leo," said Lorenzo. "You and I have a lot in common."
"In what way, my lord?" asked Leo.
"We’re both young," began Lorenzo. "We’re both intelligent. And we both love art."
Leo nodded, but remained quiet.
"One day, I will make Florence the most beautiful city in the world," Lorenzo said confidently. "And I believe you and I can do that together."
"Florence is already magnificent," replied Leo.
"I agree. But I intend to make it more so." Lorenzo laughed. "Then people will say, ‘He is Lorenzo, the one who made Florence magnificent!’"
Mandy choked on her cake. Finally she realized who this man was. "He’s Lorenzo the Magnificent!" she wanted to scream. She was eating cake with the future ruler of Florence, Italy!
The young Lorenzo gave Leo a bag of coins. Mandy and Vinnie ate their cake politely.
"Leo, take this to Master Verrocchio," Lorenzo said. "And come back tomorrow. I hear you are a genius with machines. I want you to do something for me."
As they left the Medici Palace, Mandy was excited. "He’s going to be a great ruler!" she blurted out.
"He’s only seventeen," said Leo, staring curiously at her.
But Mandy had learned about Lorenzo in school. Under his rule, Florence became the most important city of the time.
"If I were you, I would take his offer," she said to Leo.
He laughed and replied, "Are you a fortune teller? Can you tell the future?"
Vinnie squeezed Mandy’s arm. "Hey, don’t say any more," he whispered.
"I want to show you something," Leo said. He took them to a huge dome-shaped building. "Isn’t it beautiful?"
The building was a large cathedral. The marble panels outside were light green and pink. The huge dome was made of red brick. A tall bell tower rose beside it.
"I come here every day to sketch," Leo said, showing them his drawings.
"What are these machines?" asked Vinnie. He expected to see drawings of the cathedral, but the pages were filled with machines. One sketch showed a large wooden wheel. Another sketch was of a crane.
"Machines built this cathedral," Leo replied. "To me machines are more fascinating than the buildings they make."
Again Vinnie and Mandy were amazed at his talent.
"Come inside," said Leo. "There are beautiful paintings and stained glass."
As they followed Leo inside, Mandy whispered, "There’s something special about Leo."
"He’s just a kid with talent," said Vinnie.

"I don’t think so, Vinnie," Mandy said. She stopped and looked around. "Vinnie! I think we’re close to the end of our journey." They could see beautiful stained-glass windows. Tall arches curved above them.
"I think this is the place in the photo," Mandy whispered.
"Come look," Leo called. He sat, opened his notebook, and began to draw with his left hand.
Mandy watched him sketch and said, "You’re so talented!"
"Even for a lefty?" Leo grinned.
"Who cares if you are left-handed?" asked Vinnie.
"Many people think left-handed people are weird," replied Leo. "But it doesn’t bother me."
He got up, leaving his notebook open on the floor.
"I want to see some paintings in the dome," he said and walked off.
Mandy leaned over the open notebook and tried to read the writing.
"I can’t tell what it says," she said. "The writing is so strange!"
Mandy looked closer at Leo’s writing. "Can you read this, Vinnie?" she said.
But Vinnie was looking at the photo. It was glowing blue. They were standing where the old man had stood!

A well-dressed woman suddenly walked past the children. She seemed to be in a rush. As she hurried toward the cathedral door, something fell from her neck. It landed softly on the open page of Leo’s notebook. It was a mirror locket.
Mandy noticed the small mirror on the notebook. "Vinnie, look!" she whispered excitedly. She picked up the book and held the mirror to the page. Now Mandy could read the writing!
"The thoughts and ideas of Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci!" she read.
"Leonardo da Vinci!" the children shouted.
The photo glowed red as they fell down the dark tunnel. They landed with a thump in the attic.
"Wow, the greatest artist of all time! It’s too bad we didn’t get to talk to him more!" cried Mandy.
"I could tell he was special," said Vinnie.
Mandy rolled her eyes.
"Vinnie! Mandy! Come downstairs!" shouted Mom.
The children ran down to their parents, who were still in the kitchen. "We need to talk," said Mom.
The children sat quietly and listened.
"We’re moving again," began Dad. "The company needs me in California."
"California!" the children shouted together.
"We just moved here!" said Vinnie.
"I know," said Dad. "But this can’t be helped."
For the next few days, the children were busy packing.
"Kids, would you mind clearing out the attic for me?" Dad asked one morning.
With heavy hearts Vinnie and Mandy went upstairs.
"I’m sad to leave," cried Mandy.
"Well, at least we got to the end of the album," said Vinnie.
He took the album out again. Each page had a photo of their travels. In the pictures the old man was gone, replaced by Vinnie and Mandy. The objects were not glowing anymore.
"We had some great adventures," said Vinnie.
"And we made many friends," added Mandy. "What was your favorite journey?"
Vinnie thought for a moment. "I liked every one. I learned so much about the world—its different people and their special cultures."
"Me too," agreed Mandy.
"What should we do now?" asked Vinnie.
The children sat and thought.
"Someone else will be living here, right?" said Mandy. "Maybe they’ll find this album. Maybe they’ll go on photo travels too."
"Should we leave a note?" asked Vinnie.
"Great idea!" Mandy said. She grabbed a pen and turned to the first page of the album.
"On our first trip to Egypt, a glowing pyramid called to us . . . ," Mandy wrote. They finished the note and closed the photo album. Then they put it in a corner of the attic.

A week later, the family shut the door of their house. Vinnie and Mandy looked up at the attic window. Exciting adventures were waiting for whoever would find the album next. For Vinnie and Mandy, another adventure was about to begin.
